entries.title: Preferences as consistent answers to a questionnaire

statements.title: Preferences as consistent answers to a questionnaire
statements.statement:
*Preferences* on a set $X$ are a function $f$ that assigns to every pair ${(x,y)}$ of distinct elements of $X$ one of three answers, ${x \succ y}$, ${y \succ x}$ or $I$ (indifference), such that:

- **No order effect:** ${f(x,y) = f(y,x)}$ for all distinct ${x, y \in X}$.
- **Transitivity:** for all pairwise distinct ${x, y, z \in X}$, if ${f(x,y) = x \succ y}$ and ${f(y,z) = y \succ z}$ then ${f(x,z) = x \succ z}$; and if ${f(x,y) = I}$ and ${f(y,z) = I}$ then ${f(x,z) = I}$.

Here ${x \succ y}$ and $I$ are labels for verbal answers, not relations given in advance.

assumptions.text: Every pair of distinct alternatives receives exactly one of the answers ${x \succ y}$, ${y \succ x}$, $I$; nothing is asked about a pair ${(x,x)}$.
No order effect: ${f(x,y) = f(y,x)}$.
Transitivity of strict answers across distinct triples.
Transitivity of indifference answers across distinct triples.

statements.title: Strict preference followed by indifference is strict
statements.statement: Let $f$ be preferences on $X$ in the sense of Definition 1, and let ${x, y, z \in X}$ be pairwise distinct. If ${f(x,y) = x \succ y}$ and ${f(y,z) = I}$, then ${f(x,z) = x \succ z}$.

assumptions.text: $f$ is a preference on $X$ in the sense of Definition 1.
$x$, $y$, $z$ are pairwise distinct.
${f(x,y) = x \succ y}$.

statements.conclusion: ${f(x,z) = x \succ z}$.

statements.title: Indifference followed by strict preference is strict
statements.statement: Let $f$ be preferences on $X$ in the sense of Definition 1, and let ${x, y, z \in X}$ be pairwise distinct. If ${f(x,y) = I}$ and ${f(y,z) = y \succ z}$, then ${f(x,z) = x \succ z}$.

assumptions.text: $f$ is a preference on $X$ in the sense of Definition 1.
$x$, $y$, $z$ are pairwise distinct.
${f(y,z) = y \succ z}$.

statements.conclusion: ${f(x,z) = x \succ z}$.

statements.title: Preference relation: reflexive, complete and transitive

assumptions.text: Reflexivity: ${x \succsim x}$ for every $x$.
Completeness: any two distinct alternatives are comparable.
Transitivity: ${x \succsim y}$ and ${y \succsim z}$ imply ${x \succsim z}$.

entries.title: Equivalence of the two definitions of preferences

statements.title: The two definitions of preferences are equivalent

assumptions.text: $f$, $f_1$, $f_2$ are preferences on $X$ in the sense of Definition 1.
For the onto part, $\succsim$ is any preference relation on $X$ in the sense of Definition 2.

statements.conclusion: $\mathrm{Translation}$ is a well-defined, one-to-one and onto map from Definition-1 preferences to preference relations, and it sends strict answers to strict preference and indifference answers to indifference.

statements.title: Utility function representing a preference relation
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on $X$. A function ${U : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ *represents* $\succsim$ if for all ${x, y \in X}$,

$$x \succsim y \iff U(x) \ge U(y).$$

Such a $U$ is a *utility function* for $\succsim$, and $\succsim$ *has a utility representation* if some $U$ represents it.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
$U$ is a real-valued function on $X$.

entries.title: Utility is ordinal: strictly increasing transformations
entries.name: Utility is ordinal

statements.title: Strictly increasing transformations preserve the representation
statements.statement: Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on $X$, let ${U : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ represent $\succsim$, and let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be strictly increasing. Then ${V = f \circ U}$ also represents $\succsim$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
$U$ represents $\succsim$.
$f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is strictly increasing.

statements.conclusion: $x \succsim y \iff f(U(x)) \ge f(U(y))$ for all ${x, y \in X}$.

entries.title: Best and worst elements of finite sets

statements.title: Every nonempty finite set has a best and a worst element
statements.statement: Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on $X$ and let ${A \subseteq X}$ be finite and nonempty. Then $A$ has a minimal element under $\succsim$, some ${a \in A}$ with ${x \succsim a}$ for all ${x \in A}$, and a maximal element under $\succsim$, some ${b \in A}$ with ${b \succsim x}$ for all ${x \in A}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
$A$ is a finite subset of $X$.
$A$ is nonempty.

statements.conclusion: There are ${a, b \in A}$ with ${x \succsim a}$ and ${b \succsim x}$ for every ${x \in A}$.

statements.title: On a finite set, every preference has a natural-number utility
statements.statement:
Let $X$ be finite and let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on $X$. Then there is ${N : X \to \mathbb{N}}$ such that for all ${x, y \in X}$,

$$x \succsim y \iff N(x) \ge N(y).$$

assumptions.text: $X$ is finite.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.

statements.conclusion: $\succsim$ has a utility representation with values in $\mathbb{N}$.

statements.title: On a countable set, every preference has a utility in (0, 1)
statements.statement: Let $X$ be countable (finite or countably infinite) and let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on $X$. Then there is ${U : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ that represents $\succsim$ and satisfies ${0 < U(x) < 1}$ for every ${x \in X}$.

assumptions.text: $X$ is countable (finite or countably infinite).
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.

statements.conclusion: Some $U$ represents $\succsim$ and takes all its values in the open interval ${(0,1)}$.

statements.title: Lexicographic preference induced by a list of preferences
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim_1, \dots, \succsim_K$ be preference relations on $X$. The *lexicographic preference* $\succsim_L$ they induce is defined by ${x \succsim_L y}$ if either

1. there is $k^*$ such that ${x \sim_k y}$ for all ${k < k^*}$ and ${x \succ_{k^*} y}$, or
2. ${x \sim_k y}$ for all $k$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim_1, \dots, \succsim_K$ is a finite list of preference relations on $X$ (any length $K$).

entries.title: The lexicographic preference on the unit square

statements.title: The lexicographic order on the unit square
statements.statement:
On the unit square ${X = [0,1] \times [0,1]}$, the lexicographic preference induced by the two coordinate orders (${x \succsim_k y}$ iff ${x_k \ge y_k}$, for ${k = 1, 2}$) is

$$\begin{aligned} & (a_1, a_2) \succsim_L (b_1, b_2) \iff \\ & \quad a_1 > b_1, \text{ or} \\ & \quad a_1 = b_1 \text{ and } a_2 \ge b_2. \end{aligned}$$

assumptions.text: The domain is the closed unit square ${[0,1]^2}$.
Each coordinate is ranked by the usual order of the real numbers.

statements.title: The lexicographic order on the square is a preference relation
statements.statement: The lexicographic relation $\succsim_L$ on ${[0,1]^2}$ is a preference relation: it is reflexive, complete and transitive.

assumptions.text: $\succsim_L$ is the lexicographic relation on ${[0,1]^2}$.

statements.conclusion: $\succsim_L$ is reflexive, complete and transitive.

statements.title: A lexicographic preference is a preference relation
statements.statement: Let $\succsim_1, \dots, \succsim_K$ be preference relations on $X$. The lexicographic preference $\succsim_L$ they induce is a preference relation on $X$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim_1, \dots, \succsim_K$ is a finite list of preference relations on $X$.

statements.conclusion: $\succsim_L$ is reflexive, complete and transitive.

entries.title: No utility representation for the lexicographic preference on the unit square
entries.name: The lexicographic counterexample

statements.title: The lexicographic preference on the unit square has no utility representation
statements.statement: Let $\succsim_L$ be the lexicographic preference on ${[0,1]^2}$: $(a_1,a_2) \succsim_L (b_1,b_2)$ if ${a_1 > b_1}$, or ${a_1 = b_1}$ and ${a_2 \ge b_2}$. There is no function ${u : [0,1]^2 \to \mathbb{R}}$ such that $x \succsim_L y \iff u(x) \ge u(y)$ for all ${x, y}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim_L$ is the lexicographic preference on the unit square ${[0,1]^2}$.

statements.conclusion: $\succsim_L$ has no utility representation.

statements.title: Continuous preference relation (open-ball definition)
statements.statement: Let $X$ be a metric space (for example a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$) and $\succsim$ a preference relation on $X$. Then $\succsim$ is *continuous* if whenever ${a \succ b}$ (that is, not ${b \succsim a}$) there are balls $B_a$ around $a$ and $B_b$ around $b$ such that ${x \succ y}$ for all ${x \in B_a}$ and ${y \in B_b}$.

assumptions.text: $X$ carries a metric, so that balls ${B(a, r) = \{z : d(z,a) < r\}}$, ${r > 0}$, are defined.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.

statements.title: Continuous preference relation (closed-graph definition)
statements.statement: Let $X$ be a metric space and $\succsim$ a preference relation on $X$. Then $\succsim$ is *continuous* if its graph $\{(x,y) \in X \times X : x \succsim y\}$ is a closed subset of ${X \times X}$; equivalently, whenever ${a_n \succsim b_n}$ for all $n$, ${a_n \to a}$ and ${b_n \to b}$, also ${a \succsim b}$.

assumptions.text: $X$ is a metric space, which supplies the topology of ${X \times X}$ and convergence of sequences.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.

entries.title: Equivalence of the two definitions of continuity

statements.title: The two definitions of continuity coincide
statements.statement: Let $X$ be a metric space and $\succsim$ a preference relation on $X$. Then $\succsim$ is continuous in the open-ball sense if and only if its graph ${\{(x,y) : x \succsim y\}}$ is closed in ${X \times X}$.

assumptions.text: $X$ is a metric space.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.

statements.conclusion: Open-ball continuity $\iff$ closed-graph continuity.

statements.title: Debreu’s theorem on a convex domain
statements.statement: Let ${X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n}$ be convex and let $\succsim$ be a continuous preference relation on $X$. Then there is a continuous function ${U : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ that represents $\succsim$.

assumptions.text: $X$ is a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
$X$ is convex.
$\succsim$ is continuous.

statements.conclusion: Some continuous ${U : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ represents $\succsim$.

statements.title: Debreu’s theorem on a connected domain
statements.statement: Let ${X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n}$ be connected and let $\succsim$ be a continuous preference relation on $X$. Then there is a continuous function ${U : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ that represents $\succsim$.

assumptions.text: $X$ is a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
$X$ is connected.
$\succsim$ is continuous.

statements.conclusion: Some continuous ${U : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ represents $\succsim$.

statements.title: Choice problems and the domain of a choice context
statements.statement: A *choice problem* is a nonempty subset of a grand set $X$. A *context* ${(X, D)}$ consists of $X$ and a set $D$ of subsets of $X$, each of which is a choice problem; $D$ is the domain on which the agent’s behavior is defined.

assumptions.text: $D$ is a collection of subsets of $X$.
Every member of $D$ is nonempty, i.e. a choice problem.

statements.title: Choice function
statements.statement: Given a context ${(X, D)}$, a *choice function* $C$ assigns to every ${A \in D}$ an element ${C(A) \in A}$.

assumptions.text: ${(X, D)}$ is a context: $D$ is a set of nonempty subsets of $X$.
$C$ assigns exactly one element to every ${A \in D}$.
The chosen element belongs to the problem: ${C(A) \in A}$.

statements.title: The choice function induced by a preference relation
statements.statement: Let ${(X, D)}$ be a context and $\succsim$ a preference relation on $X$, and assume that every ${A \in D}$ has a unique best element under $\succsim$, an ${a \in A}$ with ${a \succsim x}$ for all ${x \in A}$. The *induced* (rational) choice function $C_\succsim$ assigns to each ${A \in D}$ its best element under $\succsim$.

assumptions.text: ${(X, D)}$ is a context.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
Every ${A \in D}$ has exactly one best element under $\succsim$.

statements.title: Rationalizable choice function
statements.statement: A choice function $C$ for a context ${(X, D)}$ *can be rationalized* if there is a preference relation $\succsim$ on $X$ such that every ${A \in D}$ has a unique best element under $\succsim$ and ${C(A) = C_\succsim(A)}$ for every ${A \in D}$.

assumptions.text: $C$ is a choice function for a context ${(X, D)}$.

statements.title: Condition α (contraction consistency)
statements.statement: A choice function $C$ for a context ${(X, D)}$ satisfies *condition* $\alpha$ if for all ${A, B \in D}$ with ${A \subset B}$ and ${C(B) \in A}$, we have ${C(A) = C(B)}$.

assumptions.text: $C$ is a choice function for a context ${(X, D)}$.

statements.title: Rational choice functions satisfy condition α
statements.statement: Let ${(X, D)}$ be a context and $\succsim$ a preference relation on $X$ such that every ${A \in D}$ has a unique best element under $\succsim$. Then the induced choice function $C_\succsim$ satisfies condition $\alpha$.

assumptions.text: ${(X, D)}$ is a context.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
Every ${A \in D}$ has exactly one best element under $\succsim$.

statements.conclusion: $C_\succsim$ satisfies condition $\alpha$.

entries.title: Rationalizability of choice functions satisfying condition α

statements.title: Condition α implies rationalizability on a rich domain
statements.statement: Let $C$ be a choice function for a context ${(X, D)}$ in which $D$ contains every nonempty subset of $X$ with at most three elements. If $C$ satisfies condition $\alpha$, then $C$ can be rationalized: there is a preference relation $\succsim$ on $X$ with ${C = C_\succsim}$ on $D$.

assumptions.text: $C$ is a choice function for a context ${(X, D)}$.
$D$ contains every nonempty subset of $X$ with at most three elements.
$C$ satisfies condition $\alpha$.

statements.conclusion: $C$ is rationalizable.

statements.title: Condition α implies rationalizability on a union-closed domain
statements.statement: Let $C$ be a choice function for a context ${(X, D)}$ in which ${A \cup B \in D}$ whenever ${A, B \in D}$. If $C$ satisfies condition $\alpha$, then $C$ can be rationalized.

assumptions.text: $C$ is a choice function for a context ${(X, D)}$.
$D$ is closed under unions of two problems.
$C$ satisfies condition $\alpha$.

statements.conclusion: $C$ is rationalizable.

statements.title: The satisficing choice procedure

assumptions.text: ${(X, D)}$ is a context.
${v : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ is a valuation of the alternatives.
${v^* \in \mathbb{R}}$ is the threshold of satisfaction.
$O$ is an ordering of $X$ (complete, asymmetric and transitive): the order in which alternatives are examined.
Every ${A \in D}$ has exactly one satisficing choice.

statements.title: Satisficing choice satisfies condition α
statements.statement: Let ${(X, D)}$ be a context, $v$ a valuation, $v^*$ a threshold and $O$ an ordering of $X$ such that every ${A \in D}$ has a unique satisficing choice. Then the satisficing choice function ${C_{v,v^*,O}}$ satisfies condition $\alpha$.

assumptions.text: ${(X, D)}$ is a context.
${v : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ is a valuation and ${v^* \in \mathbb{R}}$ a threshold.
$O$ is an ordering of $X$ (complete, asymmetric and transitive).
Every ${A \in D}$ has exactly one satisficing choice.

statements.conclusion: ${C_{v,v^*,O}}$ satisfies condition $\alpha$.

statements.title: Satisficing choice is rationalizable
statements.statement: Let ${(X, D)}$ be a context, $v$ a valuation, $v^*$ a threshold and $O$ an ordering of $X$ such that every ${A \in D}$ has a unique satisficing choice. Then ${C_{v,v^*,O}}$ can be rationalized: there is a preference relation $\succsim$ on $X$ such that every ${A \in D}$ has a unique best element under $\succsim$ and $C_{v,v^*,O}(A) = C_\succsim(A)$ for all ${A \in D}$.

assumptions.text: ${(X, D)}$ is a context.
${v : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ is a valuation and ${v^* \in \mathbb{R}}$ a threshold.
$O$ is an ordering of $X$ (complete, asymmetric and transitive).
Every ${A \in D}$ has exactly one satisficing choice.

statements.conclusion: ${C_{v,v^*,O}}$ is rationalizable.

statements.title: Choice correspondence
statements.statement: Given a context ${(X, D)}$, a *choice correspondence* $C$ assigns to every ${A \in D}$ a set $C(A)$ with $\emptyset \ne C(A) \subseteq A$.

assumptions.text: ${(X, D)}$ is a context.
${C(A) \subseteq A}$ for every ${A \in D}$.
${C(A) \ne \emptyset}$ for every ${A \in D}$.

statements.title: The choice correspondence induced by a preference relation
statements.statement:
Let ${(X, D)}$ be a context and $\succsim$ a preference relation on $X$ such that every ${A \in D}$ has at least one best element under $\succsim$. The *induced choice correspondence* is

$$C_\succsim(A) = \{x \in A : x \succsim y \ \forall y \in A\}.$$

assumptions.text: ${(X, D)}$ is a context.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
$C_\succsim(A)$ is never empty: every ${A \in D}$ has a best element under $\succsim$.

entries.title: Weak axiom of revealed preference (choice correspondences)

statements.title: The weak axiom of revealed preference (WA)
statements.statement: A choice correspondence $C$ for a context ${(X, D)}$ satisfies the *weak axiom* (WA) if for all ${A, B \in D}$ and all ${x, y \in A \cap B}$: if ${x \in C(A)}$ and ${y \in C(B)}$, then ${x \in C(B)}$.

assumptions.text: $C$ is a choice correspondence for a context ${(X, D)}$.

statements.title: Condition α for choice correspondences
statements.statement: A choice correspondence $C$ for a context ${(X, D)}$ satisfies *condition* $\alpha$ if for all ${A, B \in D}$ with ${A \subset B}$ and every ${a \in A}$: if ${a \in C(B)}$, then ${a \in C(A)}$.

assumptions.text: $C$ is a choice correspondence for a context ${(X, D)}$.

statements.title: Condition β for choice correspondences
statements.statement: A choice correspondence $C$ for a context ${(X, D)}$ satisfies *condition* $\beta$ if for all ${A, B \in D}$ with ${A \subset B}$ and all ${a, b \in A}$: if ${a, b \in C(A)}$ and ${b \in C(B)}$, then ${a \in C(B)}$.

assumptions.text: $C$ is a choice correspondence for a context ${(X, D)}$.

entries.title: Rationalizable choice correspondences (conditions α and β)
entries.name: Rationalizability by α and β

statements.title: Conditions α and β imply rationalizability of a correspondence
statements.statement: Let $C$ be a choice correspondence for a context ${(X, D)}$ in which $D$ contains every nonempty subset of $X$ with at most three elements. If $C$ satisfies conditions $\alpha$ and $\beta$, then there is a preference relation $\succsim$ on $X$ such that $C_\succsim(A)$ is nonempty and ${C(A) = C_\succsim(A)}$ for every ${A \in D}$.

assumptions.text: $C$ is a choice correspondence for a context ${(X, D)}$.
$D$ contains every nonempty subset of $X$ with at most three elements.
$C$ satisfies condition $\alpha$.
$C$ satisfies condition $\beta$.

statements.conclusion: $C$ is rationalizable: ${C = C_\succsim}$ on $D$ for some preference relation $\succsim$.

entries.title: Conditions α and β versus the weak axiom
entries.name: The weak axiom (WARP)

statements.title: On intersection-closed domains, conditions α and β together are equivalent to the weak axiom
statements.statement: Let $C$ be a choice correspondence for a context ${(X, D)}$ in which ${A \cap B \in D}$ whenever ${A, B \in D}$ and ${A \cap B \ne \emptyset}$. Then $C$ satisfies conditions $\alpha$ and $\beta$ if and only if $C$ satisfies WA.

assumptions.text: $C$ is a choice correspondence for a context ${(X, D)}$.
$D$ is closed under nonempty intersections.

statements.conclusion: $C$ satisfies $\alpha$ and $\beta$ $\iff$ $C$ satisfies WA.

statements.title: Choice with a default option
statements.statement: An *extended choice function* on $X$ assigns to every pair ${(A, a)}$ with ${A \subseteq X}$ and ${a \in A}$ an element ${c(A, a) \in A}$. Read ${c(A, a) = b}$ as: facing the set $A$ with default $a$, the decision maker chooses $b$.

assumptions.text: $c$ assigns exactly one element to every pair ${(A, a)}$ with ${a \in A}$.
The choice lies in the available set: ${c(A, a) \in A}$.

statements.title: The default-bias procedure

assumptions.text: ${u : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ describes the decision maker’s underlying preferences.
${\beta : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ is a bias function.
The bias is non-negative: ${\beta(x) \ge 0}$ for every $x$.
Every pair ${(A, a)}$ has exactly one choice under the procedure.

entries.title: Weak axiom for choice with defaults

statements.title: The weak axiom for choice with defaults

assumptions.text: $c$ is an extended choice function on $X$.

statements.title: Default tendency
statements.statement: An extended choice function $c$ satisfies *default tendency* (DT) if for every set $A$ and every default ${x \in A}$: if ${c(A, x) = a}$, then ${c(A, a) = a}$.

assumptions.text: $c$ is an extended choice function on $X$.

statements.title: Weak axiom and default tendency characterize default bias
statements.statement: Let $X$ be finite and let $c$ be an extended choice function on $X$. Then $c$ satisfies WA and default tendency if and only if ${c = DBP_{u,\beta}}$ for some utility ${u : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ and some bias ${\beta : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ with ${\beta \ge 0}$ for which the procedure is well defined.

assumptions.text: $X$ is finite.
$c$ is an extended choice function on $X$.

statements.conclusion: $c$ satisfies WA and DT $\iff$ $c$ is a default-bias procedure. The “if” direction holds on any set $X$, finite or not.

statements.title: Monotone preferences

assumptions.text: The commodity space is ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, bundles of $K$ goods.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.

statements.title: Strongly monotone preferences
statements.statement: A preference relation $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ is *strongly monotone* if for all bundles ${x, y \in X}$: if ${x_k \ge y_k}$ for every $k$ and ${x \ne y}$, then ${x \succ y}$.

assumptions.text: The commodity space is ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, bundles of $K$ goods.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.

statements.title: Nonsatiation at a bundle
statements.statement: A preference relation $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ is *nonsatiated at* the bundle $y$ if for every ${\varepsilon > 0}$ there is ${x \in X}$ with ${d(x, y) < \varepsilon}$ and ${x \succ y}$, where $d(x,y) = \sqrt{\sum_k (x_k - y_k)^2}$ is the Euclidean distance.

assumptions.text: The commodity space is ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, bundles of $K$ goods.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
$y$ is a bundle in $X$.

statements.title: Continuous preferences on the commodity space
statements.statement: A preference relation $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ is *continuous* if for all ${a, b \in X}$ with ${a \succ b}$ there is ${\varepsilon > 0}$ such that ${x \succ y}$ for all ${x, y \in X}$ with ${d(x,a) < \varepsilon}$ and ${d(y,b) < \varepsilon}$, where $d$ is the Euclidean distance.

assumptions.text: The commodity space is ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ with the Euclidean distance.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.

entries.title: Utility representation of monotone continuous preferences

statements.title: Monotone continuous preferences have a continuous utility
statements.statement: Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ that is monotone and continuous. Then there is a continuous function ${u : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ that represents $\succsim$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$\succsim$ is monotone.
$\succsim$ is continuous.

statements.conclusion: Some continuous ${u : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ represents $\succsim$.

statements.title: Convex preferences (first definition)
statements.statement: A preference relation $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ satisfies *convexity 1* if for all bundles ${x, y}$ and all ${\alpha \in (0,1)}$: ${x \succsim y}$ implies $\alpha x + (1-\alpha) y \succsim y$.

assumptions.text: The commodity space is ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, bundles of $K$ goods.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.

statements.title: Convex preferences (second definition)
statements.statement: A preference relation $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ satisfies *convexity 2* if for all bundles ${x, y, z}$ such that ${z = \alpha x + (1-\alpha) y}$ for some ${\alpha \in (0,1)}$: ${z \succsim x}$ or ${z \succsim y}$.

assumptions.text: The commodity space is ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, bundles of $K$ goods.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.

statements.title: Convex preferences (third definition)
statements.statement: A preference relation $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ satisfies *convexity 3* if for every ${y \in X}$ the upper contour set ${\{z \in X : z \succsim y\}}$ is convex: for all bundles ${a, b}$ and all ${\alpha \in (0,1)}$, ${a \succsim y}$ and ${b \succsim y}$ imply $\alpha a + (1-\alpha) b \succsim y$.

assumptions.text: The commodity space is ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, bundles of $K$ goods.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.

entries.title: Equivalence of the three definitions of convexity

statements.title: The three definitions of convex preferences are equivalent
statements.statement: Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$. Then $\succsim$ satisfies convexity 1 if and only if it satisfies convexity 2, if and only if it satisfies convexity 3.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.

statements.conclusion: Convexity 1 $\iff$ convexity 2 $\iff$ convexity 3.

statements.title: Strictly convex preferences
statements.statement: A preference relation $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ is *strictly convex* if for all bundles ${a, b, y}$ with ${a \ne b}$ and all ${\lambda \in (0,1)}$: ${a \succsim y}$ and ${b \succsim y}$ imply $\lambda a + (1-\lambda) b \succ y$.

assumptions.text: The commodity space is ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, bundles of $K$ goods.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.

statements.title: Reminder: concave and quasi-concave functions
statements.statement: A function $u$ is *concave* if $u(\lambda x + (1-\lambda) y) \ge \lambda u(x) + (1-\lambda) u(y)$ for all ${x, y}$ and ${\lambda \in [0,1]}$, and *quasi-concave* if for every $y$ the set ${\{x : u(x) \ge u(y)\}}$ is convex. Every concave function is quasi-concave.

statements.title: Convex preferences are exactly those with quasi-concave utility
statements.statement: Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ and let ${u : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ represent $\succsim$. Then $\succsim$ is convex if and only if $u$ is quasi-concave, that is, for every ${y \in X}$ the set ${\{x \in X : u(x) \ge u(y)\}}$ is convex.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
${u : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ represents $\succsim$.

statements.conclusion: $\succsim$ is convex $\iff$ $u$ is quasi-concave.

entries.title: Convex preferences need not have a concave utility

statements.title: A continuous convex preference with no concave utility
statements.statement: As printed: continuous and convex preferences might not have a utility representation by any concave function; for example, the relation on $\mathbb{R}$ defined by ${x \succsim y}$ if ${x \ge y}$ or ${y < 0}$. Read as a claim about this relation: it is continuous, it is convex, and no concave function represents it.

assumptions.text: The relation is defined on the whole real line $\mathbb{R}$.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation.
${x \succsim y}$ if ${x \ge y}$ or ${y < 0}$.

statements.conclusion: The relation is continuous, convex, and has no concave utility representation. Convexity and the absence of a concave representation hold; continuity does not hold for this relation (see the counterexample).

statements.title: The printed example relation is not continuous
statements.statement: The relation on $\mathbb{R}$ defined by ${x \succsim y}$ if and only if ${x \ge y}$ or ${y < 0}$ is a preference relation, and it is not continuous: ${0 \succ -1}$, yet every ${x < 0}$, however close to $0$, satisfies ${x \sim -1}$. It violates each of the formulations of continuity used in the library: the open-ball forms of Lectures 2 and 4 and the closed-graph form.
statements.conclusion: The relation is a preference relation on $\mathbb{R}$ and is not continuous under any of these formulations.

statements.title: A continuous, convex preference on ℝ with no concave utility
statements.statement:
There exists a preference relation $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}}$ that is continuous and convex but is represented by no concave utility function. One such relation is

$$x \succsim y \iff x \ge y \ \text{or}\ y \le 0.$$

**Change from the printed example:** ${y \le 0}$ replaces ${y < 0}$; nothing else differs.
statements.conclusion: $\succsim$ is a continuous preference relation satisfying convexity 1 (${x \succsim y}$ implies $\alpha x + (1-\alpha) y \succsim y$ for ${\alpha \in (0,1)}$), and no concave $u : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ represents it.

statements.title: Λ-convex preferences and critical orderings
statements.statement:
Let $\Lambda$ be a set of orderings (criteria) on $X$, each criterion $\unrhd$ with strict part $\rhd$. A preference relation $\succsim$ on $X$ is *Λ-convex* if for every ${y \in X}$ there is ${\unrhd \in \Lambda}$ with

$$\{x : x \succ y\} \subseteq \{x : x \rhd y\}.$$

Such a criterion is a *critical ordering* at $y$; it need not be unique.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$ (an arbitrary set).
$\Lambda$ is a given set of criteria on $X$; each criterion enters through its strict part $\rhd$.

statements.title: Λ-strictly convex preferences
statements.statement:
With $\Lambda$ as above, a preference relation $\succsim$ on $X$ is *Λ-strictly convex* if for every ${y \in X}$ there is ${\unrhd \in \Lambda}$ with

$$\{x : x \succsim y,\ x \ne y\} \subseteq \{x : x \rhd y\}.$$

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$ (an arbitrary set).
$\Lambda$ is a given set of criteria on $X$; each criterion enters through its strict part $\rhd$.

entries.title: Λ-convexity on finite sets: the bottom-up construction

statements.title: On a finite set, Λ-convex preferences are built from the bottom up
statements.statement: Let $X$ be finite and $\Lambda$ a set of strict orderings on $X$. A preference relation $\succsim$ on $X$ is Λ-convex if and only if it can be constructed from the bottom up as follows: at each step, choose an alternative that is minimal, according to one of the orderings in $\Lambda$, among the alternatives not yet ranked, and place it weakly or strictly above those already ranked.

assumptions.text: $X$ is finite.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
$\Lambda$ is a set of criteria on $X$.
Every criterion in $\Lambda$ is a strict ordering (complete, asymmetric and transitive).

statements.conclusion: $\succsim$ is Λ-convex $\iff$ $\succsim$ can be constructed from the bottom up.

statements.title: Single-peaked preferences on an interval

assumptions.text: ${X = [0,1]}$ with its usual order.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.

entries.title: Single-peaked preferences as Λ-strictly convex preferences

statements.title: For continuous preferences on an interval, single-peakedness is Λ-strict convexity
statements.statement: Let $\succsim$ be a continuous preference relation on ${X = [0,1]}$ and let $\Lambda = \{\unrhd_L, \unrhd_R\}$, where $\unrhd_R$ ranks points farther to the right higher (${x \rhd_R y}$ iff ${x > y}$) and $\unrhd_L$ ranks points farther to the left higher (${x \rhd_L y}$ iff ${x < y}$). Then $\succsim$ is Λ-strictly convex if and only if it is single-peaked.

assumptions.text: ${X = [0,1]}$ with its usual order and the distance ${|x - y|}$.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
$\succsim$ is continuous.
$\Lambda$ consists of the two criteria “farther left is better” and “farther right is better”.

statements.conclusion: $\succsim$ is Λ-strictly convex $\iff$ $\succsim$ is single-peaked.

statements.title: Algebraic linear orderings
statements.statement: For a vector ${v \in \mathbb{R}^K}$ with ${v \ne 0}$, the *algebraic linear ordering* $\ge_v$ on bundles in ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ is defined by ${x \ge_v y}$ iff ${v \cdot x \ge v \cdot y}$; its strict part is ${x >_v y}$ iff ${v \cdot x > v \cdot y}$. Let $\Psi$ be the set of all algebraic linear orderings.

assumptions.text: The commodity space is ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, bundles of $K$ goods.
$v$ is any nonzero vector in $\mathbb{R}^K$; negative components are allowed.

statements.title: Convexity and Ψ-convexity are equivalent
statements.statement: As printed: let $\succsim$ be a continuous preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$. Then $\succsim$ is convex by the standard definition if and only if it is Ψ-convex, that is, for every $y$ some algebraic linear ordering $\ge_v$ satisfies $\{x : x \succ y\} \subseteq \{x : x >_v y\}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$\succsim$ is continuous.

statements.conclusion: $\succsim$ is convex $\iff$ $\succsim$ is Ψ-convex. As printed, the “if” direction holds; the “only if” direction does not hold in full generality (see the counterexample).

statements.title: Ψ-convexity implies convexity; the converse can fail at the boundary
statements.statement:
1. For every preference relation $\succsim$ on ${\mathbb{R}^K_+}$: if $\succsim$ is Ψ-convex, then $\succsim$ is convex. No continuity is needed.
2. The converse does not hold, even for strongly monotone preferences: on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$, the preference represented by $u(x_1, x_2) = x_2 + \sqrt{x_1}$ is continuous, strongly monotone and convex, but has no critical ordering in $\Psi$ at the boundary bundle ${y = (0, 1)}$.

assumptions.text: (Part 1) $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${\mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
(Part 1) $\succsim$ is Ψ-convex.

statements.conclusion: Part 1: $\succsim$ is convex. Part 2: some continuous, strongly monotone and convex preference on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ is not Ψ-convex.

statements.title: Convex preferences have critical orderings at interior bundles
statements.statement: Let there be **at least one good** (${K \ge 1}$) and let $\succsim$ be a continuous, convex preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$. Then at every **interior** bundle $y$, one with ${y_k > 0}$ for all $k$, there is a nonzero ${v \in \mathbb{R}^K}$ such that ${v \cdot x > v \cdot y}$ for every ${x \succ y}$; that is, the algebraic linear ordering ${\ge_v \in \Psi}$ is a critical ordering at $y$.

assumptions.text: There is at least one good, ${K \ge 1}$.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$\succsim$ is continuous.
$\succsim$ is convex.
$y$ is a bundle in $X$.
$y$ is interior: ${y_k > 0}$ for every $k$.

statements.conclusion: Some algebraic linear ordering in $\Psi$ is critical at $y$.

statements.title: Homothetic preferences
statements.statement: A preference relation $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ is *homothetic* if for all bundles ${x, y}$ and all ${t \ge 0}$: ${x \succsim y}$ implies ${tx \succsim ty}$.

assumptions.text: The commodity space is ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, bundles of $K$ goods.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.

statements.title: Continuous, monotone homothetic preferences have a degree-one homogeneous utility
statements.statement: Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ that is homothetic, continuous and monotone. Then there is a continuous ${u : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ that represents $\succsim$ and is homogeneous of degree one: ${u(tx) = t\,u(x)}$ for every bundle $x$ and every ${t \ge 0}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$\succsim$ is homothetic.
$\succsim$ is continuous.
$\succsim$ is monotone.

statements.conclusion: Some continuous, degree-one homogeneous $u$ represents $\succsim$.

statements.title: Quasi-linearity in commodity 1
statements.statement: As printed (2025 edition): a preference relation $\succsim$ on ${\mathbb{R}^K_+}$ is quasi-linear in commodity 1 if ${x \succsim y}$ implies $(x + \varepsilon e_1) \succsim (y + \varepsilon e_1)$, where ${e_1 = (1, 0, \dots, 0)}$ and $\varepsilon$. The sentence ends there, so the range of $\varepsilon$ is not stated. The earlier 2020 printing completes it: “$\varepsilon$ is a real number”.

statements.title: Quasi-linear preferences (in commodity 1)
statements.statement:
A preference relation $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ is *quasi-linear in commodity 1* if for all bundles ${x, y}$ and every real $\varepsilon$ for which ${x + \varepsilon e_1}$ and ${y + \varepsilon e_1}$ are bundles,

$$x \succsim y \implies x + \varepsilon e_1 \succsim y + \varepsilon e_1,$$

where ${e_1 = (1, 0, \dots, 0)}$.

assumptions.text: The commodity space is ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, bundles of $K$ goods.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
$\varepsilon$ ranges over all real numbers, positive or negative (the range of the 2020 printing).

statements.title: A utility linear in good 1 for quasi-linear preferences
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ that is monotone, continuous, strongly monotone in commodity 1 (${x + \varepsilon e_1 \succ x}$ for every bundle $x$ and every ${\varepsilon > 0}$) and quasi-linear in commodity 1. Then there is a function $v$ such that

$$u(x) = x_1 + v(x_2, \dots, x_K)$$

represents $\succsim$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$\succsim$ is monotone.
$\succsim$ is continuous.
$\succsim$ is strongly monotone in commodity 1: ${x + \varepsilon e_1 \succ x}$ for every $x$ and ${\varepsilon > 0}$.
$\succsim$ is quasi-linear in commodity 1.

statements.conclusion: For some $v$, the function ${x_1 + v(x_2, \dots, x_K)}$ represents $\succsim$.

entries.title: Valuing a bundle in units of the numeraire

statements.title: Every bundle without good 1 is worth some amount of good 1
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ that is monotone, continuous, quasi-linear in commodity 1 and strongly monotone in commodity 1. Then for every bundle $x$ there is ${v \ge 0}$ with

$$(0, x_2, \dots, x_K) \sim (v, 0, \dots, 0).$$

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$\succsim$ is monotone.
$\succsim$ is continuous.
$\succsim$ is quasi-linear in commodity 1.
$\succsim$ is strongly monotone in commodity 1.

statements.conclusion: For every $x$ there is ${v \ge 0}$ with $(0, x_2, \dots, x_K) \sim (v, 0, \dots, 0)$.

statements.title: Quasi-linearity in all commodities
statements.statement: A preference relation $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ is *quasi-linear in all commodities* if for every commodity $k$, all bundles ${x, y}$ and every real $\varepsilon$ for which ${x + \varepsilon e_k}$ and ${y + \varepsilon e_k}$ are bundles: ${x \succsim y}$ implies $x + \varepsilon e_k \succsim y + \varepsilon e_k$, where $e_k$ is the unit vector of commodity $k$.

assumptions.text: The commodity space is ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, bundles of $K$ goods.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
The condition is required for every commodity $k$ and every real $\varepsilon$.

entries.title: Linear utility from quasi-linearity in all goods

statements.title: Continuous, strongly monotone preferences quasi-linear in every good have a linear utility
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ that is continuous, strongly monotone and quasi-linear in all commodities. Then there is ${\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^K}$ with ${\alpha_k > 0}$ for every $k$ such that

$$u(x) = \alpha \cdot x = \sum_k \alpha_k x_k$$

represents $\succsim$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$\succsim$ is continuous.
$\succsim$ is strongly monotone.
$\succsim$ is quasi-linear in all commodities.

statements.conclusion: Some $\alpha$ with all ${\alpha_k > 0}$ makes ${\alpha \cdot x}$ a utility representation.

entries.title: Directions valued by subjective marginal values

statements.title: Improvement directions according to subjective values
statements.statement:
Let ${v : X \to \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ assign to each bundle a vector of non-negative “subjective values”. For a bundle $x$, $D_v(x)$ is the set of directions ${d \in \mathbb{R}^K}$ that are feasible at $x$ (for some ${\lambda^* > 0}$, $x + \lambda d \in \mathbb{R}^K_+$ for all ${\lambda \in (0, \lambda^*)}$) and satisfy

$$d \cdot v(x) = \sum_k d_k\, v_k(x) > 0.$$

assumptions.text: ${v : X \to \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ is a value function on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$x$ is a bundle in $X$.

statements.title: Improvements and improvement directions
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ and ${x \in X}$.

1. A vector ${z \in \mathbb{R}^K}$ is an *improvement* at $x$ if ${x + z \in X}$ and ${x + z \succ x}$.
2. A vector ${d \in \mathbb{R}^K}$ is an *improvement direction* at $x$ if there is ${\lambda^* > 0}$ such that ${\lambda d}$ is an improvement at $x$ for every ${\lambda \in (0, \lambda^*)}$.
3. $D_\succsim(x)$ is the set of improvement directions at $x$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$x$ is a bundle; the vectors $z$ and $d$ range over all of $\mathbb{R}^K$, negative components allowed.

statements.title: Four properties of improvement directions
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ and ${x \in X}$.

1. If ${d \in D_\succsim(x)}$ and ${\lambda > 0}$, then ${\lambda d \in D_\succsim(x)}$.
2. If $\succsim$ is strictly convex, every improvement at $x$ is an improvement direction at $x$.
3. If $\succsim$ is strongly monotone, continuous and convex, every improvement at $x$ is an improvement direction at $x$.
4. If $\succsim$ is monotone, every $d$ with ${d_k > 0}$ for all $k$ belongs to $D_\succsim(x)$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, and $x$ is a bundle.
Part 1: ${d \in D_\succsim(x)}$ and ${\lambda > 0}$.
Part 2: $\succsim$ is strictly convex, and $z$ is an improvement at $x$.
Part 3: $\succsim$ is strongly monotone, continuous and convex, and $d$ is an improvement at $x$.
Part 4: $\succsim$ is monotone, and ${d_k > 0}$ for every $k$.

statements.conclusion: Part 1: ${\lambda d \in D_\succsim(x)}$. Parts 2 and 3: the given improvement belongs to $D_\succsim(x)$. Part 4: ${d \in D_\succsim(x)}$.

statements.title: Differentiable preferences
statements.statement: A preference relation $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ is *differentiable at* $x$ if there is a function ${v : X \to \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ with ${D_\succsim(x) = D_v(x)}$. It is *differentiable* if it is differentiable at every ${x \in X}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$x$ is a bundle in $X$.

statements.title: Differentiability of preferences with a smooth quasi-concave utility
statements.statement: Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ that is represented by a utility function $u$ which is differentiable, strongly increasing (${x_k \ge y_k}$ for all $k$ and ${x \ne y}$ imply ${u(x) > u(y)}$) and quasi-concave. Then $\succsim$ is differentiable: at every ${x \in X}$, boundary bundles included, there is ${v : X \to \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ with ${D_\succsim(x) = D_v(x)}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$u$ represents $\succsim$.
$u$ is differentiable: it has a gradient ${\nabla u}$ that gives every directional derivative.
$u$ is strongly increasing.
$u$ is quasi-concave.

statements.conclusion: $\succsim$ is differentiable at every bundle.

entries.title: Existence of a solution to the consumer problem
entries.name: Existence of demand

statements.title: Continuous preferences guarantee a solution to the consumer problem
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a continuous preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$. Then for every price vector $p$ with ${p_k > 0}$ for all $k$ and every wealth ${w > 0}$, the budget set

$$B(p,w) = \{x \in X : p \cdot x \le w\}$$

contains a bundle $x^*$ with ${x^* \succsim y}$ for every ${y \in B(p,w)}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$\succsim$ is continuous.
Prices are strictly positive, ${p_k > 0}$ for every $k$, and wealth is positive, ${w > 0}$.

statements.conclusion: The consumer problem at ${(p,w)}$ has a solution.

entries.title: Convexity and uniqueness of the consumer’s solution
entries.name: Uniqueness of demand

statements.title: Convexity and uniqueness of the consumer’s optimum
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, and let ${p_k > 0}$ for all $k$ and ${w > 0}$.

1. If $\succsim$ is convex, the set of solutions of the consumer problem at ${(p,w)}$ is convex. More generally, for every convex set $A$ of bundles, the set of best elements of $A$ under $\succsim$ is convex.
2. If $\succsim$ is strictly convex, the consumer problem at ${(p,w)}$ has at most one solution.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
Part 1: $\succsim$ is convex (and, in the general form, $A$ is a convex set of bundles).
Part 2: $\succsim$ is strictly convex.
Prices are strictly positive, ${p_k > 0}$ for every $k$, and wealth is positive, ${w > 0}$.

statements.conclusion: Part 1: the set of solutions is convex (possibly empty). Part 2: any two solutions coincide. Neither part asserts that a solution exists.

entries.title: First-order conditions for the consumer problem

statements.title: At an optimum, a consumed good has the highest value per unit of price
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a differentiable preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ with subjective value function $v$, so that ${D_\succsim(x) = D_v(x)}$ for every $x$. Let ${p_k > 0}$ for all $k$, ${w > 0}$, and let $x^*$ solve the consumer problem at ${(p,w)}$. If ${x^*_k > 0}$, then

$$\frac{v_k(x^*)}{p_k} \ge \frac{v_j(x^*)}{p_j} \quad \text{for every } j \ne k.$$

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
${v : X \to \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ is a subjective value function with ${D_\succsim(x) = D_v(x)}$ at every bundle ($\succsim$ is differentiable).
Prices are strictly positive, ${p_k > 0}$ for every $k$, and wealth is positive, ${w > 0}$.
$x^*$ solves the consumer problem at ${(p,w)}$.
Commodity $k$ is consumed: ${x^*_k > 0}$.

statements.conclusion: $v_k(x^*)/p_k \ge v_j(x^*)/p_j$ for every ${j \ne k}$.

entries.title: The marginal rate of substitution equals the price ratio
entries.name: MRS equals the price ratio

statements.title: When two goods are consumed at an optimum, their value ratio equals their price ratio
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a differentiable preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ with subjective value function $v$, so that ${D_\succsim(x) = D_v(x)}$ for every $x$; let ${p_k > 0}$ for all $k$, ${w > 0}$, and let $x^*$ solve the consumer problem at ${(p,w)}$. If ${x^*_k > 0}$ and ${x^*_j > 0}$, then $v_k(x^*)\, p_j = p_k\, v_j(x^*)$; when ${v_j(x^*) \ne 0}$ this is the ratio condition

$$\frac{v_k(x^*)}{v_j(x^*)} = \frac{p_k}{p_j}.$$

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
${v : X \to \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ is a subjective value function with ${D_\succsim(x) = D_v(x)}$ at every bundle.
Prices are strictly positive, ${p_k > 0}$ for every $k$, and wealth is positive, ${w > 0}$.
$x^*$ solves the consumer problem at ${(p,w)}$.
Both goods are consumed: ${x^*_k > 0}$ and ${x^*_j > 0}$.

entries.title: First-order conditions are sufficient under convexity

statements.title: Sufficient conditions for optimality in the consumer problem
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ that is strongly monotone, convex, continuous and differentiable with subjective value function $v$. Let ${p_k > 0}$ for all $k$, ${w > 0}$, and let $x^*$ be a bundle such that

- ${p \cdot x^* = w}$, and
- $v_k(x^*)/p_k \ge v_j(x^*)/p_j$ for every $k$ with ${x^*_k > 0}$ and every $j$.

Then $x^*$ solves the consumer problem at ${(p,w)}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$\succsim$ is strongly monotone.
$\succsim$ is convex.
$\succsim$ is continuous.
$\succsim$ is differentiable, with value function $v$: ${D_\succsim(x) = D_v(x)}$ for all $x$.
Prices are strictly positive, ${p_k > 0}$ for every $k$, and wealth is positive, ${w > 0}$.
$x^*$ exhausts the budget: ${p \cdot x^* = w}$.
$v_k(x^*)/p_k \ge v_j(x^*)/p_j$ whenever ${x^*_k > 0}$, for all $j$.

statements.conclusion: $x^*$ is a solution of the consumer problem at ${(p,w)}$.

statements.title: Walras’ law: monotone consumers exhaust their budget
statements.statement: Let $\succsim$ be a monotone preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, and let ${p_k > 0}$ for all $k$ and ${w > 0}$. If $x$ solves the consumer problem at ${(p,w)}$, then ${p \cdot x = w}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$\succsim$ is monotone.
Prices are strictly positive, ${p_k > 0}$ for every $k$, and wealth is positive, ${w > 0}$.
$x$ solves the consumer problem at ${(p,w)}$.

statements.conclusion: ${p \cdot x = w}$.

statements.title: Continuous preferences give continuous demand
statements.statement: Let $\succsim$ be a continuous preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, and let ${x(p,w)}$ be a demand function such that, for every ${p \in \mathbb{R}^K_{++}}$ and ${w > 0}$, ${x(p,w)}$ is the unique solution of the consumer problem at ${(p,w)}$. Then $x$ is continuous on ${\mathbb{R}^{K+1}_{++}}$: for every ${(p,w)}$ and ${\varepsilon > 0}$ there is ${\delta > 0}$ such that $\|x(p',w') - x(p,w)\| < \varepsilon$ for every $(p',w') \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}_{++}$ within distance $\delta$ of ${(p,w)}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$\succsim$ is continuous.
${x(p,w)}$ solves the consumer problem at every ${(p,w)}$ with positive prices and wealth.
That solution is unique.

statements.conclusion: The demand function is continuous in ${(p,w)}$ jointly.

entries.title: Closed graph of the demand correspondence

statements.title: The demand correspondence has a closed graph
statements.statement: Let $\succsim$ be a continuous preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, and let ${x(p,w)}$ denote the set of solutions of the consumer problem at ${(p,w)}$. If ${(p^n, w^n) \to (p^*, w^*)}$, where all prices and wealth levels are strictly positive, ${x^n \in x(p^n, w^n)}$ for every $n$, and ${x^n \to x^*}$, then $x^*$ is a bundle and ${x^* \in x(p^*, w^*)}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$\succsim$ is continuous.
The pairs ${(p^n, w^n)}$ and ${(p^*, w^*)}$ have strictly positive prices and wealth.
${x^n \in x(p^n, w^n)}$ for every $n$.

statements.conclusion: ${x^* \in \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ and $x^*$ solves the consumer problem at ${(p^*, w^*)}$.

statements.title: What a rationalized demand function reveals
statements.statement: Let $x$ be a demand function (with ${x(p,w) \in B(p,w)}$ and homogeneous of degree zero), and let $\succsim$ be a monotone preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ that rationalizes $x$: for every ${(p,w)}$, ${x(p,w) \succsim y}$ for all ${y \in B(p,w)}$. If ${a = x(p,w)}$ and ${b \in B(p,w)}$ for some ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$, then ${a \succsim b}$; if in addition ${p \cdot b < w}$, then ${a \succ b}$.

assumptions.text: $x$ is a demand function: ${x(p,w) \in B(p,w)}$ for all positive prices and wealth.
$x$ is homogeneous of degree zero: $x(\lambda p, \lambda w) = x(p,w)$ for ${\lambda > 0}$.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$\succsim$ is monotone.
$\succsim$ rationalizes $x$.
${a = x(p,w)}$ and ${b \in B(p,w)}$ for some ${p \gg 0}$, ${w > 0}$.
For the strict conclusion: ${p \cdot b < w}$.

statements.conclusion: ${a \succsim b}$; and ${a \succ b}$ when ${p \cdot b < w}$.

statements.title: The compensated law of demand
statements.statement:
Let $x$ be a demand function (with ${x(p,w) \in B(p,w)}$, homogeneous of degree zero) that satisfies Walras’ law and the weak axiom of revealed preference. Let ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$, let ${p' \gg 0}$, and let ${w' = p' \cdot x(p,w)}$ be the compensated wealth. Then either ${x(p',w') = x(p,w)}$, or

$$(p' - p) \cdot \big(x(p',w') - x(p,w)\big) < 0.$$

assumptions.text: $x$ is a demand function: ${x(p,w) \in B(p,w)}$ for all positive prices and wealth.
$x$ is homogeneous of degree zero.
Walras’ law: ${p \cdot x(p,w) = w}$ for all ${(p,w)}$.
Weak axiom: if ${x(p,w) \ne x(p',w')}$ and ${p \cdot x(p',w') \le w}$, then ${p' \cdot x(p,w) > w'}$.
${w' = p' \cdot x(p,w)}$.

statements.title: Indirect preferences over choice sets
statements.statement:
Let $D$ be a set of nonempty subsets of $X$ and $\succsim$ a preference relation on $X$ such that every ${A \in D}$ has a unique best element under $\succsim$, written $C_\succsim(A)$. The *indirect preference* $\succsim^*$ on $D$ is defined by

$$A \succsim^* B \iff C_\succsim(A) \succsim C_\succsim(B).$$

assumptions.text: $D$ is a set of nonempty subsets of $X$ (choice problems).
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
Every ${A \in D}$ has exactly one best element under $\succsim$, written $C_\succsim(A)$.

statements.title: Indirect preferences form a preference relation
statements.statement: Let $D$ be a set of nonempty subsets of $X$ and $\succsim$ a preference relation on $X$ such that every ${A \in D}$ has a unique best element under $\succsim$. Then the indirect preference $\succsim^*$ is a preference relation on $D$.

assumptions.text: $D$ is a set of nonempty subsets of $X$ (choice problems).
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
Every ${A \in D}$ has exactly one best element under $\succsim$, written $C_\succsim(A)$.

statements.conclusion: $\succsim^*$ is reflexive, complete and transitive on $D$.

statements.title: Indirect utility of a choice set
statements.statement:
In the setting of indirect preferences, let ${u : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ represent $\succsim$. The *indirect utility function* is the function $v$ on $D$ defined by

$$v(A) = u(C_\succsim(A)).$$

assumptions.text: $D$ is a set of nonempty subsets of $X$ (choice problems).
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
Every ${A \in D}$ has exactly one best element under $\succsim$, written $C_\succsim(A)$.
${u : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ represents $\succsim$.

statements.title: Indirect utility represents indirect preferences
statements.statement:
In the setting of indirect preferences, if $u$ represents $\succsim$, then ${v(A) = u(C_\succsim(A))}$ represents $\succsim^*$: for all ${A, B \in D}$,

$$A \succsim^* B \iff v(A) \ge v(B).$$

assumptions.text: $D$ is a set of nonempty subsets of $X$ (choice problems).
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
Every ${A \in D}$ has exactly one best element under $\succsim$, written $C_\succsim(A)$.
${u : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ represents $\succsim$.

statements.conclusion: $v$ represents $\succsim^*$.

statements.title: Recovering the choice from indirect preferences
statements.statement: In the setting of indirect preferences, let ${A \in D}$ and ${a \in A}$ with ${A \setminus \{a\} \in D}$. If ${A \succ^* A \setminus \{a\}}$, then ${C_\succsim(A) = a}$.

assumptions.text: $D$ is a set of nonempty subsets of $X$ (choice problems).
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
Every ${A \in D}$ has exactly one best element under $\succsim$, written $C_\succsim(A)$.
${A \in D}$ and ${a \in A}$.
The smaller menu is admissible: ${A \setminus \{a\} \in D}$.
${A \succ^* A \setminus \{a\}}$: removing $a$ makes the menu strictly worse.

statements.conclusion: ${C_\succsim(A) = a}$.

statements.title: Indirect preferences over budget sets
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ and ${x(p,w)}$ a demand function. The *indirect preference* over price–wealth pairs is defined by

$$\begin{aligned} &(p,w) \succsim^* (p',w') \\ &\quad\iff x(p,w) \succsim x(p',w'). \end{aligned}$$

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$x$ is a demand function from price–wealth pairs to bundles.

entries.title: Properties of indirect preferences over budget sets

statements.title: Properties of indirect preferences over budget sets
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${\mathbb{R}^K_+}$ and $x$ a demand function; all prices and wealth levels below are strictly positive.

1. If $x$ is homogeneous of degree zero, then $(\lambda p, \lambda w) \sim^* (p,w)$ for every ${\lambda > 0}$.
2. If ${x(p,w)}$ is a best bundle of ${B(p,w)}$ under $\succsim$ for every ${(p,w)}$, then ${p \le p'}$ (coordinatewise) implies ${(p,w) \succsim^* (p',w)}$; if moreover $\succsim$ is monotone, then ${w < w'}$ implies ${(p,w') \succ^* (p,w)}$.
3. If $\succsim$ is continuous and ${x(p,w)}$ is the unique best bundle of ${B(p,w)}$ under $\succsim$ for every ${(p,w)}$, then $\succ^*$ is preserved nearby: if ${(p,w) \succ^* (p',w')}$, the same holds for all pairs close enough to ${(p,w)}$ and to ${(p',w')}$.
4. If ${x(p,w)}$ is a best bundle of ${B(p,w)}$ under $\succsim$ for every ${(p,w)}$ and $(p^1,w^1) \succsim^* (p^2,w^2)$, then $(p^1,w^1) \succsim^* (\lambda p^1 + (1-\lambda) p^2,\ \lambda w^1 + (1-\lambda) w^2)$ for every ${\lambda \in [0,1]}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${\mathbb{R}^K_+}$ and $x$ is a demand function.
Part 1: $x$ is homogeneous of degree zero.
Parts 2 and 4: ${x(p,w)}$ is a best bundle of ${B(p,w)}$ under $\succsim$ at every positive ${(p,w)}$.
Part 2, wealth: $\succsim$ is monotone.
Part 3: $\succsim$ is continuous, and ${x(p,w)}$ is the unique best bundle of ${B(p,w)}$ under $\succsim$.

statements.conclusion: Properties 1 to 4.

statements.title: Roy’s identity and the tangent hyperplane
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a monotone preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, let ${x(p,w)}$ be a best bundle of ${B(p,w)}$ under $\succsim$ for every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$, and fix ${p^* \gg 0}$ and ${w^* > 0}$.

1. The point ${(p^*, w^*)}$ lies on $H = \{(p,w) : p \cdot x(p^*,w^*) = w\}$, and every ${(p,w) \in H}$ with ${p \gg 0}$, ${w > 0}$ satisfies ${(p,w) \succsim^* (p^*,w^*)}$.
2. (Roy’s identity.) If $\succsim^*$ is represented by a differentiable indirect utility function ${v(p,w)}$, then for every $k$:

$$-\frac{\partial v / \partial p_k\,(p^*,w^*)}{\partial v / \partial w\,(p^*,w^*)} = x_k(p^*,w^*).$$

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$\succsim$ is monotone.
${x(p,w)}$ is a best bundle of ${B(p,w)}$ under $\succsim$ for all ${p \gg 0}$, ${w > 0}$.
Part 2: $v$ is differentiable in prices and wealth.
Part 2: $v$ represents $\succsim^*$ on price–wealth pairs with ${p \gg 0}$, ${w > 0}$.

statements.conclusion: Part 1: $H$ is a supporting hyperplane of the indirect preference at ${(p^*,w^*)}$. Part 2: Roy’s identity holds.

statements.title: Maximal distance and minimal time are dual problems
statements.statement: Let $M : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be strictly increasing and continuous, where $M(t)$ is the maximal distance a turtle can travel in time $t$. Then for all ${t, x \in \mathbb{R}}$, ${M(t) = x}$ if and only if $t$ is the least $s$ with ${x \le M(s)}$.

assumptions.text: $M : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ gives the maximal distance traveled in each time.
$M$ is strictly increasing.
$M$ is continuous.

statements.conclusion: The prime statement (the maximal distance in time $t$ is $x$) and the dual statement (the minimal time to travel $x$ is $t$) are equivalent.

entries.title: The prime problem and the demand

statements.title: The demand: solution of the prime problem
statements.statement: Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, and let $p$ and $w$ be such that the *prime problem* ${P(p,w)}$, which is to choose a bundle in the budget set $B(p,w) = \{x \in X : p \cdot x \le w\}$ that is best under $\succsim$, has a unique solution. The *demand* ${x(p,w)}$ is that solution.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$p$ is a price vector and $w$ a wealth level.
The prime problem at ${(p,w)}$ has exactly one solution.

entries.title: Hicksian demand and the expenditure function

statements.title: Hicksian demand and the expenditure function
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, $p$ a price vector and ${z \in X}$ a target bundle. The *dual problem* ${D(p,z)}$ is

$$\min_x \{\, p \cdot x : x \succsim z \,\}.$$

When it has a unique solution, that solution is the *Hicksian demand* ${h(p,z)}$, and ${e(p,z) = p \cdot h(p,z)}$ is the *expenditure function*.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$p$ is a price vector and $z$ a bundle.
The dual problem ${D(p,z)}$ has exactly one solution.

entries.title: Properties of Hicksian demand and the expenditure function

statements.title: Properties of Hicksian demand and the expenditure function
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$. All prices are strictly positive, and each statement assumes that the dual problems it mentions have unique solutions.

1. ${h(\lambda p, z) = h(p,z)}$ and $e(\lambda p, z) = \lambda\, e(p,z)$ for every ${\lambda > 0}$.
2. ${e(p,z) \le p \cdot h(p',z)}$ for every $p'$. Hence $(p' - p) \cdot (h(p',z) - h(p,z)) \le 0$; raising only the price of good $k$ weakly lowers $h_k$; and ${p \le p'}$ implies ${e(p,z) \le e(p',z)}$.
3. If $\succsim$ is monotone and continuous, then ${h(p,z) \sim z}$.
4. If $\succsim$ is monotone and continuous and the dual problem has a unique solution at every ${(p,z)}$, then $h$ and $e$ are continuous in ${(p,z)}$.
5. $e$ is concave in $p$: $e(\lambda p^1 + (1-\lambda) p^2, z) \ge \lambda\, e(p^1,z) + (1-\lambda)\, e(p^2,z)$ for ${\lambda \in [0,1]}$.
6. (Dual of Roy’s identity.) The hyperplane $\{(p,e) : e = p \cdot h(p^*,z)\}$ passes through ${(p^*, e(p^*,z))}$ and lies weakly above the graph of ${e(\cdot, z)}$: ${p \cdot h(p^*,z) \ge e(p,z)}$ for all $p$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
Prices are strictly positive.
The dual problems involved have unique solutions.
Part 1: ${\lambda > 0}$. Part 5: ${\lambda \in [0,1]}$.
Parts 3 and 4: $\succsim$ is monotone and continuous.

statements.conclusion: Properties 1 to 6.

entries.title: Duality of utility maximization and expenditure minimization
entries.name: Consumer duality

statements.title: For monotone, continuous preferences, a bundle solves the prime problem exactly when it solves the dual
statements.statement: Let $\succsim$ be a monotone and continuous preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, and let ${p \gg 0}$, ${x^* \in X}$ and ${w^* > 0}$. Then $x^*$ solves the prime problem ${P(p, w^*)}$ if and only if $w^*$ solves the dual problem ${D(p, x^*)}$: $x^*$ is a cheapest bundle among those at least as good as $x^*$, and ${p \cdot x^* = w^*}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$.
$\succsim$ is monotone.
$\succsim$ is continuous.
$x^*$ is a bundle.

statements.conclusion: $x^*$ is best in ${B(p,w^*)}$ under $\succsim$ if and only if $x^*$ solves ${D(p,x^*)}$ and ${p \cdot x^* = w^*}$.

statements.title: Technology and its standard assumptions

assumptions.text: $Z$ is a subset of $\mathbb{R}^K$.
Scaling claim: $Z$ is convex.
Scaling claim: ${0 \in Z}$.
Scaling claim: ${0 \le \lambda < 1}$.

statements.conclusion: If $Z$ is convex and ${0 \in Z}$, then ${\lambda z \in Z}$ for all ${z \in Z}$ and ${\lambda \in [0,1)}$.

statements.title: Production functions and technologies, each derived from the other
statements.statement:
Consider the single-output case: commodity $K$ is produced from commodities ${1, \dots, K-1}$, i.e. every ${z \in Z}$ has ${z_K \ge 0}$ and ${z_k \le 0}$ for ${k \ne K}$.

1. From a technology $Z$, the *production function* is $f(v) = \max\{x : (-v, x) \in Z\}$ for input vectors ${v \in \mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+}$.
2. From a production function $f$, the derived “technology” is $Z(f) = \{(-w, x) : x \le f(v) \text{ and } w \ge v \text{ for some } v \in \mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+\}$.

assumptions.text: ${Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^K}$ is a technology.
Single output: every ${z \in Z}$ has ${z_K \ge 0}$ and ${z_k \le 0}$ for ${k \ne K}$.
Input vectors $v$ are non-negative.
In part 2, $f$ is any real-valued function on input vectors.

entries.title: The technology derived from a production function

statements.title: A well-behaved production function gives a well-behaved technology
statements.statement: Let $f$ be a real-valued function on ${\mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+}$ that is increasing (nondecreasing), continuous and concave, with ${f(0) = 0}$. Then the derived technology $Z(f)$ satisfies all five conditions: ${0 \in Z(f)}$; $Z(f) \cap \mathbb{R}^K_+ \subseteq \{0\}$; free disposal; $Z(f)$ is closed; $Z(f)$ is convex.

assumptions.text: $f$ is a real-valued function on input vectors in ${\mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+}$.
$f$ is increasing (nondecreasing) on ${\mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+}$.
$f$ is continuous on ${\mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+}$.
$f$ is concave on ${\mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+}$.

statements.conclusion: $Z(f)$ satisfies conditions 1 to 5.

statements.title: The producer as a decision maker over plans and profits
statements.statement:
Let ${Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^K}$ be a technology and let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on ${X = Z \times \mathbb{R}}$, the pairs ${(z, \pi)}$ of a plan and a profit. At prices $p$ the producer faces

$$B(p) = \{(z, \pi) : z \in Z,\ \pi = p \cdot z\}$$

and chooses ${z \in Z}$ such that ${(z, p \cdot z)}$ is best in $B(p)$ under $\succsim$. In the case ${K = 2}$, with commodity 1 the input and commodity 2 the output, a *returns maximizer* instead chooses ${z \in Z}$ maximizing the ratio ${\pi / (p_1 a)}$ of profit to cost, where ${a = -z_1}$.

assumptions.text: ${Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^K}$ is a technology, with no further conditions.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on ${Z \times \mathbb{R}}$.
The price vector $p$ is any vector in $\mathbb{R}^K$.
Returns maximizer: ${K = 2}$, commodity 1 is the input and commodity 2 the output.

entries.title: The returns maximizer and preference maximization

statements.title: The returns maximizer cannot be represented
statements.statement: As printed (example 6): with ${K = 2}$, commodity 1 the input and commodity 2 the output, a returns maximizer, who maximizes the ratio of profits to costs ${\pi/(p_a a)}$, cannot be represented as maximizing a preference relation on ${X = Z \times \mathbb{R}}$, since the behavior depends on the breakdown of profit into revenues and costs and not just on profit.

assumptions.text: Two commodities: commodity 1 is the input and commodity 2 the output.
The returns maximizer chooses a plan maximizing ${\pi / (p_a a)}$.

statements.conclusion: No preference on ${Z \times \mathbb{R}}$ reproduces the returns maximizer’s choices. With a single input, as printed, this does not hold (see the counterexample).

statements.title: With one input, the returns maximizer is representable
statements.statement: Let ${K = 2}$, with commodity 1 the input. For every technology ${Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2}$ there is a preference relation $\succsim$ on ${Z \times \mathbb{R}}$ such that, at every price vector with ${p_1 > 0}$, a plan $z$ maximizes ${\pi / (p_1 a)}$ over $Z$, where ${a = -z_1}$, if and only if ${(z, p \cdot z)}$ is best in $B(p)$ under $\succsim$. One such preference ranks pairs by ${g(z, \pi) = \pi / a}$, the profit per unit of input.

assumptions.text: ${Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2}$ is any technology.

statements.conclusion: The returns maximizer’s choices coincide with the maximization of a preference on ${Z \times \mathbb{R}}$ at every price vector with a positive input price.

statements.title: With two or more inputs, the returns maximizer is not representable
statements.statement:
Let the commodities be $L$ inputs followed by $M$ outputs, with **at least two inputs** (${L \ge 2}$) and **at least one output** (${M \ge 1}$), and let the returns maximizer choose ${z \in Z}$ to maximize profit over input cost,

$$\frac{p \cdot z}{\sum_{i \le L} p_i\,(-z_i)}.$$

Then there is a technology ${Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{L+M}}$ for which no preference relation on ${Z \times \mathbb{R}}$ reproduces the returns maximizer’s choices at every price vector with positive input prices.

assumptions.text: The commodities are $L$ inputs followed by $M$ outputs.
There are at least two inputs, ${L \ge 2}$.
There is at least one output, ${M \ge 1}$.
Input prices are positive.

statements.conclusion: For some technology $Z$, no preference on ${Z \times \mathbb{R}}$ has the returns maximizer’s choices.

entries.title: Profit maximization: profit and supply functions

statements.title: The producer’s problem, profit function and supply function
statements.statement:
Let ${Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^K}$ be a technology and ${p \in \mathbb{R}^K}$ a price vector.

1. A plan $z$ solves the *producer’s problem* ${\max_{z \in Z} p \cdot z}$ if ${z \in Z}$ and ${p \cdot z' \le p \cdot z}$ for all ${z' \in Z}$.
2. The *profit function* is $\pi(p) = \max_{z \in Z} p \cdot z$.
3. When the producer’s problem has a unique solution, that solution is the *supply function* $z(p)$.

assumptions.text: ${Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^K}$ is a technology.
$p$ is any price vector.
Supply function: the producer’s problem at $p$ has exactly one solution.

statements.title: Properties of the supply function
statements.statement:
Let ${Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^K}$ be a technology. Each statement assumes that the producer’s problems it mentions have unique solutions.

1. ${z(\lambda p) = z(p)}$ for every ${\lambda > 0}$.
2. If $Z$ is closed, convex and bounded above (there is $B$ with ${z_k \le B}$ for all ${z \in Z}$ and all $k$), then $z$ is continuous wherever it is defined.
3. (Law of supply.) If ${z(p) \ne z(p')}$, then $(p - p') \cdot (z(p) - z(p')) > 0$. In particular, if $p$ and $p'$ differ only in coordinate $k$, with ${p_k > p'_k}$, and ${z(p) \ne z(p')}$, then ${z_k(p) > z_k(p')}$.

assumptions.text: ${Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^K}$ is a technology.
The producer’s problems at the prices involved have unique solutions.
Part 1: ${\lambda > 0}$.
Part 2: $Z$ is closed, convex and bounded above.
Part 3: ${z(p) \ne z(p')}$.

statements.conclusion: Properties 1 to 3.

entries.title: Hotelling’s lemma and the profit function
entries.name: Hotelling’s lemma

statements.title: Properties of the profit function and Hotelling’s lemma
statements.statement:
Let ${Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^K}$ be a technology with profit function $\pi$ and supply function $z$. Each statement assumes that the maxima and unique solutions it mentions exist.

1. $\pi(\lambda p) = \lambda\, \pi(p)$ for every ${\lambda > 0}$.
2. If $Z$ is closed, convex and bounded above, $\pi$ is continuous wherever the supply is defined.
3. $\pi$ is convex: $\pi(\lambda p + (1-\lambda) p') \le \lambda\, \pi(p) + (1-\lambda)\, \pi(p')$ for ${\lambda \in [0,1]}$.
4. (Hotelling’s lemma.) ${p \cdot z(p^*) \le \pi(p)}$ for every $p$, with equality at ${p = p^*}$, so the hyperplane $\{(p, \pi) : \pi = p \cdot z(p^*)\}$ supports the graph of $\pi$ at $p^*$. If $\pi$ is differentiable, and the maximum defining it is attained at all prices near $p^*$, then $\partial \pi / \partial p_k\,(p^*) = z_k(p^*)$.
5. If $\pi$ is twice continuously differentiable, its mixed second derivatives are symmetric: $\partial^2 \pi / \partial p_k \partial p_j\,(p^*) = \partial^2 \pi / \partial p_j \partial p_k\,(p^*)$. The book combines this with Hotelling’s lemma to conclude $\partial z_j / \partial p_k\,(p^*) = \partial z_k / \partial p_j\,(p^*)$.

assumptions.text: ${Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^K}$ is a technology; prices are unrestricted.
The maxima defining $\pi$ at the prices involved are attained, and the supply is unique where it is used.
Part 1: ${\lambda > 0}$. Part 3: ${\lambda \in [0,1]}$.
Part 2: $Z$ is closed, convex and bounded above.
Part 4, derivative: $\pi$ is differentiable, and the maximum defining it is attained at all prices near $p^*$.
Part 5: $\pi$ is twice continuously differentiable.

statements.conclusion: Properties 1 to 5.

statements.title: The cost function
statements.statement:
Let ${Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^K}$ be a technology whose commodities are $L$ inputs followed by ${K - L}$ outputs. For input prices ${p \in \mathbb{R}^L_{++}}$ and an output combination ${y \in \mathbb{R}^{K-L}_+}$, the *cost function* is

$$c(p,y) = \min_a \{\, p \cdot a : (-a, y) \in Z \,\}.$$

assumptions.text: ${Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^K}$ is a technology.
Commodities ${1, \dots, L}$ are inputs and ${L+1, \dots, K}$ are outputs.
$p$ is the vector of input prices.
${y \in \mathbb{R}^{K-L}_+}$ is the output combination.

entries.title: Monotonicity lemma for the independence axiom

statements.title: Monotonicity of mixtures under independence
statements.statement:
Let $Z$ be a finite set of prizes and $\succsim$ a preference relation on the set $L(Z)$ of lotteries over $Z$ that satisfies the independence axiom. If ${x, y \in Z}$ and ${[x] \succ [y]}$, then for all ${1 \ge \alpha > \beta \ge 0}$,

$$\alpha x \oplus (1-\alpha) y \;\succ\; \beta x \oplus (1-\beta) y.$$

assumptions.text: $Z$ is a finite set of prizes.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $L(Z)$.
Independence: for all lotteries ${p, q, r}$ and ${\alpha \in (0,1)}$, $p \succsim q \iff \alpha p \oplus (1-\alpha) r \succsim \alpha q \oplus (1-\alpha) r$.
${x, y \in Z}$ with ${[x] \succ [y]}$.
${1 \ge \alpha > \beta \ge 0}$.

statements.conclusion: $\alpha x \oplus (1-\alpha) y \succ \beta x \oplus (1-\beta) y$.

statements.title: Expected utility representation (von Neumann–Morgenstern)
statements.statement:
Let $Z$ be a finite set of prizes and $\succsim$ a preference relation on $L(Z)$ that satisfies the independence axiom and the continuity axiom. Then there are numbers ${(v(z))_{z \in Z}}$ such that the expected value

$$U(p) = \sum_{z \in Z} p(z)\, v(z)$$

represents $\succsim$: for all ${p, q \in L(Z)}$, ${p \succsim q}$ if and only if ${U(p) \ge U(q)}$.

assumptions.text: $Z$ is a finite set of prizes.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on the set $L(Z)$ of lotteries over $Z$.
Independence: for all lotteries ${p, q, r}$ and ${\alpha \in (0,1)}$, $p \succsim q \iff \alpha p \oplus (1-\alpha) r \succsim \alpha q \oplus (1-\alpha) r$.
Continuity: if ${p \succ q}$, there are neighborhoods $B(p)$ and $B(q)$ such that ${p' \succ q'}$ for all ${p' \in B(p)}$ and ${q' \in B(q)}$.

statements.conclusion: Expected utility ${U(p) = \sum_z p(z)\, v(z)}$ represents $\succsim$.

entries.title: De Finetti’s theorem on subjective probability
entries.name: De Finetti’s theorem

statements.title: Subjective probabilities from preferences over bets (de Finetti)
statements.statement:
Let ${B = \mathbb{R}^K}$ be the set of bets on $K$ exclusive and exhaustive events, $x_k$ being the payment if event $k$ occurs, and let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on $B$. Then $\succsim$ is continuous, weakly monotone (${x_k > y_k}$ for all $k$ implies ${x \succ y}$) and additive (${x \succsim y}$ implies ${x + z \succsim y + z}$ for every bet $z$) if and only if there is ${(\pi_1, \dots, \pi_K)}$ with ${\pi_k \ge 0}$ and ${\sum_k \pi_k = 1}$ such that

$$x \succsim y \iff \sum_k \pi_k x_k \ge \sum_k \pi_k y_k.$$

assumptions.text: There are $K$ events, and bets are all vectors ${x \in \mathbb{R}^K}$.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on the set of bets.

statements.conclusion: Continuity, weak monotonicity and additivity $\iff$ $\succsim$ is represented by expected payoff under a probability vector $\pi$.

statements.title: First-order stochastic dominance via distribution functions

assumptions.text: $Z$ is a set of real numbers, possibly infinite.
$p$ and $q$ are lotteries on $Z$ with finite support.

statements.conclusion: Both characterizations of $D_1$ hold.

statements.title: Risk aversion is equivalent to concave utility
statements.statement: As printed: let $\succsim$ be a preference on $L(Z)$, ${Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}}$, represented by the vNM utility function $u$ (expected utility ${\sum_z p(z)\, u(z)}$ represents $\succsim$). The preference relation $\succsim$ is risk averse if and only if $u$ is concave.

assumptions.text: $Z$ is a set of real numbers, with no further condition.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $L(Z)$.
The expected utility ${\sum_z p(z)\,u(z)}$ represents $\succsim$.

statements.conclusion: $\succsim$ is risk averse $\iff$ $u$ is concave on $Z$. As printed, on prize sets that are not intervals this does not hold in full generality (see the counterexample).

statements.title: Risk aversion without concavity on the integer prize grid
statements.statement:
**Concavity on the prize set.** Take the prize set ${Z = \mathbb{Z}}$, which is infinite and not an interval, and ${u(x) = x}$. The preference represented by expected utility is risk averse, since ${[E(p)] \sim p}$ whenever ${E(p) \in Z}$. Yet $u$ is not concave on $Z$, because concavity on a set requires the set to be convex.

**Concavity as an inequality.** Read “$u$ is concave” instead as the inequality $u(\alpha x + (1-\alpha) y) \ge \alpha\, u(x) + (1-\alpha)\, u(y)$ for all ${x, y \in Z}$ and ${\alpha \in (0,1)}$. On ${Z = \mathbb{Z}}$, take ${u(x) = x}$ at integers and ${u(x) = x - 1}$ at all other points. The preference depends only on the values of $u$ at the prizes, so it is again risk averse, yet

$$u(\tfrac12) = -\tfrac12 < \tfrac12 = \tfrac12 u(0) + \tfrac12 u(1).$$
statements.conclusion: The equivalence between risk aversion and concavity of $u$ does not hold on some infinite prize set, under either reading of concavity.

statements.title: Risk aversion is equivalent to concave utility on an interval
statements.statement: Let ${Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}}$ be **convex** (an interval), and let $\succsim$ be a preference on $L(Z)$ represented by the vNM utility function $u$. Then $\succsim$ is risk averse, that is ${[E(p)] \succsim p}$ for every lottery $p$ with ${E(p) \in Z}$, if and only if $u$ is concave on $Z$.

assumptions.text: $Z$ is a set of real numbers.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $L(Z)$, the lotteries on $Z$ with finite support.
$u$ is a real-valued function, the vNM utility of the prizes.
The expected utility ${\sum_z p(z)\,u(z)}$ represents $\succsim$.
$Z$ is convex, i.e. an interval.

statements.conclusion: $\succsim$ is risk averse $\iff$ $u$ is concave on $Z$.

statements.title: Three definitions of “more risk averse” are equivalent

assumptions.text: $Z$ is a set of real numbers, with no further condition.
$\succsim_1$ and $\succsim_2$ are preference relations on $L(Z)$.
$u_1$ and $u_2$ are increasing on $Z$, read as strictly increasing.
$u_1$ and $u_2$ are continuous on $Z$.
The expected utility ${\sum_z p(z)\,u_i(z)}$ represents $\succsim_i$, for ${i = 1, 2}$.

statements.conclusion: Definitions 1, 2 and 3 are equivalent. As printed, on prize sets that are not intervals this does not hold in full generality (see the counterexample).
