statements.title: The definitions of “more risk averse” come apart on a grid
statements.statement:
On the prize set ${Z = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}}$, let ${u_1(x) = \max(x,\ 2x - 1)}$ and ${u_2(x) = x}$, both strictly increasing and continuous, and let $\succsim_i$ be the preference represented by the expected utility ${\sum_z p(z)\,u_i(z)}$. Then:

- definition 2 holds: whenever both certainty equivalents exist, ${CE_1(p) \le CE_2(p)}$;
- definition 1 fails: the lottery $p$ paying $0$ with probability $\tfrac25$ and $3$ with probability $\tfrac35$ satisfies ${p \sim_1 [2]}$, both having expected utility $3$ under $u_1$, while ${[2] \succ_2 p}$, since ${E(p) = \tfrac95 < 2}$.

So definitions 1 and 2 are not equivalent there, and the three-way equivalence does not hold whatever condition is used as definition 3.
statements.conclusion: On some infinite prize set the equivalence does not hold; definitions 1 and 2 already come apart.

statements.title: Three equivalent definitions of “more risk averse” on an interval

assumptions.text: $\succsim_1$ and $\succsim_2$ are preference relations on $L(Z)$.
The expected utility ${\sum_z p(z)\,u_i(z)}$ represents $\succsim_i$, for ${i = 1, 2}$.
$Z$ is convex, i.e. an interval.
$u_1$ and $u_2$ are strictly increasing on $Z$.
$u_1$ and $u_2$ are continuous on $Z$.

statements.conclusion: Definitions 1, 2 and 3 are equivalent.

entries.title: Constant absolute risk aversion and exponential utility
entries.name: Constant absolute risk aversion

statements.title: Invariance to wealth forces exponential or linear utility
statements.statement: As printed: assume that the expected utility of $u$ represents the preference $\succsim$ on $L(Z)$, ${Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}}$, which is monotonic (${a > b}$ implies ${[a] \succ [b]}$), risk averse, and invariant to wealth (${w + p \succsim w + q}$ holds or fails independently of $w$). Then $u$ is exponential or linear: ${u(x) = a + bx}$, or ${u(x) = a - b e^{-\alpha x}}$ with ${\alpha > 0}$.

assumptions.text: $Z$ is a set of real numbers, with no further condition.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $L(Z)$.
The expected utility ${\sum_z p(z)\,u(z)}$ represents $\succsim$.
Monotonicity in money: ${a > b}$ implies ${[a] \succ [b]}$.
$\succsim$ is risk averse.
Invariance to wealth, for every wealth level that keeps the prizes in $Z$.

statements.conclusion: $u$ is linear or exponential on $Z$. As printed, on prize sets other than the whole real line this does not hold in full generality (see the counterexample).

statements.title: A utility invariant to wealth, neither linear nor exponential
statements.statement:
Let $Z = \{-\tfrac13\} \cup \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ and $u(x) = \min\{2 - 2^{1-x},\ 3x\}$. Then $u$ is strictly increasing and continuous, and the preference represented by the expected utility of $u$ is monotonic, risk averse and invariant to wealth (for every wealth level that keeps the prizes in $Z$); yet on $Z$ the function $u$ is neither of the form ${a + bx}$ nor of the form ${a - b e^{-\alpha x}}$ with ${\alpha > 0}$.

Further counterexamples show that the printed statement also does not hold under narrower readings of invariance to wealth, and with the conclusion widened to include ${u(x) = a + b c^x}$. On one infinite prize set, other preferences fail invariance to wealth or risk aversion, so the hypotheses are not vacuous there.
statements.conclusion: The printed statement does not hold on some infinite prize set.

statements.title: Invariance to wealth forces CARA or linear utility on the real line
statements.statement: Let the prize space be **the whole real line** $\mathbb{R}$, and let the expected utility of $u$ represent a preference $\succsim$ on the lotteries on $\mathbb{R}$ with finite support that is monotonic in money (${a > b}$ implies ${[a] \succ [b]}$), risk averse (${[E(p)] \succsim p}$ for every $p$), and invariant to wealth (${w + p \succsim w + q}$ if and only if ${w' + p \succsim w' + q}$, for all ${w, w'}$). Then either ${u(x) = a + bx}$ for all $x$, or ${u(x) = a - b e^{-\alpha x}}$ for all $x$, for some ${\alpha > 0}$.

assumptions.text: The prize space is the whole real line, so $\succsim$ is a preference relation on the lotteries on $\mathbb{R}$ with finite support.
$u$ is a real-valued function, the vNM utility of the prizes.
The expected utility ${\sum_z p(z)\,u(z)}$ represents $\succsim$.
$\succsim$ is monotonic in money.
$\succsim$ is risk averse.
$\succsim$ is invariant to wealth (constant absolute risk aversion).

statements.conclusion: $u$ is linear, or exponential of the CARA form ${a - b e^{-\alpha x}}$ with ${\alpha > 0}$.

statements.title: The basic model of social choice

assumptions.text: $X$ is a set of alternatives, with no condition on its size.
$N$ is a finite set of individuals.
Each individual has an ordering: a preference relation with no indifference between distinct alternatives.
$F$ is defined on every profile.
The value of $F$ is a preference relation on $X$.

statements.title: The Pareto condition
statements.statement: An SWF $F$ satisfies *Par* if for all ${x, y \in X}$ and every profile ${(\succ_i)_{i \in N}}$: if ${x \succ_i y}$ for every $i$, then ${x \succ y}$, where $\succ$ is the strict part of the social preference ${F(\succ_1, \dots, \succ_n)}$.

assumptions.text: $F$ is a social welfare function.

statements.title: Independence of irrelevant alternatives
statements.statement: An SWF $F$ satisfies *IIA* if for all ${x, y \in X}$ and any two profiles ${P = (\succ_i)}$ and ${P' = (\rhd_i)}$: if ${x \succ_i y \iff x \rhd_i y}$ for every $i$, then ${x \succsim y \iff x \unrhd y}$, where ${\succsim = F(P)}$ and ${\unrhd = F(P')}$.

assumptions.text: $F$ is a social welfare function.

statements.title: Arrow’s impossibility theorem
statements.statement: Let $N$ be a finite set of individuals and let $X$ contain at least three alternatives. If a social welfare function $F$ satisfies Par and IIA, then $F$ is dictatorial: there is an individual $i^*$ such that for every profile and all ${x, y \in X}$, society strictly prefers $x$ to $y$ if and only if ${x \succ_{i^*} y}$.

assumptions.text: $N$ is a finite set of individuals.
$F$ is a social welfare function: at every profile its value is a complete, reflexive and transitive social preference.
${|X| \ge 3}$: there are three distinct alternatives.
$F$ satisfies Par.
$F$ satisfies IIA.

statements.conclusion: $F$ is dictatorial.

entries.title: Independence of the conditions of Arrow’s theorem

statements.title: Dropping Pareto or three alternatives admits nondictatorial rules
statements.statement:
1. (Par.) For any individual $i_0$ and ${|X| \ge 3}$, the anti-dictatorial SWF, whose social preference is the reverse of $i_0$’s ordering, satisfies IIA, is not dictatorial, and violates Par.
2. (${|X| \ge 3}$.) If $X$ has exactly two alternatives and $N$ is finite with **at least two individuals**, there is an SWF that satisfies Par and IIA and is not dictatorial; the majority rule is one.
3. With a single individual, no SWF satisfies Par and IIA without being dictatorial.

assumptions.text: Part 1: $i_0$ is an individual and ${|X| \ge 3}$.
Part 2: $X$ has exactly two alternatives.
Part 2: $N$ is finite.
In part 2, $N$ has at least two individuals.

statements.conclusion: Par and ${|X| \ge 3}$ cannot be dropped from Arrow’s theorem. Transitivity of the social order is treated in part (iii).

statements.title: Majority rule shows that transitivity is indispensable
statements.statement: As printed: the majority rule satisfies IIA and Par for ${|X| \ge 3}$ but can induce a relation that is not transitive regardless of the number of individuals; it is offered as an example of a nondictatorial rule showing that transitivity of the social order cannot be dropped from Arrow’s theorem.

assumptions.text: $X$ has at least three alternatives.
$N$ is a finite set of individuals, with no lower bound on their number.
Individuals have orderings.

statements.conclusion: As printed, this does not hold in full generality: with no individuals the majority rule violates Par, and with a single individual the majority relation is transitive at every profile and that individual is a dictator. The corrected statement requires at least two individuals.

statements.title: Majority rule satisfies Pareto and IIA yet may be intransitive
statements.statement:
Let $N$ be finite with **at least two individuals** and let $X$ contain at least three alternatives. The pairwise majority rule, under which $x$ is socially at least as good as $y$ when at least as many individuals strictly prefer $x$ to $y$ as $y$ to $x$, satisfies IIA and Par, is not dictatorial, and at some profile induces a relation that is not transitive.

With exactly one individual, the majority relation is transitive at every profile.

assumptions.text: $N$ is a finite set of individuals.
$X$ has at least three alternatives.
$N$ has at least two individuals.

statements.conclusion: Majority rule satisfies IIA and Par, is not dictatorial, and can be intransitive; so transitivity of the social order cannot be dropped from Arrow’s theorem.

statements.title: With two alternatives, majority rule is nondictatorial
statements.statement: As printed: for ${|X| = 2}$, the majority rule satisfies Par and IIA and induces a (trivially) transitive relation, giving a nondictatorial SWF. Read for every finite set of individuals: if $X$ has exactly two alternatives, some SWF satisfies Par and IIA and is not dictatorial.

assumptions.text: $X$ has exactly two alternatives.
$N$ is a finite set of individuals, with no lower bound on their number.

statements.conclusion: Some SWF satisfies Par and IIA and is not dictatorial. As printed, this does not hold for a single individual, since then every SWF satisfying Par and IIA is dictatorial; the corrected statement, with at least two individuals, is part 2 of the main result above.

statements.title: Social choice functions, straightforwardness and procedure invariance
statements.statement:
1. A *social choice function* (SCF) $C$ assigns an alternative $C(\succ_1, \dots, \succ_n) \in X$ to every profile.
2. $C$ is *straightforward* if no individual ever gains by misrepresenting his preferences: for every profile, every individual $i$ and every report $\succ_i'$, it is not the case that $C(\succ_1, \dots, \succ_i', \dots, \succ_n) \succ_i C(\succ_1, \dots, \succ_i, \dots, \succ_n)$.
3. Let $Ch$ assign a choice function to every profile. $Ch$ satisfies *unanimity* if for every profile, every choice set $A$ and all ${x, y \in A}$: if ${y \succ_i x}$ for every $i$, then $x$ is not chosen from $A$.
4. $Ch$ is *invariant to the procedure* if, for every profile and every choice set $A$ split into two nonempty disjoint sets $A'$ and $A''$, choosing from $A'$ and from $A''$ and then choosing between the two picks gives the same outcome as choosing from $A$ directly.

assumptions.text: $X$ is a set of alternatives, and each individual in $N$ has an ordering of $X$.
Parts 3 and 4: $Ch$ assigns a choice function to every profile.

statements.title: Unanimity and procedure invariance force a dictatorship
statements.statement: As printed: Dutta, Jackson, and Le Breton (2001) show that only dictatorships satisfy both unanimity and invariance to the procedure, for a function $Ch$ that assigns a choice function to every profile. No condition is stated on the number of alternatives or on the domain of choice sets.

assumptions.text: $X$ is a set of alternatives, and each individual of a finite set $N$ has an ordering.
$Ch$ assigns a choice function to every profile.
$Ch$ satisfies unanimity.
$Ch$ is invariant to the procedure.

statements.conclusion: $Ch$ is a dictatorship. As printed, this does not hold in full generality (see the counterexample).

statements.title: Unanimity and procedure invariance without a dictator
statements.statement:
Let ${X = \{0, 1\}}$, let $N$ have three individuals, and let the choice sets be all nonempty subsets of $X$. The rule that, from a set containing both alternatives, picks $1$ only when every individual strictly prefers $1$ to $0$, and $0$ otherwise, satisfies unanimity and invariance to the procedure; but no individual is a dictator, in the sense that the pick from every set is that individual’s best element of the set at every profile.

With two alternatives every choice function is path independent, so invariance to the procedure holds automatically, and unanimity alone already admits a rule with no dictator.
statements.conclusion: The printed statement does not hold with two alternatives and three individuals.

statements.title: Arrow’s theorem for choice rules (Dutta–Jackson–Le Breton)
statements.statement: Let $N$ be finite, let $X$ contain **at least three** alternatives, and let $Ch$ assign to every profile a choice function whose domain **contains every nonempty finite subset of** $X$. If $Ch$ satisfies unanimity, invariance to the procedure and **independence of infeasible alternatives** (whenever two profiles rank the alternatives of a choice set $A$ in the same way, the choice from $A$ is the same at both), then some individual $d$ is a dictator: at every profile, the choice from every set $A$ is $d$’s best element of $A$.

assumptions.text: $N$ is a finite set of individuals.
$Ch$ assigns a choice function to every profile.
$X$ has at least three alternatives.
Every nonempty finite subset of $X$ is an admissible choice set.
$Ch$ satisfies unanimity.
$Ch$ is invariant to the procedure.
$Ch$ satisfies independence of infeasible alternatives.

statements.conclusion: One individual’s ordering determines every choice.

statements.title: Every straightforward SCF is a dictatorship
statements.statement: As printed: the Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem states that any straightforward SCF is a dictatorship, i.e. a function that consistently picks the dictator’s most preferred alternatives. No condition is stated on the number of alternatives or on the range of the SCF.

assumptions.text: $X$ is a set of alternatives, with no condition.
$N$ is a finite set of individuals.
$C$ is a straightforward social choice function.

statements.conclusion: $C$ is a dictatorship. As printed, this does not hold in full generality (see the counterexample).

statements.title: A straightforward social choice function with no dictator
statements.statement: Let $X$ contain two distinct alternatives $a$ and $b$, and $N$ two distinct individuals. The SCF that picks $b$ when every individual strictly prefers $b$ to $a$, and $a$ otherwise, is straightforward, but there is no individual whose most preferred alternative it always picks, whether “most preferred” is taken among the alternatives the rule can select or among all of $X$. When “most preferred” means best in all of $X$, the printed statement does not hold for any number of individuals; and some SCF is not straightforward, so the hypothesis is not vacuous.
statements.conclusion: The printed statement does not hold for any such $X$ and $N$.

statements.title: Gibbard–Satterthwaite: strategy-proof onto SCFs are dictatorial
statements.statement: Let $N$ be finite and let $X$ contain **at least three** alternatives. If $C$ is a straightforward SCF that is **onto** $X$ (every alternative is chosen at some profile), then there is an individual $i$ such that at every profile $C$ picks $i$’s most preferred alternative in $X$.

assumptions.text: $N$ is a finite set of individuals.
$C$ is a social choice function.
$X$ has at least three alternatives.
$C$ is straightforward.
$C$ is onto $X$.

statements.conclusion: $C$ is dictatorial: it always picks the top alternative of one fixed individual.

statements.title: Pareto and monotonicity force a dictatorship
statements.statement: As printed: consider a change in a profile so that an alternative $a$, which individual $i$ ranked below $b$, is now ranked by $i$ above $b$. Monotonicity requires that there is no alternative $c$ such that this change lowers the ranking of $a$ relative to $c$. Muller and Satterthwaite (1977)’s theorem shows that the only SWFs satisfying Par and monotonicity are dictatorships. No condition on the number of alternatives is stated.

assumptions.text: $X$ is a set of alternatives, with no condition on its size.
$N$ is a finite set of individuals.
$F$ is a social welfare function satisfying Par.
$F$ satisfies monotonicity, as glossed above.

statements.conclusion: $F$ is dictatorial. As printed, this does not hold in full generality: it does not hold with two alternatives (see the counterexample).

statements.title: With two alternatives, majority rule is monotone and not dictatorial
statements.statement: Let $X$ have two alternatives and $N$ three individuals. The majority rule satisfies Par and monotonicity in its strongest reading (when individual $i$ moves $a$ above $b$, every strict or weak social preference for $a$ over any $c$ persists), and it is not dictatorial. The printed statement also does not hold under every weaker reading of the monotonicity gloss, under any condition implied by Par and IIA, and under any condition that the majority rule satisfies.
statements.conclusion: The printed statement does not hold with two alternatives and three individuals.

statements.title: Pareto and strong positive association force a dictatorship
statements.statement: Let $N$ be finite and let $X$ contain **at least three** alternatives. Every SWF $F$ that satisfies Par and **strong positive association** is dictatorial. Here $F$ satisfies strong positive association if, whenever profiles $P$ and $P'$ and an alternative $a$ are such that every alternative an individual ranks strictly below $a$ in $P$ is still ranked strictly below $a$ by that individual in $P'$, then for every $c$, a strict social preference for $a$ over $c$ at $P$ persists at $P'$, and so does a weak one.

assumptions.text: $N$ is a finite set of individuals.
$F$ is a social welfare function.
$X$ has at least three alternatives.
$F$ satisfies Par.
$F$ satisfies strong positive association, in place of the informally glossed monotonicity.

statements.conclusion: $F$ is dictatorial.

statements.title: Indifference classes partition the set of alternatives

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$: reflexive, complete and transitive.

statements.title: Kreps's strict preference is equivalent to a preference relation
statements.statement:
Call a relation $P$ on a set $X$ a *Kreps preference* if it is **asymmetric** (never both $x\,P\,y$ and $y\,P\,x$) and **negatively transitive** (if $x\,P\,y$, then for every $z$, $x\,P\,z$ or $z\,P\,y$).

1. If $\succsim$ is a preference relation, its strict part, ${x \succ y \iff (x \succsim y}$ and not ${y \succsim x)}$, is a Kreps preference.
2. If $P$ is a Kreps preference, the relation $x \succsim y \iff \neg\, (y\,P\,x)$ is a preference relation: reflexive, complete and transitive.
3. The two translations are mutually inverse: from $\succsim$ to its strict part and back returns $\succsim$, and from $P$ to $\succsim$ and back to the strict part returns $P$.

assumptions.text: From the traditional side: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
From Kreps's side: $P$ is asymmetric and negatively transitive.

statements.title: A menu preference satisfying both properties
statements.statement:
Let $Z$ be a finite set and $X$ the set of its nonempty subsets ("menus"). For a preference relation $\succsim$ on $X$ consider

- **Property 1**: if ${A \succsim B}$ and $C$ is disjoint from $A$ and $B$, then ${A \cup C \succsim B \cup C}$; and if ${A \succ B}$ and $C$ is disjoint from $A$ and $B$, then ${A \cup C \succ B \cup C}$.
- **Property 2**: if ${\{x\} \succ \{y\}}$ for every ${y \in A}$, then ${A \cup \{x\} \succ A}$; and if ${\{y\} \succ \{x\}}$ for every ${y \in A}$, then ${A \succ A \cup \{x\}}$.

There are a finite nonempty set $Z$ and a preference relation $\succsim$ on its menus satisfying both Property 1 and Property 2.

statements.title: Property 1 without Property 2
statements.statement: There are a finite nonempty set $Z$ and a preference relation $\succsim$ on the nonempty subsets of $Z$ that satisfies Property 1 (monotonicity under disjoint union) but not Property 2 (adding a best or worst alternative).

statements.title: Property 2 without Property 1
statements.statement: There are a finite nonempty set $Z$ and a preference relation $\succsim$ on the nonempty subsets of $Z$ that satisfies Property 2 (adding a best or worst alternative) but not Property 1 (monotonicity under disjoint union).

statements.title: Kannai–Peleg: three ranked singletons rule out both properties
statements.statement:
Let $Z$ be finite and let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on the nonempty subsets of $Z$. If there are ${x, y, z \in Z}$ with
$$\{x\} \succ \{y\} \succ \{z\},$$
then $\succsim$ does not satisfy both Property 1 and Property 2.

- **Property 1**: if ${A \succsim B}$ and $C$ is disjoint from $A$ and $B$, then ${A \cup C \succsim B \cup C}$; and if ${A \succ B}$ and $C$ is disjoint from $A$ and $B$, then ${A \cup C \succ B \cup C}$.
- **Property 2**: if ${\{x\} \succ \{y\}}$ for every ${y \in A}$, then ${A \cup \{x\} \succ A}$; and if ${\{y\} \succ \{x\}}$ for every ${y \in A}$, then ${A \succ A \cup \{x\}}$.

assumptions.text: $Z$ is a finite set.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on the nonempty subsets of $Z$.
Three singletons are strictly ranked: ${\{x\} \succ \{y\} \succ \{z\}}$ for some ${x, y, z \in Z}$.

entries.title: Extending an acyclic relation to an ordering
entries.name: Szpilrajn’s extension theorem

statements.title: An acyclic relation on a finite set extends to a complete ordering
statements.statement:
Let $X$ be a finite set and $\succ$ an asymmetric relation on $X$ with no cycle: there are no $x_1, \dots, x_K$, ${K > 2}$, with
$$x_1 \succ x_2 \succ \cdots \succ x_K \succ x_1.$$
Then there is a complete ordering ${\succ'}$ on $X$ — complete on distinct pairs, asymmetric and transitive — that extends $\succ$: ${x \succ y}$ implies ${x \succ' y}$.

assumptions.text: $X$ is finite.
$\succ$ is asymmetric: never both ${x \succ y}$ and ${y \succ x}$.
$\succ$ has no cycle $x_1 \succ x_2 \succ \cdots \succ x_K \succ\nobreak x_1$ of length ${K > 2}$.

statements.title: Unanimity over complete orderings is asymmetric and transitive
statements.statement:
Let ${\succ_1, \dots, \succ_n}$, with ${n \ge 1}$, be complete orderings (complete on distinct pairs, asymmetric and transitive) of a set $X$, and define
$$x \succ y \iff x \succ_i y \text{ for every } i.$$
Then $\succ$ is asymmetric and transitive.

assumptions.text: There is at least one criterion: ${n \ge 1}$.
Each criterion $\succ_i$ is a complete ordering: complete on distinct pairs, asymmetric and transitive.

statements.title: On {a, b, c}, ranking only a above b is an intersection of orderings
statements.statement:
Let ${X = \{a, b, c\}}$ and let $\succ$ be the relation under which only ${a \succ b}$ holds (the pairs $b, c$ and $a, c$ are not compared). There are complete orderings ${\succ_1, \dots, \succ_n}$ of $X$ such that
$$x \succ y \iff x \succ_i y \text{ for every } i.$$

statements.title: Finite strict partial orders are intersections of orderings
statements.statement:
Let $X$ be finite and $\succ$ an asymmetric, transitive relation on $X$. Then there are $n$ and complete orderings ${\succ_1, \dots, \succ_n}$ of $X$ such that
$$x \succ y \iff x \succ_i y \text{ for every } i.$$

assumptions.text: $X$ is finite.
$\succ$ is asymmetric.
$\succ$ is transitive.

statements.title: The Shepard scale and cyclic judgments
statements.statement: Listen to a demonstration of the Shepard scale, a sequence of tones that seems to rise endlessly, and look for analogies.

statements.title: Utility representations and four definitions of continuity
statements.statement:
- **(a)** It is not true that whenever $U$ and $V$ both represent a preference relation $\succsim$ on a set $X$, there is a strictly monotonic ${f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}}$ — strictly increasing or strictly decreasing on all of $\mathbb{R}$ — with ${V(x) = f(U(x))}$ for every $x$.
- **(b)** There are a set ${X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n}$, a continuous preference relation $\succsim$ on $X$ and a function ${u : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ that represents $\succsim$ but is not continuous.
- **(c)** On ${X = \mathbb{R}}$, the preference represented by ${u(x) = \lfloor x \rfloor}$, that is $x \succsim y \iff \lfloor x \rfloor \ge \lfloor y \rfloor$, is not continuous.
- **(d)** For a preference relation $\succsim$ on a metric space $X$, continuity in the sense C1 — whenever ${a \succ b}$ there are balls around $a$ and around $b$ such that ${x \succ y}$ for every $x$ in the first and $y$ in the second (equivalently C2, a closed graph) — holds if and only if (C3) the sets ${\{y : y \succsim x\}}$ and ${\{y : x \succsim y\}}$ are closed for every $x$, and if and only if (C4) the sets ${\{y : y \succ x\}}$ and ${\{y : x \succ y\}}$ are open for every $x$.

assumptions.text: In (d): $X$ is a metric space and $\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.

entries.title: Integer-valued utility on a countable set

statements.title: A preference on a countable set with no integer-valued utility
statements.statement: There are a countable set $X$ and a preference relation $\succsim$ on $X$ such that no function ${u : X \to \mathbb{Z}}$ represents $\succsim$; that is, for every ${u : X \to \mathbb{Z}}$ the equivalence $x \succsim y \iff u(x) \ge\nobreak u(y)$ fails for some $x, y$.

statements.title: Continuous preferences: an indifferent point on every segment
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a continuous preference relation on ${X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n}$, let ${x, z \in \mathbb{R}^n}$ be such that the segment $[x, z] = \{\lambda x + {(1 - \lambda)} z : \lambda \in [0,1]\}$ lies in $X$, and let ${y \in X}$ with
$$x \succsim y \succsim z.$$
Then some point ${m \in [x, z]}$ satisfies ${y \sim m}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a continuous preference relation on ${X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n}$ (C1, equivalently C2).
The segment from $x$ to $z$ lies in $X$.
${x \succsim y}$ and ${y \succsim z}$.

statements.title: Power-sum preferences converge to the max preference
statements.statement: On $\mathbb{R}^2_+$ let $\succsim^n$ be represented by $u_n(x_1, x_2) = x_1^n +\nobreak x_2^n$ and $\succsim^*$ by $u^*(x_1, x_2) = \max\{x_1, x_2\}$. Then $\succsim^n$ converges to $\succsim^*$: for all $x, y$ with ${x \succ^* y}$ there is $N$ such that ${x \succ^n y}$ for every ${n > N}$.

entries.title: Utility with a threshold for “much preferred”

statements.title: Representing an extended preference on a finite set
statements.statement:
Let $X$ be finite. An *extended preference* is a pair ${(\succsim, \succ\!\succ)}$ where $\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$ and ${\succ\!\succ}$ ("much preferred") is a transitive relation with ${x \succ\!\succ y \Rightarrow x \succ y}$, satisfying extended transitivity: if ${x \succ\!\succ y}$ and ${y \succsim z}$, or ${x \succsim y}$ and ${y \succ\!\succ z}$, then ${x \succ\!\succ z}$. Then there is ${u : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ such that for all ${x, y \in X}$:
$$\begin{aligned} u(x) = u(y) &\iff x \sim y, \\ u(x) - u(y) > 0 &\iff x \succ y, \\ u(x) - u(y) > 1 &\iff x \succ\!\succ y. \end{aligned}$$

assumptions.text: $X$ is finite.
$\succsim$ is a preference relation on $X$.
${\succ\!\succ}$ is transitive.
${\succ\!\succ}$ refines strict preference: ${x \succ\!\succ y}$ implies ${x \succ y}$.
Extended transitivity: ${x \succ\!\succ y}$ and ${y \succsim z}$ imply ${x \succ\!\succ z}$; ${x \succsim y}$ and ${y \succ\!\succ z}$ imply ${x \succ\!\succ z}$.

statements.title: A numerical representation of “approximately the same”
statements.statement:
For a relation $S$ on ${X = [0,1]}$ consider:
(S-1) $aSa$; (S-2) ${aSb \Rightarrow bSa}$; (S-3) the graph of $S$ is closed in ${X \times X}$; (S-4) if ${d \ge c \ge b \ge a}$ and $dSa$, then $cSb$; (S-5) each $a$ has an open interval around it such that $xSa$ for every ${x \in X}$ in the interval; (S-6) $M(a) = {\max\{x : xSa\}}$ and $m(a) = {\min\{x : aSx\}}$ exist, are weakly increasing, and ${f(a) < f(b)}$ for ${f = M, m}$ whenever ${a < b}$ and neither $f(a)$ nor $f(b)$ equals $0$ or $1$.

- **(b)** For every ${\varepsilon > 0}$, the relation $a S_\varepsilon b \iff |b - a| \le\nobreak \varepsilon$ satisfies (S-1)–(S-6).
- **(c)** If $S$ satisfies (S-1)–(S-6) and ${\varepsilon > 0}$, there is a strictly increasing, continuous ${H : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}}$ with $aSb \iff |H(a) - H(b)| \le\nobreak \varepsilon$ for all $a, b$.

assumptions.text: In (b): ${\varepsilon > 0}$.
In (c): $S$ satisfies (S-1)–(S-6).
In (c): ${\varepsilon > 0}$.

statements.title: Five decision procedures tested for rationality
statements.statement:
Choice problems are the sets $A$ of a domain $\mathcal{D}$ of nonempty subsets of $X$.

- **(a)** If $\succsim$ is any preference relation — for example, ranking by another person's suffering — and every ${A \in \mathcal{D}}$ has a unique $\succsim$-best element, then choosing that element is a rationalizable choice function.
- **(b)** There are a set $X$, a domain and two complete orderings (the children's rankings) such that the correspondence choosing, in each menu, the alternatives with the lowest total rank, ranks counted within the menu, is not rationalizable.
- **(c)** For any function ${d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}}$ (no metric axioms needed) and ideal point $x^*$, if every ${A \in \mathcal{D}}$ has a unique element minimizing ${d(\cdot, x^*)}$, choosing it is a rationalizable choice function.
- **(d)** Not posed formally: a choice problem is a set, in which no alternative appears more often than another.
- **(e)** There are a set $X$, a domain and a complete ordering $O$ such that a choice function selecting the $O$-median of every menu (the lower median when the menu has an even number of elements) is not rationalizable.

assumptions.text: In (a): $\succsim$ is a preference relation and every ${A \in \mathcal{D}}$ has a unique $\succsim$-best element.
In (c): every ${A \in \mathcal{D}}$ has a unique element closest to the ideal point $x^*$.

statements.title: Path independence, imposed where the sets lie in the domain

assumptions.text: In (a): $\succsim$ is a preference relation and ${C_\succsim(A) \neq \emptyset}$ for every ${A \in \mathcal{D}}$.
in (c), the domain $\mathcal{D}$ contains every nonempty subset of $X$.
In (c): $C$ is a path-independent choice function.

statements.title: Path independence with the pieces required to lie in the domain

assumptions.text: In (a): $\succsim$ is a preference relation and ${C_\succsim(A) \neq \emptyset}$ for every ${A \in \mathcal{D}}$.
in (a), the domain $\mathcal{D}$ contains every nonempty subset of $X$.
In (c): $C$ is a choice function that is path independent in this reading.

statements.title: Path independence under every reading of the domain clauses

assumptions.text: in (a) and (c), outside the cases listed, the domain $\mathcal{D}$ contains every nonempty subset of $X$.
In (a): $\succsim$ is a preference relation and ${C_\succsim(A) \neq \emptyset}$ for every ${A \in \mathcal{D}}$.
In (c): $C$ is a choice function that is path independent in the given reading.

statements.title: Rational choice is path independent, pieces required
statements.statement: As printed, read with the domain memberships required: for every context $(X, \mathcal{D})$ and every preference relation $\succsim$ whose best sets are nonempty on $\mathcal{D}$, the rational correspondence $C_\succsim$ is path independent.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation and ${C_\succsim(A) \neq \emptyset}$ for every ${A \in \mathcal{D}}$.

statements.title: Rational choice is path independent, under each reading
statements.statement: As printed, under each of the sixteen readings of the domain memberships: for every context $(X, \mathcal{D})$ and every preference relation $\succsim$ whose best sets are nonempty on $\mathcal{D}$, the rational correspondence $C_\succsim$ is path independent.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation and ${C_\succsim(A) \neq \emptyset}$ for every ${A \in \mathcal{D}}$.

statements.title: Two different choice functions that are not path independent
statements.statement: There are a set $X$, a domain $\mathcal{D}$ and two choice functions $C_1, C_2$ on $(X, \mathcal{D})$, differing at some ${A \in \mathcal{D}}$, neither of which is path independent (the equation imposed where the sets lie in $\mathcal{D}$).

statements.title: Path independence implies condition α, on any domain
statements.statement: As printed, in the reading that imposes the equation only where the sets lie in $\mathcal{D}$: on every context $(X, \mathcal{D})$, a path-independent choice function satisfies condition $\alpha$.

assumptions.text: $C$ is a choice function that is path independent in this reading.

statements.title: Path independence implies condition α, under each reading
statements.statement: As printed, under each of the sixteen readings of the domain memberships: on every context $(X, \mathcal{D})$, a choice function that is path independent in that reading satisfies condition $\alpha$.

assumptions.text: $C$ is a choice function that is path independent in the given reading.

entries.title: Three choice correspondences and the weak axiom

statements.title: Three choice correspondences and the weak axiom

assumptions.text: $X$ is finite; $V$ is an arbitrary real function on $X$, ties allowed.

entries.title: Choosing from the most common class

statements.title: The most-common-class procedure: an ordering on pairs, not always rational
statements.statement:
A decision maker has a strict ordering $\succ$ of $X$ and a class function ${\mathrm{class} : X \to \mathbb{N}}$. From a finite menu $A$ he chooses the $\succ$-best element among those whose class is the most common in $A$; when several classes are equally common, he uses the one with the highest class number.

- **(a)** The relation ${x\,P\,y \iff x \neq y}$ and $x$ is chosen from $\{x, y\}$ is a strict ordering: complete on distinct pairs, asymmetric and transitive.
- **(b)** For some $X$, $\succ$ and class function, the procedure — a choice function on the nonempty finite subsets of $X$ — is not rationalizable.

assumptions.text: In (a): $\succ$ is a strict ordering of $X$ (complete, asymmetric and transitive); the class function is arbitrary.

statements.title: Two threshold procedures: one always rational, one not
statements.statement:
Let ${u, v : X \to \mathbb{R}}$ be one-to-one and, for a menu $A$, let $a^*$ maximize $u$ and $b^*$ maximize $v$ on $A$.

- **(a)** Procedure (a) chooses $a^*$ if ${v(a^*) \ge v^*}$ and $b^*$ otherwise. For some $X$, domain, one-to-one $u, v$ and threshold $v^*$, a choice function that follows procedure (a) is not rationalizable.
- **(b)** Procedure (b) chooses $a^*$ if ${u(a^*) \ge u^*}$ and $b^*$ otherwise. On every context, for one-to-one $u, v$ and every threshold $u^*$, any choice function that follows procedure (b) is rationalizable.

assumptions.text: In (b): $u$ and $v$ are one-to-one.
In (b): from every ${A \in \mathcal{D}}$ the choice function picks $a^*$ if ${u(a^*) \ge u^*}$ and $b^*$ otherwise.

statements.title: Choice from lists: Property I and its relatives
statements.statement:
A *list* is a nonempty finite sequence of elements of $X$, and a list choice function $C$ picks an element of each list. $C$ satisfies **Property I** if $C(\langle L_1, \dots, L_m \rangle) = C(\langle C(L_1), \dots, C(L_m) \rangle)$ for all lists $L_1, \dots, L_m$, where $\langle L_1, \dots, L_m \rangle$ is their concatenation. $C$ satisfies **Order Invariance** if reordering a list leaves the choice unchanged, and **Duplication Invariance** if deleting an element that appears elsewhere in the list leaves the choice unchanged. Given a one-to-one ${u : X \to \mathbb{R}}$, $C$ *accommodates a longer list* if $u(C(L')) \ge\nobreak u(C(L))$ whenever $L'$ extends $L$ (that is, ${L' = \langle L, M \rangle}$ for a list $M$), with strict inequality for some such pair.

- **(a)** Some list choice function on a finite $X$ satisfies Property I, and some list choice function on a finite $X$ violates it.
- **(b)** Every list choice function satisfying Duplication Invariance satisfies Order Invariance, for any $X$.
- **(d)** On some finite $X$, with a one-to-one $u$, some list choice function accommodates a longer list.
- **(e)** On some finite $X$, with a one-to-one $u$, some list choice function satisfies Property I but does not accommodate a longer list.

assumptions.text: In (b): $C$ satisfies Duplication Invariance.

statements.title: Two different list choice functions with Property I
statements.statement:
A *list* is a nonempty finite sequence of elements of $X$, and a list choice function $C$ picks an element of each list. $C$ satisfies **Property I** if $C(\langle L_1, \dots, L_m \rangle) = C(\langle C(L_1), \dots, C(L_m) \rangle)$ for all lists $L_1, \dots, L_m$, where $\langle L_1, \dots, L_m \rangle$ is their concatenation.

On some finite set $X$ there are two list choice functions $C_1, C_2$, differing on some list, both satisfying Property I.

statements.title: Two different list choice functions violating Property I
statements.statement:
A *list* is a nonempty finite sequence of elements of $X$, and a list choice function $C$ picks an element of each list. $C$ satisfies **Property I** if $C(\langle L_1, \dots, L_m \rangle) = C(\langle C(L_1), \dots, C(L_m) \rangle)$ for all lists $L_1, \dots, L_m$, where $\langle L_1, \dots, L_m \rangle$ is their concatenation.

On some finite set $X$ there are two list choice functions $C_1, C_2$, differing on some list, neither of which satisfies Property I.

statements.title: Duplication Invariance and Property I mean maximizing an ordering
statements.statement:
A *list* is a nonempty finite sequence of elements of $X$, and a list choice function $C$ picks an element of each list. $C$ satisfies **Property I** if $C(\langle L_1, \dots, L_m \rangle) = C(\langle C(L_1), \dots, C(L_m) \rangle)$ for all lists $L_1, \dots, L_m$, where $\langle L_1, \dots, L_m \rangle$ is their concatenation. $C$ satisfies **Duplication Invariance** if deleting an element that appears elsewhere in a list leaves the choice unchanged.

Let $X$ be finite. A list choice function $C$ satisfies Duplication Invariance and Property I if and only if there is a complete ordering $\succ$ of $X$ such that, for every list $L$, ${C(L) \succ y}$ for every entry ${y \neq C(L)}$ of $L$.

assumptions.text: $X$ is finite.

statements.title: Two different list choice functions that reward longer lists
statements.statement:
A *list* is a nonempty finite sequence of elements of $X$, and a list choice function $C$ picks an element of each list. $C$ satisfies **Property I** if $C(\langle L_1, \dots, L_m \rangle) = C(\langle C(L_1), \dots, C(L_m) \rangle)$ for all lists $L_1, \dots, L_m$, where $\langle L_1, \dots, L_m \rangle$ is their concatenation. Given a one-to-one ${u : X \to \mathbb{R}}$, $C$ *accommodates a longer list* if $u(C(L')) \ge\nobreak u(C(L))$ whenever $L'$ extends $L$ (that is, ${L' = \langle L, M \rangle}$ for a list $M$), with strict inequality for some such pair.

On some finite set $X$, with a one-to-one ${u : X \to \mathbb{R}}$, there are two list choice functions $C_1, C_2$, differing on some list, both of which accommodate a longer list.

statements.title: Two choice functions with Property I that ignore longer lists
statements.statement:
A *list* is a nonempty finite sequence of elements of $X$, and a list choice function $C$ picks an element of each list. $C$ satisfies **Property I** if $C(\langle L_1, \dots, L_m \rangle) = C(\langle C(L_1), \dots, C(L_m) \rangle)$ for all lists $L_1, \dots, L_m$, where $\langle L_1, \dots, L_m \rangle$ is their concatenation. Given a one-to-one ${u : X \to \mathbb{R}}$, $C$ *accommodates a longer list* if $u(C(L')) \ge\nobreak u(C(L))$ whenever $L'$ extends $L$ (that is, ${L' = \langle L, M \rangle}$ for a list $M$), with strict inequality for some such pair.

On some finite set $X$, with a one-to-one ${u : X \to \mathbb{R}}$, there are two list choice functions $C_1, C_2$, differing on some list, each satisfying Property I and not accommodating a longer list.

statements.title: Lexicographic rationality is the reference-point property
statements.statement:
Let $X$ be finite and $c$ a choice function on all nonempty subsets of $X$.

- $c$ is *lexicographically rational* if there are an ordering $O$ of $X$ and orderings $\succ_a$, one for each ${a \in X}$, such that $c(A)$ is the $\succ_a$-maximal element of $A$, where $a$ is the $O$-maximal element of $A$.
- $c$ has the *reference-point property* if every $A$ contains some $a$ such that ${c(A'') = c(A')}$ whenever ${a \in A'' \subseteq A' \subseteq A}$ and ${c(A') \in A''}$.

Then $c$ is lexicographically rational if and only if it has the reference-point property.

assumptions.text: $X$ is finite.

statements.title: Part (b): a choice function with the reference-point property
statements.statement: There are a finite set $X$ and a choice function $c$ on its nonempty subsets that has the reference-point property: every $A$ contains some $a$ such that ${c(A'') = c(A')}$ whenever ${a \in A'' \subseteq A' \subseteq A}$ and ${c(A') \in A''}$.

entries.title: Choice by rationales (Cherepanov, Feddersen and Sandroni)

statements.title: The weak weak axiom characterizes choice by rationales
statements.statement:
Let $X$ be finite and $c$ a choice function on all nonempty subsets of $X$.

- $c$ satisfies **WWARP** if, whenever ${x \neq y}$, ${\{x, y\} \subseteq B_1 \subseteq B_2}$ and $c(\{x, y\}) = c(B_2) =\nobreak x$, we have ${c(B_1) \neq y}$.
- $c$ is *rationalized* if there are an asymmetric, complete (not necessarily transitive) relation $\succ$ and finitely many rationales ${\succ_1, \dots, \succ_K}$, each asymmetric and transitive, such that $c(A)$ is the $\succ$-best element among the alternatives that at least one rationale ranks above every other element of $A$.

Then $c$ satisfies WWARP if and only if it is rationalized.

assumptions.text: $X$ is finite.

statements.title: Part (b): the warm-glow procedure satisfies WWARP
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim_M$ (moral) and $\succsim_S$ (selfish) be preference relations on a finite set $X$, each with a unique best element in every nonempty ${A \subseteq X}$, and let ${l : X 	o X}$ satisfy (i) ${s \succsim_S l(s)}$ and (ii) $s \succsim_S s' \Rightarrow l(s) \succsim_S
obreak l(s')$. In each menu $A$, with $m$ the $\succsim_M$-best and $s$ the $\succsim_S$-best element, the *warm-glow procedure* chooses $m$ if ${m \succsim_S l(s)}$ and $s$ otherwise. The warm-glow procedure satisfies WWARP: whenever ${x 
eq y}$, ${\{x, y\} \subseteq B_1 \subseteq B_2}$ and $c(\{x, y\}) = c(B_2) =
obreak x$, we have ${c(B_1) 
eq y}$.

assumptions.text: $X$ is finite.
$\succsim_M$ and $\succsim_S$ are preference relations, each with a unique best element in every nonempty ${A \subseteq X}$.
(i) ${s \succsim_S l(s)}$ for every $s$.
(ii) ${s \succsim_S s'}$ implies ${l(s) \succsim_S l(s')}$.

statements.title: Part (c): the warm-glow procedure is rationalized, directly
statements.statement: Let $\succsim_M$ (moral) and $\succsim_S$ (selfish) be preference relations on a finite set $X$, each with a unique best element in every nonempty ${A \subseteq X}$, and let ${l : X \to X}$ satisfy (i) ${s \succsim_S l(s)}$ and (ii) $s \succsim_S s' \Rightarrow l(s) \succsim_S\nobreak l(s')$. In each menu $A$, with $m$ the $\succsim_M$-best and $s$ the $\succsim_S$-best element, the *warm-glow procedure* chooses $m$ if ${m \succsim_S l(s)}$ and $s$ otherwise. The warm-glow procedure is rationalized: there are an asymmetric, complete relation $\succ$ and finitely many asymmetric, transitive rationales such that the chosen element of every menu is the $\succ$-best among the alternatives that at least one rationale ranks above every other element of the menu.

assumptions.text: $X$ is finite.
$\succsim_M$ and $\succsim_S$ are preference relations, each with a unique best element in every nonempty ${A \subseteq X}$.
(i) ${s \succsim_S l(s)}$ for every $s$.
(ii) ${s \succsim_S s'}$ implies ${l(s) \succsim_S l(s')}$.

statements.title: Choice probabilities sum to one on every subset
statements.statement:
As printed: on a set $X$, a probabilistic choice function gives each ${A \subseteq X}$ and each ${a \in A}$ a weight ${C(a \mid A) > 0}$, and for each ${A \subseteq X}$ these weights add up to one:
$$\sum_{a \in A} C(a \mid A) = 1.$$

statements.title: Luce's choice axiom yields the ratio representation
statements.statement:
A probabilistic choice function assigns ${C(a \mid A) > 0}$ to each ${a \in A \subseteq X}$, with ${\sum_{a \in A} C(a \mid A) = 1}$ for every nonempty $A$; write $C{(B \mid A)} = \sum_{a \in B} C{(a \mid A)}$. It satisfies **path independence (PI)** if, whenever ${a \in B \subseteq A}$,
$$C(a \mid A) = C(a \mid B)\, C(B \mid A).$$

- **(a)** Some probabilistic choice function violates PI.
- **(b)** If $C$ satisfies PI, there is ${v : X \to (0, \infty)}$ such that, for every menu $A$ and every ${a \in A}$,
$$C(a \mid A) = \frac{v(a)}{\sum_{x \in A} v(x)}.$$

assumptions.text: the normalization ${\sum_{a \in A} C(a \mid A) = 1}$ is imposed on nonempty menus only.
In (b): $C$ satisfies PI.

statements.title: Two probabilistic choice functions that violate Luce's axiom
statements.statement: With probabilistic choice functions normalized on nonempty menus, as in the corrected definition: there are a set $X$ and two probabilistic choice functions $C_1, C_2$ on $X$, differing at some ${a \in A}$, neither of which satisfies PI, $C{(a \mid A)} = C{(a \mid B)}\, C{(B \mid A)}$ for ${a \in B \subseteq A}$.

assumptions.text: probabilistic choice functions are normalized on nonempty menus only.

entries.title: Strict convexity on the unit interval

statements.title: On the unit interval, strict convexity means a single peak
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a continuous preference relation on ${X = [0,1]}$. Then $\succsim$ is strictly convex — ${a \succsim y}$, ${b \succsim y}$, ${a \neq b}$ and ${\lambda \in (0,1)}$ imply ${\lambda a + (1 - \lambda) b \succ y}$ — if and only if there is ${x^* \in [0,1]}$ such that
$$\begin{aligned} b \succ a \quad &\text{whenever } a < b \le x^*, \\ b \succ a \quad &\text{whenever } x^* \le b < a. \end{aligned}$$

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a continuous preference relation on $[0,1]$.

statements.title: Monotone, quasi-linear, homothetic: lexicographic-linear preferences
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ be a preference relation on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$; continuity is not assumed. Then $\succsim$ is

- strongly monotone (${x \ge y}$ coordinatewise and ${x \neq y}$ imply ${x \succ y}$),
- quasi-linear in both commodities ($x \succsim y \iff x + \varepsilon e_k \succsim y + \varepsilon e_k$ for ${k = 1, 2}$ and every ${\varepsilon \ge 0}$), and
- homothetic (${x \succsim y}$ implies ${tx \succsim ty}$ for every ${t \ge 0}$)

if and only if there are ${a, b \in \mathbb{R}^2}$ such that, writing ${\ell(x) = (a \cdot x,\ b \cdot x)}$, we have ${\ell(d) >_{\mathrm{lex}} (0, 0)}$ for every nonzero ${d \in \mathbb{R}^2_+}$ and
$$x \succsim y \iff \ell(x) \ge_{\mathrm{lex}} \ell(y).$$

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a preference relation on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$; no continuity is assumed.

entries.title: Convexity as a diminishing rate of substitution

statements.title: Convexity 4 is equivalent to convexity
statements.statement:
A preference $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$ satisfies *convexity 4* if, for every bundle ${x = (x_1, x_2)}$, every ${\varepsilon > 0}$ and all $\delta_1, \delta_2$,
$$\begin{aligned} x &\sim (x_1 - \varepsilon, x_2 + \delta_1) \\ &\sim (x_1 - 2\varepsilon, x_2 + \delta_1 + \delta_2) \end{aligned}$$
implies ${\delta_2 \ge \delta_1}$. If $\succsim$ is strongly monotone and continuous, it satisfies convexity 4 if and only if it is convex: ${x \succsim y}$ and ${\alpha \in (0,1)}$ imply ${\alpha x + (1 - \alpha) y \succsim y}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is strongly monotone: ${x \ge y}$ coordinatewise and ${x \neq y}$ imply ${x \succ y}$.
$\succsim$ is continuous.

statements.title: Quasi-linearity in every commodity gives a linear utility
statements.statement:
For every number of commodities $K$: let $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ be continuous, strongly monotone, and quasi-linear in every commodity — ${x \succsim y}$ implies ${x + \varepsilon e_k \succsim y + \varepsilon e_k}$ for every $k$ and every real $\varepsilon$ that keeps both bundles in $\mathbb{R}^K_+$. Then there is ${\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^K}$ with ${\alpha_k > 0}$ for all $k$ such that
$$u(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \alpha_k x_k$$
represents $\succsim$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is continuous.
$\succsim$ is strongly monotone.
$\succsim$ is quasi-linear in every commodity.

statements.title: Every bundle is indifferent to a point on the numeraire axis
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ be continuous, monotonic, strongly monotonic in commodity 1 (${x + \varepsilon e_1 \succ x}$ for ${\varepsilon > 0}$) and quasi-linear in commodity 1. Then for every bundle $x$ there is ${v(x) \ge 0}$ with
$$x \sim (v(x), 0, \dots, 0).$$

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is continuous.
$\succsim$ is monotonic: ${x \ge y}$ coordinatewise implies ${x \succsim y}$, and ${x_k > y_k}$ for all $k$ implies ${x \succ y}$.
$\succsim$ is strongly monotonic in commodity 1: ${x + \varepsilon e_1 \succ x}$ for every ${\varepsilon > 0}$.
$\succsim$ is quasi-linear in commodity 1: ${x \succsim y}$ implies ${x + \varepsilon e_1 \succsim y + \varepsilon e_1}$ for every real $\varepsilon$ that keeps both bundles in $\mathbb{R}^K_+$.

statements.title: Separable preferences satisfy condition S
statements.statement:
A preference on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ is *separable* if it is represented by an additive utility $u(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} v_k(x_k)$ for some functions ${v_k : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}}$. It satisfies *condition S* if for every set of commodities $J$ and all bundles $a, b, c, d$,
$$\begin{aligned} &(a_J, c_{-J}) \succsim (b_J, c_{-J}) \\ \iff {} &(a_J, d_{-J}) \succsim (b_J, d_{-J}), \end{aligned}$$
where $(x_J, y_{-J})$ takes the coordinates of $x$ in $J$ and those of $y$ outside $J$.

Every separable preference on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ satisfies condition S.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is separable: ${u(x) = \sum_k v_k(x_k)}$ represents it.

statements.title: Separable preferences on two goods satisfy the hexagon condition
statements.statement:
A preference on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ is *separable* if it is represented by an additive utility $u(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} v_k(x_k)$ for some functions ${v_k : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}}$. With ${K = 2}$, every separable preference satisfies the *hexagon condition*: for all nonnegative $a, b, c, d, e, f$,
$$\begin{gathered} (a, b) \succsim (c, d), \quad (c, e) \succsim (f, b) \\ \implies (a, e) \succsim (f, d). \end{gathered}$$

assumptions.text: ${K = 2}$ and $\succsim$ is separable.

statements.title: Condition S without separability
statements.statement:
A preference on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ is *separable* if it is represented by an additive utility $u(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} v_k(x_k)$ for some functions ${v_k : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}}$. It satisfies *condition S* if for every set of commodities $J$ and all bundles $a, b, c, d$,
$$\begin{aligned} &(a_J, c_{-J}) \succsim (b_J, c_{-J}) \\ \iff {} &(a_J, d_{-J}) \succsim (b_J, d_{-J}), \end{aligned}$$
where $(x_J, y_{-J})$ takes the coordinates of $x$ in $J$ and those of $y$ outside $J$.

There are $K$ and a continuous preference relation on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ that satisfies condition S but is not separable.

statements.title: The lexicographic preference is not differentiable
statements.statement:
For a preference $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ and a bundle $x$, $D(x)$ is the set of *improvement directions*: vectors $d$ such that, for some ${\lambda^* > 0}$, ${x + \lambda d \in X}$ and ${x + \lambda d \succ x}$ for all ${\lambda \in (0, \lambda^*)}$. In the book's sense, $\succsim$ is *differentiable* if at every $x$ there is a value vector ${v(x) \in \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ such that $D(x)$ is the set of directions $d$ with ${d \cdot v(x) > 0}$, among those that keep ${x + \lambda d}$ in $X$ for small ${\lambda > 0}$.

The lexicographic preference on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$, $x \succsim_L y \iff x_1 >\nobreak y_1$ or (${x_1 = y_1}$ and ${x_2 \ge y_2}$), is not differentiable: at some bundle $x$, no value vector $v(x)$ describes $D(x)$.

statements.title: Improvements as directions: flat indifference sets
statements.statement:
For a preference $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ and a bundle $x$, $D(x)$ is the set of *improvement directions*: vectors $d$ such that, for some ${\lambda^* > 0}$, ${x + \lambda d \in X}$ and ${x + \lambda d \succ x}$ for all ${\lambda \in (0, \lambda^*)}$. In the book's sense, $\succsim$ is *differentiable* if at every $x$ there is a value vector ${v(x) \in \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ such that $D(x)$ is the set of directions $d$ with ${d \cdot v(x) > 0}$, among those that keep ${x + \lambda d}$ in $X$ for small ${\lambda > 0}$.

Let $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ be monotonic, convex and differentiable, and let $F(x) = {\{d : x + d \in X\}}$ be the feasible full steps from $x$. Then $\succsim$ satisfies condition **(\*)**, $D(x) \cap F(x) = {\{d \in F(x) : x + d \succ x\}}$ at every $x$, if and only if it has flat indifference sets: for every $x$ there is ${v \in \mathbb{R}^K_+}$, ${v \neq 0}$, with
$$\{y : y \succ x\} = \{y : v \cdot y > v \cdot x\}.$$

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is monotonic: ${x \ge y}$ coordinatewise implies ${x \succsim y}$, and ${x_k > y_k}$ for all $k$ implies ${x \succ y}$.
$\succsim$ is convex: ${x \succsim y}$ and ${\alpha \in (0,1)}$ imply ${\alpha x + (1 - \alpha) y \succsim y}$.
$\succsim$ is differentiable in the book's sense.

condition (*) compares only full steps $d$ with ${x + d \in X}$. Without this restriction the equality $D(x) = {\{d : x + d \succ x\}}$ cannot hold for a monotonic, differentiable preference on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$, even at the bundle $(1,1)$.

statements.title: Negated improvement directions worsen, at every bundle
statements.statement:
For a preference $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ and a bundle $x$, $D(x)$ is the set of *improvement directions*: vectors $d$ such that, for some ${\lambda^* > 0}$, ${x + \lambda d \in X}$ and ${x + \lambda d \succ x}$ for all ${\lambda \in (0, \lambda^*)}$. In the book's sense, $\succsim$ is *differentiable* if at every $x$ there is a value vector ${v(x) \in \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ such that $D(x)$ is the set of directions $d$ with ${d \cdot v(x) > 0}$, among those that keep ${x + \lambda d}$ in $X$ for small ${\lambda > 0}$. $E(x)$ is the set of *worsening directions*: vectors $d$ such that, for some ${\varepsilon^* > 0}$, ${x + \varepsilon d \in X}$ and ${x + \varepsilon d \prec x}$ for all ${\varepsilon \in (0, \varepsilon^*]}$.

As printed: for a monotonic, convex and differentiable $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$, ${\{-d : d \in D(x)\}} \subseteq\nobreak E(x)$. The problem does not say at which bundles; here it is read at every bundle $x$.

$\succsim$ is convex: ${x \succsim y}$ and ${\alpha \in (0,1)}$ imply ${\alpha x + (1 - \alpha) y \succsim y}$.
$\succsim$ is differentiable in the book's sense.

statements.title: At interior bundles, negated improvement directions worsen
statements.statement:
For a preference $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ and a bundle $x$, $D(x)$ is the set of *improvement directions*: vectors $d$ such that, for some ${\lambda^* > 0}$, ${x + \lambda d \in X}$ and ${x + \lambda d \succ x}$ for all ${\lambda \in (0, \lambda^*)}$. In the book's sense, $\succsim$ is *differentiable* if at every $x$ there is a value vector ${v(x) \in \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ such that $D(x)$ is the set of directions $d$ with ${d \cdot v(x) > 0}$, among those that keep ${x + \lambda d}$ in $X$ for small ${\lambda > 0}$. $E(x)$ is the set of *worsening directions*: vectors $d$ such that, for some ${\varepsilon^* > 0}$, ${x + \varepsilon d \in X}$ and ${x + \varepsilon d \prec x}$ for all ${\varepsilon \in (0, \varepsilon^*]}$.

Let $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ be monotonic, convex and differentiable, and let $x$ be an interior bundle: ${x_k > 0}$ for every $k$. Then
$$\{-d : d \in D(x)\} \subseteq E(x).$$

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is monotonic: ${x \ge y}$ coordinatewise implies ${x \succsim y}$, and ${x_k > y_k}$ for all $k$ implies ${x \succ y}$.
$\succsim$ is convex: ${x \succsim y}$ and ${\alpha \in (0,1)}$ imply ${\alpha x + (1 - \alpha) y \succsim y}$.

$x$ is interior, ${x_k > 0}$ for every $k$.

statements.title: Worsening directions can be more than negated improvements
statements.statement:
For a preference $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ and a bundle $x$, $D(x)$ is the set of *improvement directions*: vectors $d$ such that, for some ${\lambda^* > 0}$, ${x + \lambda d \in X}$ and ${x + \lambda d \succ x}$ for all ${\lambda \in (0, \lambda^*)}$. In the book's sense, $\succsim$ is *differentiable* if at every $x$ there is a value vector ${v(x) \in \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ such that $D(x)$ is the set of directions $d$ with ${d \cdot v(x) > 0}$, among those that keep ${x + \lambda d}$ in $X$ for small ${\lambda > 0}$. $E(x)$ is the set of *worsening directions*: vectors $d$ such that, for some ${\varepsilon^* > 0}$, ${x + \varepsilon d \in X}$ and ${x + \varepsilon d \prec x}$ for all ${\varepsilon \in (0, \varepsilon^*]}$.

There are $K$, a monotonic, convex and differentiable preference $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$, and a bundle $x$ with
$$\{-d : d \in D(x)\} \subsetneq E(x).$$

statements.title: A discontinuous preference that is monotone, convex and differentiable
statements.statement:
For a preference $\succsim$ on ${X = \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ and a bundle $x$, $D(x)$ is the set of *improvement directions*: vectors $d$ such that, for some ${\lambda^* > 0}$, ${x + \lambda d \in X}$ and ${x + \lambda d \succ x}$ for all ${\lambda \in (0, \lambda^*)}$. In the book's sense, $\succsim$ is *differentiable* if at every $x$ there is a value vector ${v(x) \in \mathbb{R}^K_+}$ such that $D(x)$ is the set of directions $d$ with ${d \cdot v(x) > 0}$, among those that keep ${x + \lambda d}$ in $X$ for small ${\lambda > 0}$.

On $\mathbb{R}^2_+$, the preference represented by ${u(x) = x_1 + x_2}$ where ${x_1 + x_2 \le 1}$ and $u(x) = 1 + 2x_1 +\nobreak x_2$ where ${x_1 + x_2 > 1}$ is not continuous, but it is monotonic, convex and differentiable.

entries.title: A convex but discontinuous preference on the line

statements.title: Convex and differentiable, but not continuous
statements.statement: As printed: let $u$ on $\mathbb{R}$ be ${u(x) = x}$ when ${x \le 0}$ and ${u(x) = 1 - x}$ when ${x > 0}$. The preference it represents is differentiable and convex, yet fails continuity.

statements.title: Convex and discontinuous; differentiable with a signed value function

assumptions.text: in the definition of differentiability, the value function may take any sign; the book's definition requires values in $\mathbb{R}^K_+$.

entries.title: Λ-strictly convex preferences on the unit interval

statements.title: Λ-strict convexity for the two monotone orderings of [0,1]
statements.statement: Let ${X = [0,1]}$ and let ${\Lambda = \{>, <\}}$ consist of the increasing and the decreasing ordering. A preference $\succsim$ on $X$ is *$\Lambda$-strictly convex* if for every $y$ there is ${\rhd \in \Lambda}$ with ${\{x : x \succsim y,\ x \neq y\}} \subseteq {\{x : x \rhd y\}}$. Then $\succsim$ is $\Lambda$-strictly convex if and only if it is strictly convex: ${a \succsim y}$, ${b \succsim y}$, ${a \neq b}$ and ${\lambda \in (0,1)}$ imply ${\lambda a + (1 - \lambda) b \succ y}$.

entries.title: Convexity through strict upper contour sets

statements.title: Convexity iff convex strict upper contour sets
statements.statement: As printed: when $X$ lies in a Euclidean space and $\succsim$ on $X$ is a continuous preference relation, $\succsim$ is convex exactly when ${\{x : x \succ y\}}$ is a convex set for each ${y \in X}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a continuous preference relation on $X$, a subset of a Euclidean space.

statements.title: On a convex set: convex upper contours iff convex strict ones
statements.statement: Let ${X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n}$ be convex and $\succsim$ a continuous preference relation on $X$. Then the sets ${\{x \in X : x \succsim y\}}$ are convex for every ${y \in X}$ if and only if the sets ${\{x \in X : x \succ y\}}$ are convex for every ${y \in X}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is continuous (C1).
$X$ is convex.

statements.title: Homothetic preferences give demand homogeneous of degree one in wealth
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ be homothetic — ${x \succsim y}$ implies ${tx \succsim ty}$ for every ${t \ge 0}$ — and let $x(p, w)$ be its demand function: for every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$, $x(p, w)$ is the unique $\succsim$-best bundle in $B(p, w) = {\{x \in \mathbb{R}^K_+ : p \cdot x \le w\}}$. Then, for all ${p \gg 0}$, ${w > 0}$ and ${\lambda > 0}$,
$$x(p, \lambda w) = \lambda\, x(p, w).$$

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is homothetic.
For every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$, $x(p, w)$ is a $\succsim$-best bundle in $B(p, w)$.
That best bundle is unique.

statements.title: Quasi-linear consumers: demand for the numeraire as wealth varies
statements.statement:
Fix ${p_1 > 0}$. A function $g$ of wealth is the demand for commodity 1 — ${g(w) = x_1(p, w)}$ for every ${w > 0}$, where $x(p, w)$ is a best bundle in $B(p, w)$ — of some consumer on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$ whose preference is monotonic, continuous, strictly convex and quasi-linear in commodity 1, at some prices ${p \gg 0}$ with first price $p_1$, **if and only if** either ${g(w) = 0}$ for every ${w > 0}$, or there is ${t \ge 0}$ such that, for every ${w > 0}$,
$$g(w) = \max\Big\{0,\ \frac{w - t}{p_1}\Big\}.$$

statements.title: Demand correspondence for perfect substitutes

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is represented by ${x_1 + x_2}$.

statements.title: Continuous preferences give an upper semi-continuous demand
statements.statement: Let $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ be continuous, not necessarily convex. Then the demand correspondence $X(p, w)$ is upper semi-continuous on $\mathbb{R}^{K+1}_{++}$: if ${(p^n, w^n) \to (p, w)}$ with all terms and the limit in $\mathbb{R}^{K+1}_{++}$, and ${x^n \in X(p^n, w^n)}$ converge to $x$, then ${x \in X(p, w)}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is a continuous preference relation on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$.

statements.title: Buying up to one unit of good 1 is fully rationalizable
statements.statement:
A preference relation $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$ *fully rationalizes* a demand function $x(p, w)$ if, for every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$, $x(p, w)$ is the unique $\succsim$-best bundle in $B(p, w)$. Let $x(p, w)$ satisfy, for every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$,
$$\begin{aligned} x_1(p, w) &= \min\{1,\ w/p_1\}, \\ x_2(p, w) &= \frac{w - p_1 x_1(p, w)}{p_2}. \end{aligned}$$
Then some preference relation on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$ fully rationalizes $x$.

assumptions.text: The behaviour pattern, in our reading: ${x_1 = \min\{1, w/p_1\}}$ and the remaining wealth is spent on commodity 2.

statements.title: If “up to one unit” only caps good 1, rationalizability can fail
statements.statement:
A preference relation $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$ *fully rationalizes* a demand function $x(p, w)$ if, for every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$, $x(p, w)$ is the unique $\succsim$-best bundle in $B(p, w)$. It is not the case that every demand function $x(p, w)$ that is homogeneous of degree zero and satisfies, for every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$,
$$\begin{aligned} x_1(p, w) &\le 1, \\ x_2(p, w) &= \frac{w - p_1 x_1(p, w)}{p_2}, \end{aligned}$$
is fully rationalized by some preference relation on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$.

assumptions.text: The behaviour pattern, in our reading: ${x_1 \le 1}$ and the remaining wealth is spent on commodity 2; demand is homogeneous of degree zero.

statements.title: Buying quantities in proportion to prices is not fully rationalizable
statements.statement: A preference relation $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$ *fully rationalizes* a demand function $x(p, w)$ if, for every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$, $x(p, w)$ is the unique $\succsim$-best bundle in $B(p, w)$. Let $x(p, w)$ satisfy ${x_1/x_2 = p_1/p_2}$ and ${p_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 = w}$ at every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$; so $x(p, w) = w\,(p_1, p_2)/{(p_1^2 + p_2^2)}$. Then no preference relation on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$ fully rationalizes $x$.

assumptions.text: $x(p, w)$ satisfies ${x_1/x_2 = p_1/p_2}$ and ${p_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 = w}$ at every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$.

statements.title: The sum of squares does not rationalize the price-ratio demand
statements.statement: Let $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$ be represented by ${u(x) = x_1^2 + x_2^2}$, and let $x(p, w)$ satisfy ${x_1/x_2 = p_1/p_2}$ and ${p_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 = w}$ at every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$. Then $\succsim$ does not *rationalize* $x$ in the book's sense: it is not true that $\succsim$ is monotonic and $x(p, w)$ is a $\succsim$-best bundle in $B(p, w)$ for every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is represented by ${x_1^2 + x_2^2}$.
$x(p, w)$ satisfies ${x_1/x_2 = p_1/p_2}$ and ${p_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 = w}$ at every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$.

statements.title: The price-ratio bundles are not even best for the sum of squares
statements.statement: Let $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$ be represented by ${u(x) = x_1^2 + x_2^2}$, and let $x(p, w)$ satisfy ${x_1/x_2 = p_1/p_2}$ and ${p_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 = w}$ at every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$. Then the behaviour is not *consistent with maximizing* $\succsim$: it is not true that $x(p, w)$ is a $\succsim$-best bundle in $B(p, w)$ for every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is represented by ${x_1^2 + x_2^2}$.
$x(p, w)$ satisfies ${x_1/x_2 = p_1/p_2}$ and ${p_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 = w}$ at every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$.

entries.title: A consumer with a utility floor

statements.title: The utility-floor procedure selects a unique bundle
statements.statement:
A consumer has a continuous, monotonic, strictly convex preference $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$, represented by a utility function $u$, and a utility level $u^0$. Where the floor is attainable — at prices ${p \gg 0}$ and wealth ${w > 0}$ such that $B(p, w)$ contains a bundle with ${u \ge u^0}$ — the *utility-floor procedure* selects the bundles that maximize $x_1$ over $\{x \in B(p, w) : u(x) \ge u^0\}$.

As printed: wherever the floor is attainable, exactly one bundle maximizes $x_1$ over $\{x \in B(p, w) : u(x) \ge u^0\}$.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is continuous.
$\succsim$ is monotonic: ${x \ge y}$ coordinatewise implies ${x \succsim y}$, and ${x_k > y_k}$ for all $k$ implies ${x \succ y}$.
$\succsim$ is strictly convex: ${a \succsim y}$, ${b \succsim y}$, ${a \neq b}$ and ${\lambda \in (0,1)}$ imply ${\lambda a + (1 - \lambda) b \succ y}$.
$u$ represents $\succsim$: $x \succsim y \iff u(x) \ge\nobreak u(y)$.
The floor is attainable: some bundle of $B(p, w)$ has ${u \ge u^0}$.

If the set ${\{x : u(x) \ge u^0\}}$ is closed, then wherever the floor is attainable exactly one bundle maximizes $x_1$ over $\{x \in B(p, w) : u(x) \ge u^0\}$.

statements.statement:

statements.title: The utility-floor procedure is consistent with maximization
statements.statement:
A consumer has a continuous, monotonic, strictly convex preference $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$, represented by a utility function $u$, and a utility level $u^0$. Where the floor is attainable — at prices ${p \gg 0}$ and wealth ${w > 0}$ such that $B(p, w)$ contains a bundle with ${u \ge u^0}$ — the *utility-floor procedure* selects the bundles that maximize $x_1$ over $\{x \in B(p, w) : u(x) \ge u^0\}$.

There is a preference relation ${\succsim'}$ on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ such that, wherever the floor is attainable, every bundle selected by the procedure is a ${\succsim'}$-best bundle in $B(p, w)$, not necessarily unique.

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is continuous.
$\succsim$ is monotonic: ${x \ge y}$ coordinatewise implies ${x \succsim y}$, and ${x_k > y_k}$ for all $k$ implies ${x \succ y}$.
$\succsim$ is strictly convex: ${a \succsim y}$, ${b \succsim y}$, ${a \neq b}$ and ${\lambda \in (0,1)}$ imply ${\lambda a + (1 - \lambda) b \succ y}$.
$u$ represents $\succsim$: $x \succsim y \iff u(x) \ge\nobreak u(y)$.

statements.title: The utility-floor demand satisfies Walras's law
statements.statement:
A consumer has a continuous, monotonic, strictly convex preference $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$, represented by a utility function $u$, and a utility level $u^0$. Where the floor is attainable — at prices ${p \gg 0}$ and wealth ${w > 0}$ such that $B(p, w)$ contains a bundle with ${u \ge u^0}$ — the *utility-floor procedure* selects the bundles that maximize $x_1$ over $\{x \in B(p, w) : u(x) \ge u^0\}$.

Wherever the floor is attainable, every selected bundle $x$ satisfies ${p \cdot x = w}$.

The floor is attainable at $(p, w)$, and $x$ is selected there.

statements.title: Demand for commodity 1 does not rise with its own price
statements.statement:
A consumer has a continuous, monotonic, strictly convex preference $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$, represented by a utility function $u$, and a utility level $u^0$. statements.title: The utility-floor demand is continuous
statements.statement:
A consumer has a continuous, monotonic, strictly convex preference $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$, represented by a utility function $u$, and a utility level $u^0$. Where the floor is attainable — at prices ${p \gg 0}$ and wealth ${w > 0}$ such that $B(p, w)$ contains a bundle with ${u \ge u^0}$ — the *utility-floor procedure* selects the bundles that maximize $x_1$ over $\{x \in B(p, w) : u(x) \ge u^0\}$.

The selection is continuous on the set of $(p, w)$ where the floor is attainable: for every bundle $x$ selected at $(p, w)$ and every ${\varepsilon > 0}$ there is ${\delta > 0}$ such that every bundle selected at any such $(p', w')$ within distance $\delta$ of $(p, w)$ lies within $\varepsilon$ of $x$.

statements.title: Averaging two rational consumers need not be rational
statements.statement:
There are $K$, two different budget sets ${A = B(p^A, w^A)}$ and ${B = B(p^B, w^B)}$ with ${p^A, p^B \gg 0}$ and ${w^A, w^B > 0}$, two different preference relations ${\succsim^1, \succsim^2}$ on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$, and bundles $x^i$ that are $\succsim^i$-best in $A$ and $y^i$ that are $\succsim^i$-best in $B$, with ${x^1 \neq x^2}$ and ${y^1 \neq y^2}$, such that:

- no preference relation makes ${(x^1 + x^2)/2}$ the unique best bundle in $A$ and ${(y^1 + y^2)/2}$ the unique best bundle in $B$; and
- no monotonic preference relation makes ${(x^1 + x^2)/2}$ a best bundle in $A$ and ${(y^1 + y^2)/2}$ a best bundle in $B$.

entries.title: Under the weak axiom, Giffen goods are inferior
entries.name: Giffen goods are inferior

statements.title: A Giffen good is inferior
statements.statement: As printed: Let $x(p, w)$ be a demand function on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$: for every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$, ${x(p, w) \in B(p, w)}$, and $x(\lambda p, \lambda w) =\nobreak x(p, w)$ for every ${\lambda > 0}$. If good $k$ is Giffen at some $(p, w)$ — raising $p_k$ alone raises the demand for $k$ — then at some $(p', w')$ the demand for $k$ falls when $w'$ rises.

assumptions.text: ${x(p, w) \in B(p, w)}$ for every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$.
$x$ is homogeneous of degree zero: $x(\lambda p, \lambda w) =\nobreak x(p, w)$.
Good $k$ is Giffen somewhere: at some $(p, w)$, raising $p_k$ alone raises $x_k$.

statements.title: Under the weak axiom, a Giffen good is inferior
statements.statement: Let $x(p, w)$ be a demand function on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$: for every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$, ${x(p, w) \in B(p, w)}$, and $x(\lambda p, \lambda w) =\nobreak x(p, w)$ for every ${\lambda > 0}$. Suppose $x$ satisfies the weak axiom: if ${x(p, w) \neq x(p', w')}$ and ${p \cdot x(p', w') \le w}$, then ${p' \cdot x(p, w) > w'}$. If good $k$ is Giffen at some $(p, w)$, then at some $(p', w')$ the demand for $k$ falls when $w'$ rises.

If good $k$ is Giffen at some $(p, w)$, then at some $(p', w')$ the demand for $k$ falls when $w'$ rises.

statements.title: Strict “concavity” of a preference
statements.statement: A preference $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$ is *strictly concave* if ${a \succsim b}$ implies ${a \succ \delta a + (1 - \delta) b}$ for every ${\delta \in (0, 1)}$.

statements.title: Every bundle (0, t) is indifferent to some (s, 0)
statements.statement: As printed: A preference $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$ is *strictly concave* if ${a \succsim b}$ implies ${a \succ \delta a + (1 - \delta) b}$ for every ${\delta \in (0, 1)}$. If $\succsim$ is strongly monotone, continuous and strictly concave, then for every ${t \ge 0}$ there is ${s \ge 0}$ with ${(0, t) \sim (s, 0)}$.

statements.title: Every bundle (0, t) is indifferent to some (s, 0)
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$ be strongly monotone, continuous, and strictly concave for distinct bundles: ${a \succsim b}$ and ${a \neq b}$ imply ${a \succ \delta a + (1 - \delta) b}$ for all ${\delta \in (0, 1)}$. Then for every ${t \ge 0}$ there is ${s \ge 0}$ with
$$(0, t) \sim (s, 0).$$

strict concavity is required for distinct bundles only — ${a \succsim b}$ and ${a \neq b}$ imply ${a \succ \delta a + (1 - \delta) b}$ for all ${\delta \in (0,1)}$.
