statements.title: Concave preferences: demand for good 1 jumps at a threshold price
statements.statement:
Let $\succsim$ on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$ be strongly monotone, continuous, and strictly concave for distinct bundles, and fix ${p_2 > 0}$ and ${w > 0}$. There is ${p^* > 0}$ such that, for every ${p_1 > 0}$, the set of quantities of good 1 demanded at prices $(p_1, p_2)$ and wealth $w$ is
$$\begin{cases} \{w/p_1\} & \text{if } p_1 < p^*, \\ \{0,\ w/p^*\} & \text{if } p_1 = p^*, \\ \{0\} & \text{if } p_1 > p^*. \end{cases}$$

assumptions.text: $\succsim$ is strongly monotone: ${x \ge y}$ coordinatewise and ${x \neq y}$ imply ${x \succ y}$.
$\succsim$ is continuous.
strict concavity is required for distinct bundles only — ${a \succsim b}$ and ${a \neq b}$ imply ${a \succ \delta a + (1 - \delta) b}$ for all ${\delta \in (0,1)}$.
The price of good 2 and wealth are fixed: ${p_2 > 0}$, ${w > 0}$.

statements.title: Aspiration-level saving is fully rationalizable
statements.statement:
Saving is the $K$th good, with price $1$. A consumer has a continuous, strictly concave function $v$ on $\mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+$, not necessarily increasing, and an aspiration level $v^*$. At prices ${p \in \mathbb{R}^{K-1}_{++}}$ and wealth ${w > 0}$ he chooses $x$ maximizing $v$ over the set $F(p, w)$ of ${x \in \mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+}$ with ${p \cdot x \le w}$ and ${v(x) \le v^*}$, and saves the rest, ending with the bundle ${(x,\ w - p \cdot x)}$. A preference relation on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ *fully rationalizes* this behaviour where that bundle is the unique best bundle of $\{(x, s) \in \mathbb{R}^K_+ : p \cdot x + s \le w\}$.

As printed: some preference relation on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ fully rationalizes the behaviour at every ${p \gg 0}$, ${w > 0}$ and every maximizer $x$.

assumptions.text: $v$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+$.
$v$ is strictly concave on $\mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+$.

statements.title: Aspiration-level saving is fully rationalizable where choice is unique
statements.statement:
Saving is the $K$th good, with price $1$. A consumer has a continuous, strictly concave function $v$ on $\mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+$, not necessarily increasing, and an aspiration level $v^*$. At prices ${p \in \mathbb{R}^{K-1}_{++}}$ and wealth ${w > 0}$ he chooses $x$ maximizing $v$ over the set $F(p, w)$ of ${x \in \mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+}$ with ${p \cdot x \le w}$ and ${v(x) \le v^*}$, and saves the rest, ending with the bundle ${(x,\ w - p \cdot x)}$. A preference relation on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ *fully rationalizes* this behaviour where that bundle is the unique best bundle of $\{(x, s) \in \mathbb{R}^K_+ : p \cdot x + s \le w\}$.

There is a preference relation on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ that fully rationalizes the behaviour at every ${p \gg 0}$ and ${w > 0}$ at which the maximizer $x$ of $v$ over $F(p, w)$ is unique.

assumptions.text: $v$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+$.
$v$ is strictly concave on $\mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+$.
full rationalization is required only where the maximizer of $v$ over $F(p, w)$ is unique.

statements.title: No continuous preference rationalizes aspiration-level saving
statements.statement:
Saving is the $K$th good, with price $1$. A consumer has a continuous, strictly concave function $v$ on $\mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+$, not necessarily increasing, and an aspiration level $v^*$. At prices ${p \in \mathbb{R}^{K-1}_{++}}$ and wealth ${w > 0}$ he chooses $x$ maximizing $v$ over the set $F(p, w)$ of ${x \in \mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+}$ with ${p \cdot x \le w}$ and ${v(x) \le v^*}$, and saves the rest, ending with the bundle ${(x,\ w - p \cdot x)}$. A preference relation on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ *fully rationalizes* this behaviour where that bundle is the unique best bundle of $\{(x, s) \in \mathbb{R}^K_+ : p \cdot x + s \le w\}$.

With ${K = 2}$: there are a continuous, strictly concave $v$ on $\mathbb{R}_+$ and an aspiration level $v^*$ such that no continuous preference relation on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$ fully rationalizes the behaviour at every ${p > 0}$ and ${w > 0}$ at which the maximizer is unique.

assumptions.text: full rationalization is required only where the maximizer is unique. This weakens the requirement and so strengthens the negative answer; without it, the answer would be negative for a trivial reason.

statements.title: No differentiable preference rationalizes aspiration-level saving
statements.statement:
Saving is the $K$th good, with price $1$. A consumer has a continuous, strictly concave function $v$ on $\mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+$, not necessarily increasing, and an aspiration level $v^*$. At prices ${p \in \mathbb{R}^{K-1}_{++}}$ and wealth ${w > 0}$ he chooses $x$ maximizing $v$ over the set $F(p, w)$ of ${x \in \mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+}$ with ${p \cdot x \le w}$ and ${v(x) \le v^*}$, and saves the rest, ending with the bundle ${(x,\ w - p \cdot x)}$. A preference relation on $\mathbb{R}^K_+$ *fully rationalizes* this behaviour where that bundle is the unique best bundle of $\{(x, s) \in \mathbb{R}^K_+ : p \cdot x + s \le w\}$.

With ${K = 2}$: there are a continuous, strictly concave $v$ on $\mathbb{R}_+$ and an aspiration level $v^*$ such that no preference relation on $\mathbb{R}^2_+$ that is differentiable in the book's sense — at every bundle $z$ there is a value vector ${q(z) \in \mathbb{R}^2_+}$ such that the improvement directions at $z$ are exactly the directions $d$ that keep ${z + \lambda d}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2_+$ for small ${\lambda > 0}$ and have ${d \cdot q(z) > 0}$ — fully rationalizes the behaviour at every ${p > 0}$ and ${w > 0}$ at which the maximizer is unique.

assumptions.text: full rationalization is required only where the maximizer is unique. This weakens the requirement and so strengthens the negative answer; without it, the answer would be negative for a trivial reason.

entries.title: Is v = w/p₁ + w/p₂ a rational consumer’s indirect utility?

statements.title: Roy’s identity applied to v = w/p₁ + w/p₂
statements.statement:
Let ${v(p_1,p_2,w) = w/p_1 + w/p_2}.$ Then ${v}$ is differentiable at every ${(p,w)}$ with ${p_1,p_2,w>0},$ and there, for ${\{i,j\}=\{1,2\}},$ the ratio in Roy’s identity is
$$\begin{gathered}-\frac{\partial v/\partial p_i}{\partial v/\partial w}(p,w)\\[4pt]=\frac{p_j}{p_i+p_j}\cdot\frac{w}{p_i}.\end{gathered}$$

statements.title: Any smooth utility behind this demand has slope −√x₂/√x₁
statements.statement: Let ${x(p,w)}$ be the demand of part (a) and let ${u:\mathbb{R}^2_+\to\mathbb{R}}$ be differentiable at every bundle ${x\gg 0}.$ Suppose that for all ${p\gg 0}$ and ${w>0}$ the bundle ${x(p,w)}$ maximizes ${u}$ on the budget set $B(p,w)=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^2_+ : p\cdot y\le w\}.$ Then at every demanded bundle ${x = x(p,w)}$ the indifference curve of ${u}$ has slope ${-\sqrt{x_2}/\sqrt{x_1}}$: the derivative of ${u}$ in the direction ${(1,\,-\sqrt{x_2}/\sqrt{x_1})}$ is zero.

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is differentiable at every ${x\gg 0}$: for some gradient ${\nabla u(x)},$ $\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\,[u(x+\varepsilon d)-u(x)]/\varepsilon = d\cdot\nabla u(x)$ in every direction ${d}.$
The demand of part (a) is derived from ${u}$: for all ${p\gg 0}$ and ${w>0},$ ${u(y)\le u(x(p,w))}$ for every ${y\in B(p,w)}.$

statements.title: A utility whose marginal-utility ratio is √x₂/√x₁
statements.statement:
There is a utility function ${u:\mathbb{R}^2_+\to\mathbb{R}}$ such that at every bundle ${x\gg 0}$ both partial derivatives exist and
$$\frac{\partial u/\partial x_1\,(x)}{\partial u/\partial x_2\,(x)} \;=\; \frac{\sqrt{x_2}}{\sqrt{x_1}}.$$

statements.title: A utility with that ratio has indirect utility √(w/p₁ + w/p₂)
statements.statement:
There is a utility ${u:\mathbb{R}^2_+\to\mathbb{R}}$ with the property of part (c) whose indirect utility is ${\sqrt{v}}$: for all ${p\gg 0}$ and ${w>0}$ the maximum of ${u}$ on ${B(p,w)}$ is attained and
$$\max_{x\in B(p,w)} u(x) \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{w}{p_1}+\frac{w}{p_2}}.$$

statements.title: The utility of part (c) does not return the original v
statements.statement: It is not the case that every utility ${u:\mathbb{R}^2_+\to\mathbb{R}}$ with the property of part (c) whose indirect utility is ${\sqrt{w/p_1+w/p_2}}$ also has indirect utility ${v(p_1,p_2,w) = w/p_1 + w/p_2}$ at all ${p\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$

statements.title: Another utility with the same ratio yields exactly v
statements.statement:
There is a utility ${u:\mathbb{R}^2_+\to\mathbb{R}}$ with the property of part (c) whose indirect utility is the original ${v}$: for all ${p\gg 0}$ and ${w>0}$ the maximum of ${u}$ on ${B(p,w)}$ is attained and
$$\max_{x\in B(p,w)} u(x) \;=\; \frac{w}{p_1}+\frac{w}{p_2}.$$

statements.title: Hicksian demand is continuous under strict convexity
statements.statement: Let ${\succsim}$ be a preference on ${X=\mathbb{R}^K_+}$ that is monotone, continuous and strictly convex. For prices ${p\gg 0}$ and a bundle ${z\in X},$ the dual problem ${D(p,z)}$ is ${\min_x\{p\cdot x : x\succsim z\}},$ and its solution is the Hicksian demand ${h(p,z)}.$ Then ${h}$ is continuous: for every ${p\gg 0},$ ${z\in X},$ every solution ${x}$ of ${D(p,z)}$ and every ${\varepsilon>0}$ there is ${\delta>0}$ such that every solution ${x'}$ of ${D(p',z')}$ with ${p'\gg 0}$ satisfies ${\|x'-x\|<\varepsilon}$ whenever ${\big\|(p',z')-(p,z)\big\|<\delta}.$

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is monotone: ${x\ge y}$ implies ${x\succsim y},$ and ${x\gg y}$ implies ${x\succ y}.$
${\succsim}$ is continuous: if ${a\succ b},$ then ${x\succ y}$ for all ${x}$ near ${a}$ and ${y}$ near ${b}.$
${\succsim}$ is strictly convex: if ${a\succsim y},$ ${b\succsim y}$ and ${a\neq b},$ then ${\lambda a+(1-\lambda)b\succ y}$ for every ${\lambda\in(0,1)}.$

statements.title: Compensating variation with perfect substitutes
statements.statement:
Let ${\succsim}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ be represented by ${u(x)=x_1+x_2},$ and let ${p,p'\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$ Define ${CV(p,p',w) = w - e(p',z)},$ where ${z}$ is an optimal bundle in ${B(p,w)}$ and ${e(p',z)}$ is the least cost at prices ${p'}$ of a bundle at least as good as ${z}.$ Then, whichever optimal bundle ${z}$ is used,
$$CV(p,p',w) \;=\; w - w\,\frac{\min(p_1',p_2')}{\min(p_1,p_2)}.$$

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is represented by ${u(x)=x_1+x_2}.$
Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${p'\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$

statements.title: Equivalent variation with perfect substitutes
statements.statement:
Let ${\succsim}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ be represented by ${u(x)=x_1+x_2},$ and let ${p,p'\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$ Define ${EV(p,p',w) = e(p,z') - w},$ where ${z'}$ is an optimal bundle in ${B(p',w)}$ and ${e(p,z')}$ is the least cost at prices ${p}$ of a bundle at least as good as ${z'}.$ Then, whichever optimal bundle ${z'}$ is used,
$$EV(p,p',w) \;=\; w\,\frac{\min(p_1,p_2)}{\min(p_1',p_2')} - w.$$

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is represented by ${u(x)=x_1+x_2}.$
Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${p'\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$

statements.title: For a normal good, the area under demand lies between CV and EV
statements.statement:
Let ${\succsim}$ be a monotone preference on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ with demand function ${x(q,v)},$ a best bundle in ${B(q,v)}$ for all ${q\gg 0},$ ${v>0},$ and assume every dual problem has a solution. Suppose good 1 is normal. Let ${p,p'\gg 0}$ differ only in the first price (${p_2=p'_2}$), let ${w>0},$ and let ${CV}$ and ${EV}$ be the two measures of the change from ${p}$ to ${p'}.$ Then
$$CV\le\int_{p_1'}^{p_1}x_1\big((t,p_2),w\big)\,dt\le EV.$$

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is monotone.
${x(q,v)}$ is a demand function for ${\succsim}$: it is a best bundle in ${B(q,v)}$ for every ${q\gg 0}$ and ${v>0}.$
The dual problem has a solution: for every ${q\gg 0}$ and every bundle ${z},$ some bundle minimizes ${q\cdot y}$ over ${y\succsim z}.$
Good 1 is normal: ${x_1(q,v)}$ is nondecreasing in wealth ${v>0}$ at every ${q\gg 0}.$
Only the first price changes: ${p_2 = p_2'}.$
Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${p'\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$

statements.title: Quasi-linearity in good 2 makes the two measures equal
statements.statement: Original claim: suppose ${\succsim}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ is quasi-linear in good 2, take ${p,p'\gg 0}$ and ${w>0},$ and assume all bundles used by the two measures are strictly positive. Then, for the move from ${p}$ to ${p'},$ the compensating variation equals the equivalent variation: ${CV(p,p',w) = EV(p,p',w)}.$

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is quasi-linear in the second commodity: ${x\succsim y}$ implies $x+\varepsilon e_2\succsim y+\varepsilon e_2.$
Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${p'\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$
Every optimal bundle in ${B(p,w)}$ is strictly positive.
Every optimal bundle in ${B(p',w)}$ is strictly positive.
Every cost-minimizing bundle defining ${e(p',z)},$ for ${z}$ optimal in ${B(p,w)},$ is strictly positive.
Every cost-minimizing bundle defining ${e(p,z')},$ for ${z'}$ optimal in ${B(p',w)},$ is strictly positive.

statements.title: CV equals EV when only the price of the non-linear good moves
statements.statement: Let ${\succsim}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ be strictly convex and quasi-linear in the second commodity. Let ${p,p'\gg 0}$ with ${p_2=p_2'},$ let ${w>0},$ and suppose that every bundle entering the two measures is strictly positive. Then ${CV(p,p',w) = EV(p,p',w)}.$

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is strictly convex.
${\succsim}$ is quasi-linear in the second commodity: ${x\succsim y}$ implies $x+\varepsilon e_2\succsim y+\varepsilon e_2.$
Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${p'\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$
the price of the second commodity does not change: ${p_2=p_2'}.$
Every optimal bundle in ${B(p,w)}$ is strictly positive.
Every optimal bundle in ${B(p',w)}$ is strictly positive.
Every cost-minimizing bundle defining ${e(p',z)},$ for ${z}$ optimal in ${B(p,w)},$ is strictly positive.
Every cost-minimizing bundle defining ${e(p,z')},$ for ${z'}$ optimal in ${B(p',w)},$ is strictly positive.

entries.title: The envelope theorem and Roy’s identity
entries.name: The envelope theorem

statements.title: The envelope identity, with its conditions unstated
statements.statement:
Original claim: take the problem ${\max_x\{u(x,\alpha) : g(x,\alpha)=0\}},$ write ${V(\alpha)}$ for its value, ${x^*(\alpha)}$ for its solution and ${\lambda}$ for the multiplier. Then
$$\frac{\partial V}{\partial\alpha_i}(a) \;=\; \frac{\partial(u-\lambda g)}{\partial\alpha_i}\big(x^*(a),a\big).$$
The conditions that make this hold are alluded to but never spelled out.

statements.title: The envelope theorem, with its differentiability conditions
statements.statement:
Consider $\max_{x\in\mathbb{R}^M}\{u(x,\alpha) : g(x,\alpha)=0\}$ with parameters ${\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^n}.$ Let ${x^*(\alpha)}$ solve the problem for every ${\alpha}$ and let ${V(\alpha)=u(x^*(\alpha),\alpha)}.$ Fix a parameter point ${a},$ an index ${i}$ and ${\lambda\in\mathbb{R}}.$ If the Lagrangian ${u-\lambda g}$ is differentiable at ${(x^*(a),a)}$ with zero derivative in ${x}$ there, and ${x^*}$ has a partial derivative in ${\alpha_i}$ at ${a},$ then ${V}$ has a partial derivative in ${\alpha_i}$ at ${a}$ and
$$\frac{\partial V}{\partial\alpha_i}(a) \;=\; \frac{\partial(u-\lambda g)}{\partial\alpha_i}\big(x^*(a),a\big).$$

assumptions.text: ${x^*(\alpha)}$ solves the problem for every ${\alpha}$: ${g(x^*(\alpha),\alpha)=0},$ and ${u(y,\alpha)\le u(x^*(\alpha),\alpha)}$ whenever ${g(y,\alpha)=0}.$
${V}$ is the value of the problem: ${V(\alpha)=u(x^*(\alpha),\alpha)}.$
the Lagrangian ${u-\lambda g}$ is differentiable at ${(x^*(a),a)},$ jointly in ${(x,\alpha)}.$
${\lambda}$ is a Lagrange multiplier at the solution: the derivative of ${u-\lambda g}$ in ${x}$ at ${(x^*(a),a)}$ is zero.
the solution ${x^*}$ has a partial derivative in ${\alpha_i}$ at ${a}.$

statements.title: Roy’s identity derived from the envelope theorem
statements.statement:
Treat the consumer’s problem as a parametric problem with parameters ${\alpha=(p,w)\in\mathbb{R}^{K+1}}$: maximize ${u(x)}$ subject to ${g(x,p,w)=p\cdot x-w=0},$ with solution ${x^*(p,w)},$ value ${V(p,w)}$ and multiplier ${\lambda}.$ At a point ${a=(p,w)\gg 0},$ suppose ${\lambda}$ is a Lagrange multiplier at ${x^*(a)},$ the envelope identity holds in every parameter, and ${\partial(u-\lambda g)/\partial w\neq 0}$ there. Then for every commodity ${k}$ both partial derivatives below exist and
$$-\frac{\partial V/\partial p_k}{\partial V/\partial w}(a) \;=\; x^*_k(a).$$

assumptions.text: the parameter point is strictly positive: ${a=(p,w)\gg 0}.$
the objective does not depend on the parameters: ${u(x,\alpha)=u(x)}.$
the constraint is the budget equation: ${g(x,p,w)=p\cdot x-w}$ whenever ${(p,w)\gg 0}.$
${x^*(p,w)}$ solves the problem at every ${(p,w)\gg 0}.$
${V(p,w) = u(x^*(p,w))}$ at every ${(p,w)\gg 0}.$
${\lambda}$ is a Lagrange multiplier at the solution: every partial derivative of ${x\mapsto (u-\lambda g)(x,a)}$ at ${x^*(a)}$ is zero.
The partial derivatives of $\alpha\mapsto(u-\lambda g)(x^*(a),\alpha)$ at ${a}$ exist.
The envelope identity holds at ${a}$: $\partial V/\partial\alpha_i(a)=\partial(u-\lambda g)/\partial\alpha_i\,(x^*(a),a)$ for every parameter ${\alpha_i}.$
the marginal value of wealth is nonzero: ${\partial(u-\lambda g)/\partial w\neq 0}$ at ${(x^*(a),a)}.$

entries.title: Convex technologies and concave production functions

statements.title: A technology is convex iff its production function is concave
statements.statement:
Let ${Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^K}$ be a technology and ${f:\mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+\to\mathbb{R}}$ a production function describing the same producer, who produces commodity ${K}$ from inputs ${1,\dots,K-1}$: for every ${v\in\mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+},$
$$f(v)=\max\{x : (-v,x)\in Z\},$$
and ${Z}$ consists of the plans ${(-w,x)}$ with ${x\le f(v)}$ and ${w\ge v}$ for some ${v\in\mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+}.$
Then ${Z}$ is convex if and only if ${f}$ is concave on ${\mathbb{R}^{K-1}_+}.$

assumptions.text: ${f}$ is derived from ${Z}$: for every input vector ${v\ge 0}$ the maximum of ${\{x : (-v,x)\in Z\}}$ exists and equals ${f(v)}.$
${Z}$ is derived from ${f}$: ${Z}$ consists of the plans ${(-w,x)}$ with ${x\le f(v)}$ and ${w\ge v}$ for some ${v\ge 0}.$

entries.title: Properties of the cost function and Shephard’s lemma
entries.name: Shephard’s lemma

statements.title: The cost function is homogeneous of degree one in input prices
statements.statement:
For a technology ${Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^K}$ with inputs ${1,\dots,L}$ and outputs ${L+1,\dots,K},$ let $C(w,y)=\min_a\{w\cdot a : (-a,y)\in Z\}$ be the least cost of producing ${y\in\mathbb{R}^{K-L}_+}$ at input prices ${w}.$ For ${w\gg 0}$ and ${\lambda}$ with ${\lambda w\gg 0}$ (that is, ${\lambda>0}$),
$$C(\lambda w,y) \;=\; \lambda\, C(w,y).$$

assumptions.text: Input prices are positive: ${w\gg 0}$ and ${\lambda w\gg 0}.$

statements.title: The cost function is nondecreasing in each input price
statements.statement: For a technology ${Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^K}$ with inputs ${1,\dots,L}$ and outputs ${L+1,\dots,K},$ let $C(w,y)=\min_a\{w\cdot a : (-a,y)\in Z\}$ be the least cost of producing ${y\in\mathbb{R}^{K-L}_+}$ at input prices ${w}.$ Original claim: raising one input price ${w_k}$ never lowers ${C};$ that is, when ${w_k\le w_k'}$ and ${w_j=w_j'}$ for all ${j\neq k},$ we get ${C(w,y)\le C(w',y)}.$

assumptions.text: Only the price of input ${k}$ changes, and it does not fall: ${w_k\le w_k'}$ and ${w_j=w_j'}$ for ${j\ne k}.$

statements.title: Cost is nondecreasing in a price when that input is never negative
statements.statement:
For a technology ${Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^K}$ with inputs ${1,\dots,L}$ and outputs ${L+1,\dots,K},$ let $C(w,y)=\min_a\{w\cdot a : (-a,y)\in Z\}$ be the least cost of producing ${y\in\mathbb{R}^{K-L}_+}$ at input prices ${w}.$ Let ${w_k\le w_k'}$ and ${w_j=w_j'}$ for ${j\neq k}.$ If every input vector ${a}$ with ${(-a,y)\in Z}$ has ${a_k\ge 0},$ then
$$C(w,y)\;\le\; C(w',y).$$

assumptions.text: The price of input ${k}$ does not fall: ${w_k\le w_k'}.$
No other price changes: ${w_j=w_j'}$ for every ${j\neq k}.$
input ${k}$ is never negative: ${a_k\ge 0}$ for every ${a}$ with ${(-a,y)\in Z}.$

statements.title: The cost function is concave in input prices
statements.statement:
For a technology ${Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^K}$ with inputs ${1,\dots,L}$ and outputs ${L+1,\dots,K},$ let $C(w,y)=\min_a\{w\cdot a : (-a,y)\in Z\}$ be the least cost of producing ${y\in\mathbb{R}^{K-L}_+}$ at input prices ${w}.$ For all input price vectors ${w^1,w^2}$ and every ${\lambda\in[0,1]},$
$$\begin{aligned}&C\big(\lambda w^1+(1-\lambda)w^2,\,y\big)\\&\quad\ge\lambda\,C(w^1,y)+(1-\lambda)\,C(w^2,y).\end{aligned}$$

statements.title: Shephard’s lemma: the price derivative of cost is input demand
statements.statement:
For a technology ${Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^K}$ with inputs ${1,\dots,L}$ and outputs ${L+1,\dots,K},$ let $C(w,y)=\min_a\{w\cdot a : (-a,y)\in Z\}$ be the least cost of producing ${y\in\mathbb{R}^{K-L}_+}$ at input prices ${w}.$ Let ${a}$ be a cost-minimizing input vector at ${(w,y)}$: ${(-a,y)\in Z}$ and ${w\cdot a\le w\cdot a'}$ whenever ${(-a',y)\in Z}.$ If ${C(\cdot,y)}$ is defined near ${w}$ along the price of input ${k}$ and has a partial derivative in ${w_k}$ at ${w},$ then
$$\frac{\partial C}{\partial w_k}(w,y) \;=\; a_k .$$

assumptions.text: ${C}$ is defined near ${w}$ in the ${k}$-th price: the minimum is attained at every price vector obtained from ${w}$ by moving ${w_k}$ slightly.
${C}$ has a partial derivative in ${w_k}$ at ${w}.$

statements.title: Cross-price effects on input demands are symmetric
statements.statement:
For a technology ${Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^K}$ with inputs ${1,\dots,L}$ and outputs ${L+1,\dots,K},$ let $C(w,y)=\min_a\{w\cdot a : (-a,y)\in Z\}$ be the least cost of producing ${y\in\mathbb{R}^{K-L}_+}$ at input prices ${w}.$ Let ${a(w')}$ be a cost-minimizing input vector at every price vector ${w'}$ near ${w}.$ If ${C(\cdot,y)}$ is twice continuously differentiable at ${w},$ then for any two inputs ${j}$ and ${k}$
$$\frac{\partial a_k}{\partial w_j}(w) \;=\; \frac{\partial a_j}{\partial w_k}(w).$$

assumptions.text: ${C(\cdot,y)}$ is twice continuously differentiable at ${w}.$
${a(w')}$ minimizes cost at every price vector ${w'}$ near ${w}$: ${(-a(w'),y)\in Z}$ and ${w'\cdot a(w')\le w'\cdot a'}$ whenever ${(-a',y)\in Z}.$

entries.title: The output-maximizing producer with a profit target

statements.title: A unique solution at every price vector
statements.statement: Original claim: given sensible assumptions, a producer seeking the largest output with profit at least ${\rho},$ and staying inactive when that is out of reach, faces a problem with exactly one solution at each price vector. No assumptions are specified.

statements.title: Unique solution for a closed, bounded, strictly convex technology
statements.statement: A producer has a technology ${Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{L+1}}$ (inputs ${1,\dots,L},$ output ${K=L+1}$) and faces prices ${p}.$ A plan ${z}$ solves his problem at profit target ${\rho}$ if either some plan ${w\in Z}$ earns ${p\cdot w\ge\rho},$ and ${z}$ is such a plan with the largest output ${z_K};$ or no plan earns ${\rho},$ and ${z=0}.$ If ${Z}$ is closed, bounded above and strictly convex, then for every profit level ${\rho}$ and every price vector ${p\gg 0}$ the problem has exactly one solution.

assumptions.text: ${Z}$ is closed and bounded above: for some ${B},$ ${z_k\le B}$ for every ${z\in Z}$ and every ${k}.$
${Z}$ is strictly convex: for distinct ${z,z'\in Z}$ and ${0<\lambda<1},$ ${\lambda z+(1-\lambda)z'}$ is an interior point of ${Z}.$
prices are strictly positive: ${p\gg 0}.$

statements.title: Supply is monotonic in prices
statements.statement: Original claim: given sensible assumptions, this profit-target, output-maximizing producer has a supply function that is monotonic in prices. No assumptions are specified.

statements.title: Output rises with its own price and falls with an input’s price
statements.statement:
A producer has a technology ${Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{L+1}}$ (inputs ${1,\dots,L},$ output ${K=L+1}$) and faces prices ${p}.$ A plan ${z}$ solves his problem at profit target ${\rho}$ if either some plan ${w\in Z}$ earns ${p\cdot w\ge\rho},$ and ${z}$ is such a plan with the largest output ${z_K};$ or no plan earns ${\rho},$ and ${z=0}.$ Suppose every plan in ${Z}$ yields a nonnegative output, ${z_K\ge 0}.$ Let ${z}$ solve the problem at prices ${p}$ and ${z'}$ at prices ${p'},$ with the same ${\rho}.$

- (i) If only the output price changes and it does not fall (${p_K\le p'_K},$ ${p_j=p'_j}$ for ${j\neq K}$), then ${z_K\le z'_K}.$
- (ii) If every plan uses commodity ${j}$ as an input (${z_j\le 0}$ for all ${z\in Z}$) and only ${p_j}$ changes and it does not fall, then ${z'_K\le z_K}.$

assumptions.text: every plan yields a nonnegative output: ${z_K\ge 0}$ for all ${z\in Z}.$
In (i): ${p_K\le p_K'}$ and ${p_j=p_j'}$ for every ${j\neq K}.$
in (ii): every plan uses commodity ${j}$ as an input, ${z_j\le 0}$ for all ${z\in Z}.$
In (ii): ${p_j\le p_j'}$ and ${p_i=p_i'}$ for every ${i\neq j}.$

statements.title: Supply is continuous in prices when ρ = 0
statements.statement: Original claim: given sensible assumptions, with ${\rho=0}$ this profit-target, output-maximizing producer has a supply function that is continuous in prices. No assumptions are specified.

statements.title: Supply is continuous at ρ = 0 for closed, strictly convex technologies
statements.statement: A producer has a technology ${Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{L+1}}$ (inputs ${1,\dots,L},$ output ${K=L+1}$) and faces prices ${p}.$ A plan ${z}$ solves his problem at profit target ${\rho}$ if either some plan ${w\in Z}$ earns ${p\cdot w\ge\rho},$ and ${z}$ is such a plan with the largest output ${z_K};$ or no plan earns ${\rho},$ and ${z=0}.$ Suppose ${Z}$ is closed, strictly convex and contains ${0},$ let ${\rho=0},$ let ${p\gg 0}$ and let ${z}$ solve the problem at ${p}.$ Then for every ${\varepsilon>0}$ there is ${\delta>0}$ such that every solution ${z'}$ at any price vector ${p'}$ with ${\|p'-p\|<\delta}$ satisfies ${\|z'-z\|<\varepsilon}.$

assumptions.text: ${Z}$ is closed.
${Z}$ contains the idle plan ${0}.$
${Z}$ is strictly convex.
The profit target is zero: ${\rho=0}.$
the base price vector is strictly positive: ${p\gg 0}.$
${z}$ solves the problem at ${p}.$

statements.title: Supply is monotonic in the profit target
statements.statement: Original claim: given sensible assumptions, this profit-target, output-maximizing producer has a supply function that is monotonic in ${\rho}.$ No assumptions are specified.

statements.title: Output falls weakly as the profit target rises
statements.statement: A producer has a technology ${Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{L+1}}$ (inputs ${1,\dots,L},$ output ${K=L+1}$) and faces prices ${p}.$ A plan ${z}$ solves his problem at profit target ${\rho}$ if either some plan ${w\in Z}$ earns ${p\cdot w\ge\rho},$ and ${z}$ is such a plan with the largest output ${z_K};$ or no plan earns ${\rho},$ and ${z=0}.$ Suppose every plan in ${Z}$ yields a nonnegative output. If ${\rho\le\rho'},$ ${z}$ solves the problem at ${\rho}$ and ${z'}$ solves it at ${\rho'},$ both at the same prices ${p},$ then ${z'_K\le z_K}.$

assumptions.text: every plan yields a nonnegative output: ${z_K\ge 0}$ for all ${z\in Z}.$
The profit targets are ordered: ${\rho\le\rho'}.$

entries.title: Information gathering and a non-convex cost function

statements.title: The survey firm’s product, and a best schedule exists
statements.statement: A firm with ${n\ge 1}$ workers runs a survey over four periods. In each period a worker either talks to one respondent, or takes part in one transfer of information with one colleague, or is idle; what a worker knows grows only through his own interview or through what his transfer partner knew. At the end, everything collected must be held by one worker, the announcer. The firm’s product is the number of distinct respondents interviewed. For every workforce size ${n},$ the set of products the firm can achieve has a largest element.

statements.title: The survey firm’s cost function
statements.statement:
A firm with ${n\ge 1}$ workers runs a survey over four periods. In each period a worker either talks to one respondent, or takes part in one transfer of information with one colleague, or is idle; what a worker knows grows only through his own interview or through what his transfer partner knew. At the end, everything collected must be held by one worker, the announcer. The firm’s product is the number of distinct respondents interviewed. Each worker costs ${w>0},$ busy or idle, and ${C(y)}$ is the least wage bill of a workforce that can achieve the product ${y}.$ The least wage bill exists exactly when some workforce achieves ${y},$ and then
$$C(y)=\begin{cases} w, & y\le 4,\\ 2w, & y\in\{5,6\},\\ 3w, & y=7,\\ 4w, & y\ge 8.\end{cases}$$

assumptions.text: The wage is positive: ${w>0}.$

statements.title: The survey firm’s cost function is not convex
statements.statement:
For the survey firm above, it is not the case that for every population of respondents, every wage ${w>0}$ and every product level ${y},$ the least wage bills satisfy
$$\begin{aligned}&C(y+1)-C(y)\\&\qquad\le C(y+2)-C(y+1).\end{aligned}$$
That is, the cost function is not convex.

entries.title: A firm that aggregates expert recommendations

statements.title: The best report quality with one, two and three experts
statements.statement:
An event occurs with probability ${1/2}.$ Each of ${k}$ experts independently gives a recommendation that is correct with probability ${p},$ ${1/2<p<1};$ the firm reports according to a rule ${r:\{0,1\}^k\to\{0,1\}},$ and ${f(k)}$ is the greatest probability of a correct report over all rules. Then
$$\begin{gathered}f(1)=f(2)=p,\\ f(3)=3p^2-2p^3.\end{gathered}$$

assumptions.text: Experts are better than chance: ${p>1/2}.$
Experts are fallible: ${p<1}.$

statements.title: The expert production function is not concave
statements.statement: An event occurs with probability ${1/2}.$ Each of ${k}$ experts independently gives a recommendation that is correct with probability ${p},$ ${1/2<p<1};$ the firm reports according to a rule ${r:\{0,1\}^k\to\{0,1\}},$ and ${f(k)}$ is the greatest probability of a correct report over all rules. It is not the case that for every ${p\in(1/2,1)}$ the marginal products are nonincreasing, i.e. that $f(k+2)-f(k+1)\le f(k+1)-f(k)$ for every ${k}.$

statements.title: With concave production, hire while marginal revenue exceeds the wage
statements.statement:
Let ${f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be a discrete production function, ${M}$ the revenue per unit of output and ${w}$ the wage. Suppose the marginal products of ${f}$ are nonincreasing, and let ${k^*}$ be the last worker whose marginal revenue exceeds the wage: the largest ${j\ge 1}$ with ${w<M\,[f(j)-f(j-1)]}.$ Then ${k^*}$ workers earn the greatest profit: for every ${k\in\mathbb{N}},$
$$Mf(k^*)-wk^*\ge Mf(k)-wk.$$

assumptions.text: Marginal products are nonincreasing: $f(j+2)-f(j+1)\le f(j+1)-f(j)$ for every ${j}.$
${k^*}$ is the largest ${j\ge 1}$ with ${w<M\,[f(j)-f(j-1)]}.$

statements.title: For the expert firm, the marginal hiring rule can fail
statements.statement: An event occurs with probability ${1/2}.$ Each of ${k}$ experts independently gives a recommendation that is correct with probability ${p},$ ${1/2<p<1};$ the firm reports according to a rule ${r:\{0,1\}^k\to\{0,1\}},$ and ${f(k)}$ is the greatest probability of a correct report over all rules. It is not the case that for every ${p\in(1/2,1)},$ every prize ${M}$ and every wage ${w},$ the largest ${k^*\ge 1}$ with ${w<M\,[f(k^*)-f(k^*-1)]}$ maximizes the profit ${Mf(k)-wk}.$

entries.title: A producer–consumer run by three centers

statements.title: Profit maximization at harmony prices yields the agent’s optimum
statements.statement: An agent owns ${a_0}$ units of good 1 and can turn ${a\in[0,a_0]}$ of them into ${f(a)}$ units of good 2, so he can consume any bundle in $F=\{(a_0-a,\,f(a)) : 0\le a\le a_0\}.$ The function ${f}$ is nondecreasing, continuous and strictly concave on ${[0,a_0]},$ and his preference ${\succsim}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ is monotone, continuous and convex. Prices ${p}$ create harmony at a bundle ${x}$ if ${x}$ is a best bundle in the budget set ${B(p,\,p\cdot x)}.$ Let ${a^*}$ maximize profit ${p_2f(a)-p_1a}$ over ${[0,a_0]}$ (Rule 1) and let ${x^*=(a_0-a^*,\,f(a^*))}.$ If ${p}$ creates harmony at ${x^*},$ then ${x^*}$ is a best bundle in ${F}$: ${x^*\succsim (a_0-a,\,f(a))}$ for every ${a\in[0,a_0]}.$

assumptions.text: ${f}$ is nondecreasing on ${[0,a_0]}.$
${f}$ is continuous on ${[0,a_0]}.$
${f}$ is strictly concave on ${[0,a_0]}.$
${\succsim}$ is monotone.
${\succsim}$ is continuous.
${\succsim}$ is convex.
Rule 1: ${a^*\in[0,a_0]}$ maximizes ${p_2f(a)-p_1a}$ over ${[0,a_0]}.$
${x^*}$ is the production center’s outcome: ${x^*=(a_0-a^*,\,f(a^*))}.$
Harmony: ${x^*}$ is a best bundle in ${B(p,\,p\cdot x^*)}.$

statements.title: Under Rule 2 the agent buys as if his wealth were max{p₁a₀, p₂f(a₀)}
statements.statement:
An agent owns ${a_0}$ units of good 1 and can turn ${a\in[0,a_0]}$ of them into ${f(a)}$ units of good 2, so he can consume any bundle in $F=\{(a_0-a,\,f(a)) : 0\le a\le a_0\}.$ The function ${f}$ is nondecreasing, continuous and strictly concave on ${[0,a_0]},$ and his preference ${\succsim}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ is monotone, continuous and convex. Prices ${p}$ create harmony at a bundle ${x}$ if ${x}$ is a best bundle in the budget set ${B(p,\,p\cdot x)}.$ Say that ${a}$ follows Rule 2 at prices ${p}$ if it maximizes ${f(a)}$ over the ${a\in[0,a_0]}$ with ${p_2f(a)-p_1a\ge 0},$ and that ${x}$ is a Rule-2 outcome if ${x=(a_0-a,f(a))}$ for such an ${a}.$ Then for every bundle ${x}$: ${x}$ is a Rule-2 outcome at which ${p}$ creates harmony if and only if ${x}$ is a Rule-2 outcome that is a best bundle in
$$B\big(p,\ \max\{p_1a_0,\ p_2f(a_0)\}\big).$$

assumptions.text: ${f}$ is nondecreasing on ${[0,a_0]}.$
${f}$ is continuous on ${[0,a_0]}.$
${f}$ is strictly concave on ${[0,a_0]}.$
${\succsim}$ is monotone.
${\succsim}$ is continuous.
${\succsim}$ is convex.

statements.title: Rule 1 leaves the agent better off, at a smaller scale
statements.statement: An agent owns ${a_0}$ units of good 1 and can turn ${a\in[0,a_0]}$ of them into ${f(a)}$ units of good 2, so he can consume any bundle in $F=\{(a_0-a,\,f(a)) : 0\le a\le a_0\}.$ The function ${f}$ is nondecreasing, continuous and strictly concave on ${[0,a_0]},$ and his preference ${\succsim}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ is monotone, continuous and convex. Prices ${p}$ create harmony at a bundle ${x}$ if ${x}$ is a best bundle in the budget set ${B(p,\,p\cdot x)}.$ Two such agents share ${a_0},$ ${f}$ and ${\succsim}.$ The first follows Rule 1 at prices ${p},$ with input ${a_1}$ and bundle ${x_1=(a_0-a_1,f(a_1))};$ the second follows Rule 2 at prices ${q},$ with input ${a_2}$ and bundle ${x_2=(a_0-a_2,f(a_2))};$ and each price vector creates harmony at its own agent’s bundle. Then ${x_1\succsim x_2},$ ${a_1\le a_2}$ and ${f(a_1)\le f(a_2)}.$

assumptions.text: ${f}$ is nondecreasing on ${[0,a_0]}.$
${f}$ is continuous on ${[0,a_0]}.$
${f}$ is strictly concave on ${[0,a_0]}.$
${\succsim}$ is monotone.
${\succsim}$ is continuous.
${\succsim}$ is convex.
Rule 1: ${a_1}$ maximizes ${p_2f(a)-p_1a}$ over ${[0,a_0]}.$
${x_1}$ is the first agent’s outcome: ${x_1=(a_0-a_1,\,f(a_1))}.$
Harmony for the first agent: ${x_1}$ is a best bundle in ${B(p,\,p\cdot x_1)}.$
Rule 2: ${a_2}$ maximizes ${f(a)}$ over the ${a\in[0,a_0]}$ with ${q_2f(a)-q_1a\ge 0}.$
${x_2}$ is the second agent’s outcome: ${x_2=(a_0-a_2,\,f(a_2))}.$
Harmony for the second agent: ${x_2}$ is a best bundle in ${B(q,\,q\cdot x_2)}.$

statements.title: Ranking lotteries by support size violates independence
statements.statement: Let ${Z}$ be a finite set of prizes and let ${\succsim}$ rank lotteries ${p,q\in L(Z)}$ by the size of their support: ${p\succsim q}$ if and only if $|\operatorname{supp}(p)|\le|\operatorname{supp}(q)|,$ where ${\operatorname{supp}(p)=\{z : p(z)>0\}}.$ If ${Z}$ has at least two prizes, ${\succsim}$ violates independence, the requirement that ${p\succsim q}$ if and only if $\alpha p\oplus(1-\alpha)r\succsim\alpha q\oplus(1-\alpha)r,$ for all lotteries ${p,q,r}$ and ${\alpha\in(0,1)}.$

assumptions.text: The set of prizes ${Z}$ is finite.
${Z}$ contains two distinct prizes.

statements.title: Ranking lotteries by support size violates continuity
statements.statement: Let ${Z}$ be a finite set of prizes and let ${\succsim}$ rank lotteries ${p,q\in L(Z)}$ by the size of their support: ${p\succsim q}$ if and only if $|\operatorname{supp}(p)|\le|\operatorname{supp}(q)|,$ where ${\operatorname{supp}(p)=\{z : p(z)>0\}}.$ If ${Z}$ has at least two prizes, ${\succsim}$ violates continuity, the requirement that whenever ${p\succ q},$ every ${p'}$ close to ${p}$ and every ${q'}$ close to ${q}$ satisfy ${p'\succ q'}.$

assumptions.text: The set of prizes ${Z}$ is finite.
${Z}$ contains two distinct prizes.

statements.title: Ranking lotteries by their most likely prize can violate independence
statements.statement: Let ${Z}$ be a finite set of prizes. A most-likely-prize preference is given by a preference ${\succsim_Z}$ over prizes and a rule ${m}$ that picks, for each lottery ${p},$ a prize ${m(p)}$ of maximal probability (ties broken arbitrarily); it ranks ${p\succsim q}$ if and only if ${m(p)\succsim_Z m(q)}.$ If ${Z}$ has at least two prizes, it is not the case that every such preference satisfies independence, the requirement that ${p\succsim q}$ if and only if $\alpha p\oplus(1-\alpha)r\succsim\alpha q\oplus(1-\alpha)r,$ for all lotteries ${p,q,r}$ and ${\alpha\in(0,1)}.$

assumptions.text: The set of prizes ${Z}$ is finite.
${Z}$ contains two distinct prizes.

statements.title: Ranking lotteries by their most likely prize can violate continuity
statements.statement: Let ${Z}$ be a finite set of prizes. A most-likely-prize preference is given by a preference ${\succsim_Z}$ over prizes and a rule ${m}$ that picks, for each lottery ${p},$ a prize ${m(p)}$ of maximal probability (ties broken arbitrarily); it ranks ${p\succsim q}$ if and only if ${m(p)\succsim_Z m(q)}.$ If ${Z}$ has at least two prizes, it is not the case that every such preference satisfies continuity, the requirement that whenever ${p\succ q},$ every ${p'}$ close to ${p}$ and every ${q'}$ close to ${q}$ satisfy ${p'\succ q'}.$

assumptions.text: The set of prizes ${Z}$ is finite.
${Z}$ contains two distinct prizes.

statements.title: The support-size preference is not immune to reframing
statements.statement: Call a preference over ${L(Z)}$ immune to reframing if, for every map ${\varphi:Z\to Z}$ that replaces each prize by one it regards as equally good (${[\varphi(z)]\sim[z]}$ for all ${z}$), it ranks any two lotteries ${p,q}$ exactly as it ranks their re-described versions ${\varphi(p),\varphi(q)},$ where ${\varphi(p)}$ gives each prize ${z'}$ the total probability ${p}$ assigns to the prizes mapped to ${z'}.$ Then for some finite prize set ${Z},$ the support-size preference (${p\succsim q}$ iff $|\operatorname{supp}(p)|\le|\operatorname{supp}(q)|$) is not immune to reframing.

statements.title: A most-likely-prize preference is not immune to reframing
statements.statement: Call a preference over ${L(Z)}$ immune to reframing if, for every map ${\varphi:Z\to Z}$ that replaces each prize by one it regards as equally good (${[\varphi(z)]\sim[z]}$ for all ${z}$), it ranks any two lotteries ${p,q}$ exactly as it ranks their re-described versions ${\varphi(p),\varphi(q)},$ where ${\varphi(p)}$ gives each prize ${z'}$ the total probability ${p}$ assigns to the prizes mapped to ${z'}.$ Then for some finite prize set ${Z},$ some preference ${\succsim_Z}$ over prizes and some rule ${m}$ selecting a most likely prize, the most-likely-prize preference (${p\succsim q}$ iff ${m(p)\succsim_Z m(q)}$) is not immune to reframing.

statements.title: Mean minus a quarter of the variance violates the vNM assumptions
statements.statement:
There is a finite set of monetary prizes on which the preference over lotteries represented by
$$u(L)=\mathrm{Ex}(L)-\tfrac14\,\mathrm{var}(L)$$
is not consistent with the vNM assumptions: it violates independence or continuity.

statements.title: Mean minus squared mean minus variance is an expected utility
statements.statement:
For every finite set of monetary prizes, the preference over lotteries represented by
$$u(L)=\mathrm{Ex}(L)-\big(\mathrm{Ex}(L)\big)^2-\mathrm{var}(L)$$
satisfies the vNM assumptions: independence and continuity.

assumptions.text: The set of prizes is finite, each prize being a sum of money.

entries.title: Deciding on Sunday or on Monday

statements.title: A contingent plan is a choice among mixed lotteries
statements.statement: Let ${Z}$ be finite, let ${L_1,L_2,L_3,L_4\in L(Z)}$ and ${0<\alpha<1}.$ Approach 2 is a choice problem over ${L(Z)}$: a choice from the nonempty menu of the mixtures ${\alpha p\oplus(1-\alpha)q}$ with ${p\in\{L_1,L_2\}}$ and ${q\in\{L_3,L_4\}},$ each plan corresponding to the mixture of the two lotteries it would pick.

assumptions.text: The set of prizes ${Z}$ is finite.
The first contingency has probability ${\alpha},$ with ${0<\alpha<1}.$

statements.title: Under independence, planning ahead and waiting choose alike
statements.statement: Let ${Z}$ be finite, let ${\succsim}$ be a preference on ${L(Z)}$ satisfying the independence axiom, and let ${L_1,\dots,L_4\in L(Z)}$ and ${0<\alpha<1}.$ Then the best elements of the menu $\{\alpha p\oplus(1-\alpha)q : p\in\{L_1,L_2\},\ q\in\{L_3,L_4\}\}$ are exactly the mixtures ${\alpha p\oplus(1-\alpha)q}$ in which ${p}$ is a best element of ${\{L_1,L_2\}}$ and ${q}$ a best element of ${\{L_3,L_4\}}.$

assumptions.text: The set of prizes ${Z}$ is finite.
The first contingency has probability ${\alpha},$ with ${0<\alpha<1}.$
${\succsim}$ satisfies independence: ${p\succsim q}$ if and only if $\beta p\oplus(1-\beta)r\succsim\beta q\oplus(1-\beta)r,$ for all ${p,q,r}$ and ${\beta\in(0,1)}.$

statements.title: With vNM preferences and Bayes’ rule, the decision never changes
statements.statement:
Let ${Z}$ be a finite set of consequences, ${z^*\in Z},$ and ${A}$ a set of actions. Action ${a}$ leads to the lottery ${p_a\in L(Z)}$ with ${p_a(z^*)=\alpha}$ for every ${a}$ and ${p_a(z)=(1-\alpha)\,q(a,z)}$ for ${z\neq z^*}.$ After learning that ${z^*}$ will not occur, action ${a}$ leads to a lottery ${p'_a}.$ Suppose the decision maker’s preference ${\succsim}$ on ${L(Z)}$ satisfies the vNM axioms (independence and continuity) and that he updates by Bayes’ rule: ${p'_a(z^*)=0}$ and ${p'_a(z)=p_a(z)/(1-p_a(z^*))}$ for ${z\ne z^*}.$ Then an action is a best action before the news if and only if it is a best action after it:
$$\begin{aligned}&\{a : p_a\succsim p_b\text{ for all } b\}\\&\qquad=\{a : p'_a\succsim p'_b\text{ for all } b\}.\end{aligned}$$

assumptions.text: The set of consequences ${Z}$ is finite.
Every action gives ${z^*}$ the same probability: ${p_a(z^*)=\alpha}.$
The other consequences have probability ${p_a(z)=(1-\alpha)\,q(a,z)}.$
After the news, ${z^*}$ has probability zero: ${p'_a(z^*)=0}.$
After the news, beliefs are updated by Bayes’ rule: ${p'_a(z)=p_a(z)/(1-p_a(z^*))}$ for ${z\neq z^*}.$
${\succsim}$ satisfies the vNM axioms: independence and continuity.

statements.title: Without expected utility, time consistency can fail
statements.statement: Let ${Z}$ be a finite set of consequences, ${z^*\in Z},$ and ${A}$ a set of actions. Action ${a}$ leads to the lottery ${p_a\in L(Z)}$ with ${p_a(z^*)=\alpha}$ for every ${a}$ and ${p_a(z)=(1-\alpha)\,q(a,z)}$ for ${z\neq z^*}.$ After learning that ${z^*}$ will not occur, action ${a}$ leads to a lottery ${p'_a}.$ The decision maker is time-consistent if every action that is best among ${\{p_a\}}$ remains best among ${\{p'_a\}}.$ There is such a situation, with a preference ${\succsim}$ on ${L(Z)},$ in which the decision maker updates by Bayes’ rule (${p'_a(z^*)=0}$ and ${p'_a(z)=p_a(z)/(1-p_a(z^*))}$ for ${z\ne z^*}$), ${\succsim}$ is not represented by any expected utility ${\sum_z p(z)v(z)},$ and the decision maker is not time-consistent.

statements.title: Without Bayesian updating, time consistency can fail
statements.statement: Let ${Z}$ be a finite set of consequences, ${z^*\in Z},$ and ${A}$ a set of actions. Action ${a}$ leads to the lottery ${p_a\in L(Z)}$ with ${p_a(z^*)=\alpha}$ for every ${a}$ and ${p_a(z)=(1-\alpha)\,q(a,z)}$ for ${z\neq z^*}.$ After learning that ${z^*}$ will not occur, action ${a}$ leads to a lottery ${p'_a}.$ The decision maker is time-consistent if every action that is best among ${\{p_a\}}$ remains best among ${\{p'_a\}}.$ There is such a situation, with a preference ${\succsim}$ on ${L(Z)}$ satisfying the vNM axioms, in which the post-news lotteries are not the Bayesian conditionals of the original ones and the decision maker is not time-consistent.

statements.title: An egalitarian ranking of income distributions violates independence
statements.statement: Call a preference ${\succsim}$ over income distributions on a finite set ${Z}$ of income levels *egalitarian* if every perfectly equal distribution ${[z]},$ in which everybody earns ${z},$ is weakly preferred to every distribution and strictly preferred to every distribution that is not perfectly equal. There are a finite set of income levels and an egalitarian preference on its distributions that violates the independence axiom.

statements.title: A proposed axiom: mixture quasi-convexity
statements.statement:
Our proposal: a preference ${\succsim}$ over income distributions on a finite set of income levels satisfies *mixture quasi-convexity* if for all distributions ${p,q}$ and every ${\alpha\in(0,1)},$
$$\begin{gathered}p\succsim\alpha p\oplus(1-\alpha)q\\ \text{or}\quad q\succsim\alpha p\oplus(1-\alpha)q.\end{gathered}$$

assumptions.text: The set of income levels is finite.

statements.title: Two different rankings satisfy mixture quasi-convexity
statements.statement: There are a finite set of income levels and two distinct preferences ${\succsim_1\neq\succsim_2}$ over its income distributions, each satisfying mixture quasi-convexity.

entries.title: Trading off quality and length of life

statements.title: Maximizing E[v(q)·t] satisfies the three conditions
statements.statement:
Outcomes are pairs ${(q,t)}$ with ${q,t\ge 0}$: a life of quality ${q}$ and length ${t}.$ Preferences are over lotteries with finite support on these outcomes, and ${[(q,t)]}$ is the sure outcome. The conditions are:
(1) ${[(q,0)]\sim[(q',0)]}$ for all ${q,q'};$
(2) for each ${q},$ every lottery on outcomes ${(q,t)}$ with expected length ${T}$ is indifferent to ${[(q,T)]};$
(3) ${[(q,t)]\succ[(q,t')]}$ whenever ${t>t'}.$ Let ${v}$ satisfy ${v(q)>0}$ for every ${q\ge 0},$ and rank lotteries by the expectation of ${v(q)\,t}.$ Then this preference has an expected-utility representation (the form the vNM assumptions take here) and satisfies conditions (1), (2) and (3).

assumptions.text: ${v}$ is positive: ${v(q)>0}$ for every quality ${q\ge 0}.$

statements.title: The three conditions force the form v(q)·t
statements.statement:
Outcomes are pairs ${(q,t)}$ with ${q,t\ge 0}$: a life of quality ${q}$ and length ${t}.$ Preferences are over lotteries with finite support on these outcomes, and ${[(q,t)]}$ is the sure outcome. The conditions are:
(1) ${[(q,0)]\sim[(q',0)]}$ for all ${q,q'};$
(2) for each ${q},$ every lottery on outcomes ${(q,t)}$ with expected length ${T}$ is indifferent to ${[(q,T)]};$
(3) ${[(q,t)]\succ[(q,t')]}$ whenever ${t>t'}.$ Let ${\succsim}$ have an expected-utility representation and satisfy conditions (1), (2) and (3). Then there is a function ${v}$ with ${v(q)>0}$ for all ${q\ge 0}$ such that ${\succsim}$ is represented by the expectation of ${v(q)\,t}.$

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ has an expected-utility representation: it ranks lotteries by the expectation of some ${U(q,t)}.$
Condition (1): ${[(q,0)]\sim[(q',0)]}$ for all qualities ${q,q'}.$
Condition (2): at a fixed quality, only expected length matters.
Condition (3): at a fixed quality, longer life is strictly better.

entries.title: A money pump against someone who believes 2 + 3 = 6
entries.name: A money pump

statements.title: A money pump exists, and it extracts unboundedly
statements.statement: Model the decision maker by his arithmetic ${\oplus}$ on amounts: ${2\oplus 3=6},$ and ${x\oplus y=x+y}$ for every other pair. Holding ${h}$ units of a good, he accepts a trade that changes his holding by ${\delta}$ at a price ${c}$ whenever ${c<(h\oplus\delta)-h}.$ A money pump is a finite sequence of trades, each accepted at the holding it finds, that returns him to his initial holding while he pays a positive total. Then for some initial holding there is a money pump against him; moreover, money pumps from that holding extract more than any given amount.

statements.title: A schedule is a finite list of timed activities
statements.statement: A schedule over a set ${A}$ of activities is a finite list ${\big((a_1,t_1),\dots,(a_n,t_n)\big)}$ of pairs, each an activity and a duration: activity ${a_1}$ runs from ${0}$ to ${t_1},$ activity ${a_2}$ from ${t_1}$ to ${t_1+t_2},$ and so on.

statements.title: Two properties necessary for time-additive utility
statements.statement:
A schedule over a set ${A}$ of activities is a finite list ${s=\big((a_1,t_1),\dots,(a_n,t_n)\big)}$ of blocks: activity ${a_1}$ for duration ${t_1},$ then ${a_2}$ for duration ${t_2},$ and so on. Write ${T_a(s)}$ for the total time ${s}$ gives to activity ${a}.$ Our proposal for the two properties:

- (i) **Time-allocation invariance.** If ${T_a(s)=T_a(s')}$ for every activity ${a},$ then ${s\succsim s'}.$
- (ii) **Concatenation independence.** If ${s\succsim s'},$ then ${s}$ followed by ${t}$ is weakly preferred to ${s'}$ followed by ${t},$ for every schedule ${t}.$

If ${\succsim}$ is represented by ${U(s)=\sum_{a\in A}v(a)\,T_a(s)}$ for some ${v},$ it satisfies (i) and (ii); and the two properties are different.

assumptions.text: The set of activities ${A}$ is finite.
${\succsim}$ is represented by ${U(s)=\sum_{a\in A}v(a)\,T_a(s)}$ for some values ${v(a)}.$

statements.title: A taste for balance has no time-additive representation
statements.statement: A schedule over a set ${A}$ of activities is a finite list ${s=\big((a_1,t_1),\dots,(a_n,t_n)\big)}$ of blocks: activity ${a_1}$ for duration ${t_1},$ then ${a_2}$ for duration ${t_2},$ and so on. Write ${T_a(s)}$ for the total time ${s}$ gives to activity ${a}.$ There are a finite set of activities and a preference ${\succsim}$ over schedules that is not represented by ${U(s)=\sum_{a\in A}v(a)\,T_a(s)}$ for any values ${v}.$

statements.title: Nonnegative on positive vectors iff all coefficients are nonnegative
statements.statement:
For real numbers ${a_1,\dots,a_n},$ the inequality
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_kx_k\ge 0$$
holds for every ${x\gg 0}$ if and only if ${a_k\ge 0}$ for every ${k}.$

statements.title: Nonnegative on decreasing positive vectors iff partial sums are
statements.statement:
For real numbers ${a_1,\dots,a_n},$ the inequality
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_kx_k\ge 0$$
holds for every ${x}$ with ${x_1>x_2>\dots>x_n>0}$ if and only if every partial sum of the coefficients is nonnegative:
$$\sum_{k=1}^{l}a_k\ge 0\qquad\text{for every } l.$$

statements.title: First-order dominance implies second-order dominance
statements.statement: Prizes are sums of money in a set ${Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}},$ and lotteries have finite support. ${pD_2q}$ means that ${p\succsim q}$ for every preference ${\succsim}$ represented by an expected utility ${\mathbb{E}u}$ that is monotone (${a>b}$ implies ${[a]\succ[b]}$) and risk averse (${[\mathbb{E}p]\succsim p}$ for every ${p}$ whose expectation lies in ${Z}$). If ${p}$ first-order stochastically dominates ${q}$ (${pD_1q}$: every expected-utility preference that is monotone in money weakly prefers ${p}$ to ${q}$), then ${pD_2q}.$

assumptions.text: ${p}$ first-order stochastically dominates ${q}.$

statements.title: Adding zero-mean noise yields a second-order dominated lottery
statements.statement:
Prizes are sums of money in a set ${Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}},$ and lotteries have finite support. ${pD_2q}$ means that ${p\succsim q}$ for every preference ${\succsim}$ represented by an expected utility ${\mathbb{E}u}$ that is monotone (${a>b}$ implies ${[a]\succ[b]}$) and risk averse (${[\mathbb{E}p]\succsim p}$ for every ${p}$ whose expectation lies in ${Z}$). For lotteries ${p}$ and ${\varepsilon},$ let ${p+\varepsilon}$ yield ${t}$ with probability $\sum_{\alpha+\beta=t}p(\alpha)\varepsilon(\beta)$: the distribution of the sum of independent draws from ${p}$ and ${\varepsilon}.$ If ${\varepsilon}$ has expectation ${0},$ then
$$p\;D_2\;(p+\varepsilon).$$

assumptions.text: ${\varepsilon}$ has expectation zero: ${\sum_z\varepsilon(z)\,z=0}.$

statements.title: A partial-sum test for second-order stochastic dominance
statements.statement:
Prizes are sums of money in a set ${Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}},$ and lotteries have finite support. ${pD_2q}$ means that ${p\succsim q}$ for every preference ${\succsim}$ represented by an expected utility ${\mathbb{E}u}$ that is monotone (${a>b}$ implies ${[a]\succ[b]}$) and risk averse (${[\mathbb{E}p]\succsim p}$ for every ${p}$ whose expectation lies in ${Z}$). Let ${x_0<x_1<\dots<x_K}$ be all the prizes in the support of ${p}$ or ${q},$ and ${G(p,x)=\sum_{z\ge x}p(z)}.$ Then ${pD_2q}$ if and only if, for every ${t<K},$
$$\sum_{k=0}^{t}\Delta_{k+1}\,(x_{k+1}-x_k)\ge 0,$$
where ${\Delta_k=G(p,x_k)-G(q,x_k)}.$

assumptions.text: Each ${x_i}$ is a prize in the support of ${p}$ or of ${q}.$
The ${x_i}$ are strictly increasing.
Every prize in the support of ${p}$ or of ${q}$ is one of the ${x_i}.$

statements.title: Preference reversal, a question for discussion
statements.statement: The problem asks for a discussion of the preference-reversal phenomenon for ${L_1=(8/9)[\$4]\oplus(1/9)[\$0]}$ and ${L_2=(1/9)[\$40]\oplus(8/9)[\$0]}.$ It contains no formal statement to check.

entries.title: Preferences over portfolios of risky assets

statements.title: The induced preference over portfolios is monotone
statements.statement: Take ${K}$ assets whose random returns ${Z_1,\dots,Z_K}$ are independent, positive and finitely valued. A holding ${x\in\mathbb{R}^K_+}$ yields wealth ${\sum_k x_kZ_k},$ and the investor compares holdings by expected utility: ${x\succsim y}$ if and only if $\mathbb{E}\,v\big(\sum_k x_kZ_k\big)\ge\mathbb{E}\,v\big(\sum_k y_kZ_k\big).$ The claim: for ${v}$ increasing and concave, this preference on ${\mathbb{R}^K_+}$ is monotone (${x\ge y}$ gives ${x\succsim y},$ and ${x\gg y}$ gives ${x\succ y}$), for any number ${K}$ of assets.

assumptions.text: The returns are independent and positive, each taking finitely many values.
${v}$ is strictly increasing on ${[0,\infty)}.$
${v}$ is concave on ${[0,\infty)}.$

statements.title: With at least one asset, the induced preference is monotone
statements.statement: There are ${K}$ assets with independent random returns ${Z_1,\dots,Z_K},$ each positive and taking finitely many values. An investor holding ${x\in\mathbb{R}^K_+}$ receives wealth ${\sum_k x_kZ_k}$ and ranks holdings by expected utility, ${x\succsim y}$ if and only if $\mathbb{E}\,v\big(\sum_k x_kZ_k\big)\ge\mathbb{E}\,v\big(\sum_k y_kZ_k\big).$ If ${K\ge 1}$ and ${v}$ is strictly increasing and concave on ${[0,\infty)},$ the induced preference on ${\mathbb{R}^K_+}$ is monotone: ${x\ge y}$ implies ${x\succsim y},$ and ${x\gg y}$ implies ${x\succ y}.$

assumptions.text: there is at least one asset: ${K\ge 1}.$
The returns are independent and positive, each taking finitely many values.
${v}$ is strictly increasing on ${[0,\infty)}.$
${v}$ is concave on ${[0,\infty)}.$

statements.title: The induced preference over portfolios is convex
statements.statement: There are ${K}$ assets with independent random returns ${Z_1,\dots,Z_K},$ each positive and taking finitely many values. An investor holding ${x\in\mathbb{R}^K_+}$ receives wealth ${\sum_k x_kZ_k}$ and ranks holdings by expected utility, ${x\succsim y}$ if and only if $\mathbb{E}\,v\big(\sum_k x_kZ_k\big)\ge\mathbb{E}\,v\big(\sum_k y_kZ_k\big).$ If ${v}$ is strictly increasing and concave on ${[0,\infty)},$ the induced preference is convex: ${x\succsim y}$ implies ${\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y\succsim y}$ for every ${\alpha\in(0,1)}.$

assumptions.text: The returns are independent and positive, each taking finitely many values.
${v}$ is strictly increasing on ${[0,\infty)}.$
${v}$ is concave on ${[0,\infty)}.$

statements.title: One apple today beats two apples a day from day 4 on

assumptions.text: Adam likes up to two apples a day: raising ${x_t}$ by one when ${x_t\le 1}$ is strictly better.
Adam cannot bear three apples a day: raising ${x_t}$ from ${2}$ to ${3}$ is strictly worse.
Adam is impatient: when ${x_t\le 1}$ and ${x_{t+1}\ge 1},$ moving an apple from day ${t+1}$ to day ${t}$ is strictly better.
On a day without an apple, Adam prefers one apple now to two tomorrow: when ${x_t=0}$ and ${x_{t+1}\ge 2},$ taking one apple on day ${t}$ for two on day ${t+1}$ is strictly better.

statements.title: The dual functional W induces a preference relation
statements.statement:
Let prizes be sums of money in a set ${Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}}$ and lotteries have finite support. For a lottery ${p}$ whose support is ${z_0<z_1<\dots<z_K},$ let ${G_p(z_k)=\sum_{j\ge k}p(z_j)}$ and
$$W(p)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}f\big(G_p(z_k)\big)\,(z_k-z_{k-1}),$$
where ${f:[0,1]\to[0,1]}$ is continuous and strictly increasing. Then some preference relation on lotteries is represented by ${W}.$

assumptions.text: ${f}$ is continuous on ${[0,1]}.$
${f}$ is strictly increasing on ${[0,1]}.$

statements.title: The dual functional can violate independence
statements.statement:
For a lottery ${p}$ whose support is ${z_0<z_1<\dots<z_K},$ let ${G_p(z_k)=\sum_{j\ge k}p(z_j)}$ and
$$W(p)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}f\big(G_p(z_k)\big)\,(z_k-z_{k-1}),$$
where ${f:[0,1]\to[0,1]}$ is continuous and strictly increasing. There are a set of monetary prizes ${Z}$ and such an ${f}$ for which the preference represented by ${W}$ violates independence: the equivalence $p\succsim q\iff\alpha p\oplus(1-\alpha)r\succsim\alpha q\oplus(1-\alpha)r$ fails for some lotteries ${p,q,r}$ and some ${\alpha\in(0,1)}.$

statements.title: Weighting each prize’s probability can violate stochastic dominance
statements.statement: For lotteries with monetary prizes, let ${V(p)=\sum_{z}f\big(p(z)\big)\,u(z)}.$ There are a set of prizes, a continuous strictly increasing ${f:[0,1]\to[0,1]},$ a strictly increasing ${u},$ and lotteries ${p,q}$ such that ${p}$ first-order stochastically dominates ${q}$ and yet ${V(q)>V(p)}.$

statements.title: Your friend’s envelope is always worth more
statements.statement: Draw ${n\in\{0,1,2,\dots\}}$ with probability ${2^n/3^{n+1}},$ and place ${2^n}$ and ${2^{n+1}}$ in two envelopes, one for you and one for your friend. The claim: your envelope is assigned at random, and for any amount found in it, your friend's envelope has a higher expected amount.

statements.title: With a fair coin, your friend’s envelope is always worth more
statements.statement:
A number ${n\in\{0,1,2,\dots\}}$ is drawn with probability ${2^n/3^{n+1}},$ and the amounts ${2^n}$ and ${2^{n+1}}$ are put into two envelopes; one envelope goes to you and the other to your friend. If each of the two envelopes is given to you with probability ${1/2},$ independently of ${n},$ then, writing ${X}$ and ${Y}$ for the amounts in your envelope and in your friend’s, for every amount ${x}$ your envelope can hold
$$\mathbb{E}[\,Y\mid X=x\,]>x.$$

assumptions.text: the envelopes are assigned by a fair coin: you receive each of the two with probability ${1/2},$ whatever ${n}$ is.

statements.title: More risk aversion can raise or lower the value of information
Every Borda rule violates independence of irrelevant alternatives
statements.statement:
Let the sets of alternatives ${X}$ and individuals ${N}$ be finite, with ${|X|\ge 3}$ and ${|N|\ge 2},$ and let the weights satisfy ${w(1)>w(2)>\dots>w(|X|)}.$ Each individual has a strict ordering ${\succ_i}$ of ${X},$ and ${r_i(x)}$ is the number of alternatives ${i}$ ranks at least as high as ${x},$ so his top alternative has ${r_i=1}.$ The Borda rule ranks ${x\succsim y}$ if and only if
$$\sum_{i\in N}w\big(r_i(x)\big)\ge\sum_{i\in N}w\big(r_i(y)\big).$$
Then the Borda rule violates IIA: for some two profiles in which every individual ranks ${x}$ against ${y}$ in the same way, society ranks ${x}$ against ${y}$ differently.

assumptions.text: The set of alternatives ${X}$ is finite.
The set of individuals ${N}$ is finite.
The weights are strictly decreasing: ${w(1)>w(2)>\dots>w(|X|)}.$
There are at least three alternatives.
There are at least two individuals.

statements.title: Majority rule is anonymous, neutral and positively responsive
statements.statement: Let ${X=\{a,b\}}$ with ${a\neq b},$ and let ${N}$ be a finite set of individuals, each with a preference on ${X}$ (indifference allowed). A social welfare function ${F}$ assigns a preference ${\succsim=F(p)}$ on ${X}$ to every profile ${p}.$ The majority rule ranks ${x\succsim y}$ if and only if at least as many individuals strictly prefer ${x}$ to ${y}$ as strictly prefer ${y}$ to ${x}.$ Anonymity: permuting the individuals’ preferences leaves ${F(p)}$ unchanged. Neutrality: reversing every individual’s preference reverses ${F(p)}.$ Positive responsiveness: if a single individual moves toward ${x},$ from indifference to ${x\succ y}$ or from ${y\succ x}$ to indifference, and society ranked ${x\succsim y}$ before, then society ranks ${x\succ y}$ after. Then the majority rule satisfies anonymity, neutrality and positive responsiveness.

assumptions.text: The set of individuals ${N}$ is finite.
The two alternatives are distinct: ${a\neq b}.$
There is no third alternative: every ${x\in X}$ is ${a}$ or ${b}.$

statements.title: May’s theorem: only majority rule satisfies the three axioms
statements.statement: Let ${X=\{a,b\}}$ with ${a\neq b},$ and let ${N}$ be a finite set of individuals, each with a preference on ${X}$ (indifference allowed). A social welfare function ${F}$ assigns a preference ${\succsim=F(p)}$ on ${X}$ to every profile ${p}.$ The majority rule ranks ${x\succsim y}$ if and only if at least as many individuals strictly prefer ${x}$ to ${y}$ as strictly prefer ${y}$ to ${x}.$ Anonymity: permuting the individuals’ preferences leaves ${F(p)}$ unchanged. Neutrality: reversing every individual’s preference reverses ${F(p)}.$ Positive responsiveness: if a single individual moves toward ${x},$ from indifference to ${x\succ y}$ or from ${y\succ x}$ to indifference, and society ranked ${x\succsim y}$ before, then society ranks ${x\succ y}$ after. Then an SWF ${F}$ satisfies anonymity, neutrality and positive responsiveness if and only if it is the majority rule: at every profile, ${x\succsim y}$ under ${F}$ exactly when at least as many individuals strictly prefer ${x}$ to ${y}$ as strictly prefer ${y}$ to ${x}.$

Let ${\succsim}$ be a binary relation on a set ${X},$ let ${u:X\to\mathbb{R}}$ represent it, ${x\succsim y\iff u(x)\ge u(y)},$ and let ${f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be strictly increasing. Then ${v=f\circ u}$ also represents ${\succsim}$:
$$x\succsim y\iff f\big(u(x)\big)\ge f\big(u(y)\big).$$

statements.title: Optimal coverage equates marginal benefit and marginal cost
statements.statement:
A consumer with a strictly concave von Neumann–Morgenstern utility ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ and wealth ${w}$ loses ${L}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ Coverage ${q\in\mathbb{R}}$ costs ${\pi q},$ so her final wealth is ${w-\pi q}$ without the loss and ${w-L+(1-\pi)q}$ with it, and her expected utility is
$$\begin{aligned}U(q)&=(1-p)\,u(w-\pi q)\\&\quad+p\,u\big(w-L+(1-\pi)q\big).\end{aligned}$$
Coverage ${q}$ is optimal if it maximizes ${U}$ over all real ${q}.$ Then ${q}$ is optimal if and only if ${u}$ has supporting slopes ${s_0}$ at ${w-\pi q}$ and ${s_1}$ at ${w-L+(1-\pi)q}$ (so that ${u(t)\le u(a)+s\,(t-a)}$ for all ${t}$ at the corresponding point ${a}$) with
$$p\,(1-\pi)\,s_1=\pi\,(1-p)\,s_0 .$$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is strictly concave: the consumer is strictly risk averse.
${p}$ is a probability: ${0\le p\le 1}.$

$$\begin{aligned}U(q)&=(1-p)\,u(w-\pi q)\\&\quad+p\,u\big(w-L+(1-\pi)q\big).\end{aligned}$$
Coverage ${q}$ is optimal if it maximizes ${U}$ over all real ${q}.$ If insurance is actuarially fair, ${\pi=p},$ then ${q}$ is optimal if and only if ${q=L}$ or ${p\in\{0,1\}}.$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is strictly concave: the consumer is strictly risk averse.
${p}$ is a probability: ${0\le p\le 1}.$

statements.title: With loaded insurance, coverage is on one side of full
statements.statement:
A consumer with a strictly concave von Neumann–Morgenstern utility ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ and wealth ${w}$ loses ${L}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ Coverage ${q\in\mathbb{R}}$ costs ${\pi q},$ so her final wealth is ${w-\pi q}$ without the loss and ${w-L+(1-\pi)q}$ with it, and her expected utility is
$$\begin{aligned}U(q)&=(1-p)\,u(w-\pi q)\\&\quad+p\,u\big(w-L+(1-\pi)q\big).\end{aligned}$$
Coverage ${q}$ is optimal if it maximizes ${U}$ over all real ${q}.$ If ${\pi>p},$ then ${q}$ is optimal if and only if the marginal condition of part (a) holds and, writing ${\bar w=w-\pi L}$ for the wealth full coverage guarantees:

- if ${u}$ is higher at some wealth above ${\bar w},$ then ${q\le L};$
- if ${\bar w}$ maximizes ${u},$ then ${q=L};$
- if ${u}$ is higher at some wealth below ${\bar w},$ then ${q\ge L}.$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is strictly concave: the consumer is strictly risk averse.
${p}$ is a probability: ${0\le p\le 1}.$

statements.title: The elasticity of the gain from paying with respect to detection
statements.statement:
Let ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be infinitely differentiable, strictly increasing and concave. A citizen with wealth ${w}$ who feeds the meter pays ${m};$ one who parks illegally is fined ${f}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ The gain from feeding the meter is
$$\begin{gathered}\Delta(w)=u(w-m)\\-\big[p\,u(w-f)+(1-p)\,u(w)\big].\end{gathered}$$ Then the elasticity of ${\Delta}$ with respect to ${p}$ is
$$\begin{aligned}\varepsilon_p&=\frac{p}{\Delta}\,\frac{\partial\Delta}{\partial p}\\[4pt]&=\frac{p\,\big[u(w)-u(w-f)\big]}{\Delta}.\end{aligned}$$
