statements.title: If violators strictly prefer to park, both groups force m > pf
statements.statement:
Let ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be infinitely differentiable, strictly increasing and concave. A citizen with wealth ${w}$ who feeds the meter pays ${m};$ one who parks illegally is fined ${f}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ The gain from feeding the meter is
$$\begin{gathered}\Delta(w)=u(w-m)\\-\big[p\,u(w-f)+(1-p)\,u(w)\big].\end{gathered}$$ Citizens’ wealth ranges over ${[\underline w,\bar w]}.$ If ${\Delta}$ is decreasing in wealth on that range, some citizen has ${\Delta>0}$ and some citizen has ${\Delta<0},$ then ${pf<m}.$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is differentiable as many times as needed.
${u}$ is strictly increasing.
${u}$ is concave.
${p}$ is a probability: ${0\le p\le 1}.$
${\Delta}$ is decreasing in wealth on ${[\underline w,\bar w]}.$
Some citizen in the range feeds the meter: ${\Delta(w)>0}.$
Some citizen in the range strictly prefers to park illegally: ${\Delta(w)<0}.$

statements.title: A higher fine never shrinks the set of meter-feeders
statements.statement:
Let ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be infinitely differentiable, strictly increasing and concave. A citizen with wealth ${w}$ who feeds the meter pays ${m};$ one who parks illegally is fined ${f}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ The gain from feeding the meter is
$$\begin{gathered}\Delta(w)=u(w-m)\\-\big[p\,u(w-f)+(1-p)\,u(w)\big].\end{gathered}$$ Let ${F(f,m,p)}$ be the set of wealth levels ${w\in[\underline w,\bar w]}$ with ${\Delta(w)>0}$: the citizens who feed the meter. Then ${F}$ is weakly increasing in ${f}$: ${f\le f'}$ implies ${F(f,m,p)\subseteq F(f',m,p)}.$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is differentiable as many times as needed.
${u}$ is strictly increasing.
${u}$ is concave.
${p}$ is a probability: ${0\le p\le 1}.$

statements.title: A pricier meter never enlarges the set of meter-feeders
statements.statement:
Let ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be infinitely differentiable, strictly increasing and concave. A citizen with wealth ${w}$ who feeds the meter pays ${m};$ one who parks illegally is fined ${f}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ The gain from feeding the meter is
$$\begin{gathered}\Delta(w)=u(w-m)\\-\big[p\,u(w-f)+(1-p)\,u(w)\big].\end{gathered}$$ Let ${F(f,m,p)}$ be the set of wealth levels ${w\in[\underline w,\bar w]}$ with ${\Delta(w)>0}$: the citizens who feed the meter. Then ${F}$ is weakly decreasing in ${m}$: ${m\le m'}$ implies ${F(f,m',p)\subseteq F(f,m,p)}.$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is differentiable as many times as needed.
${u}$ is strictly increasing.
${u}$ is concave.
${p}$ is a probability: ${0\le p\le 1}.$

statements.title: With a nonnegative fine, more policing never shrinks the set of payers
statements.statement:
Let ${u:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be infinitely differentiable, strictly increasing and concave. A citizen with wealth ${w}$ who feeds the meter pays ${m};$ one who parks illegally is fined ${f}$ with probability ${p\in[0,1]}.$ The gain from feeding the meter is
$$\begin{gathered}\Delta(w)=u(w-m)\\-\big[p\,u(w-f)+(1-p)\,u(w)\big].\end{gathered}$$ Let ${F(f,m,p)}$ be the set of wealth levels ${w\in[\underline w,\bar w]}$ with ${\Delta(w)>0}$: the citizens who feed the meter. Then, as ${p}$ ranges over ${[0,1]}$: if ${f\ge 0},$ ${F}$ is weakly increasing in ${p};$ if ${f\le 0},$ it is weakly decreasing in ${p}.$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is differentiable as many times as needed.
${u}$ is strictly increasing.
${u}$ is concave.

statements.title: Independence implies betweenness
statements.statement: Lotteries are probability vectors over three outcomes, and ${\succsim}$ is a binary relation on lotteries, with ${L\sim L'}$ when ${L\succsim L'}$ and ${L'\succsim L}.$ Betweenness: ${L\sim L'}$ implies ${\lambda L+(1-\lambda)L'\sim L}$ for every ${\lambda\in(0,1)}.$ If ${\succsim}$ satisfies independence: ${L\succsim L'}$ if and only if $\alpha L+(1-\alpha)L''\succsim\alpha L'+(1-\alpha)L'',$ for all ${L,L',L''}$ and ${\alpha\in(0,1)},$ then it satisfies betweenness.

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ satisfies the independence axiom.

statements.title: Continuity and betweenness make indifference curves straight
statements.statement: Lotteries are probability vectors over three outcomes, and ${\succsim}$ is a binary relation on lotteries, with ${L\sim L'}$ when ${L\succsim L'}$ and ${L'\succsim L}.$ Betweenness: ${L\sim L'}$ implies ${\lambda L+(1-\lambda)L'\sim L}$ for every ${\lambda\in(0,1)}.$ If ${\succsim}$ satisfies continuity: for all ${L,L',L''}$ the sets $\{\alpha\in[0,1]:\alpha L+(1-\alpha)L'\succsim L''\}$ and $\{\alpha\in[0,1]:L''\succsim\alpha L+(1-\alpha)L'\}$ are closed, together with betweenness, then its indifference curves are straight lines: ${L\sim L'}$ implies ${\alpha L+(1-\alpha)L'\sim L}$ for every ${\alpha\in[0,1]}.$

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ satisfies the continuity axiom.
${\succsim}$ satisfies the betweenness axiom.

statements.title: Straight indifference curves imply betweenness
statements.statement: Lotteries are probability vectors over three outcomes, and ${\succsim}$ is a binary relation on lotteries, with ${L\sim L'}$ when ${L\succsim L'}$ and ${L'\succsim L}.$ Betweenness: ${L\sim L'}$ implies ${\lambda L+(1-\lambda)L'\sim L}$ for every ${\lambda\in(0,1)}.$ If ${\succsim}$ has the property that its indifference curves are straight lines: ${L\sim L'}$ implies ${\alpha L+(1-\alpha)L'\sim L}$ for every ${\alpha\in[0,1]},$ then it satisfies betweenness.

assumptions.text: The indifference curves of ${\succsim}$ are straight lines.

statements.title: The straight indifference lines need not be parallel
statements.statement: Lotteries are probability vectors over three outcomes, and ${\succsim}$ is a binary relation on lotteries, with ${L\sim L'}$ when ${L\succsim L'}$ and ${L'\succsim L}.$ Betweenness: ${L\sim L'}$ implies ${\lambda L+(1-\lambda)L'\sim L}$ for every ${\lambda\in(0,1)}.$ It is not the case that every relation satisfying continuity and betweenness has parallel indifference lines, that is, that any two of its indifference sets that are lines are parallel.

statements.title: Betweenness is weaker than independence
statements.statement: Lotteries are probability vectors over three outcomes, and ${\succsim}$ is a binary relation on lotteries, with ${L\sim L'}$ when ${L\succsim L'}$ and ${L'\succsim L}.$ Betweenness: ${L\sim L'}$ implies ${\lambda L+(1-\lambda)L'\sim L}$ for every ${\lambda\in(0,1)}.$ There is a relation that satisfies betweenness but not independence.

statements.title: Betweenness is compatible with the Allais paradox
statements.statement:
Lotteries are probability vectors over three outcomes, and ${\succsim}$ is a binary relation on lotteries, with ${L\sim L'}$ when ${L\succsim L'}$ and ${L'\succsim L}.$ Betweenness: ${L\sim L'}$ implies ${\lambda L+(1-\lambda)L'\sim L}$ for every ${\lambda\in(0,1)}.$ Over the prizes \$2.5 million, \$0.5 million and \$0, let
$$\begin{aligned}L_1&=(0,\,1,\,0),\\ L_1'&=(0.10,\,0.89,\,0.01),\\ L_2&=(0,\,0.11,\,0.89),\\ L_2'&=(0.10,\,0,\,0.90).\end{aligned}$$
There is a relation satisfying betweenness with ${L_1\succ L_1'}$ and ${L_2'\succ L_2}.$

entries.title: Should the young hold more stocks?

statements.title: Age and the share of wealth in stocks, a question for discussion
statements.statement: The question asks for a discussion of why younger investors might hold a larger share of their wealth in stocks. It contains no formal statement to check.

entries.title: CES demand and the elasticity of substitution

statements.title: The CES elasticity of substitution is 1/(1 − ρ)
statements.statement:
Let ${u_\rho(x)=(x_1^\rho+x_2^\rho)^{1/\rho}}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+},$ and let ${p\gg 0}$ and ${w>0}.$ Walrasian demand ${x(p,w)}$ is the set of utility-maximizing bundles in ${B(p,w)},$ and the value of the problem is the indirect utility. A number ${\xi}$ is the elasticity of substitution at ${(p,w)}$ if, for ${p_1}$ near its value with ${p_2}$ fixed, demand is a single strictly positive bundle ${(x_1,x_2)}$ whose ratio ${x_1/x_2}$ is differentiable in ${p_1},$ and
$$\xi=-\frac{\partial(x_1/x_2)}{\partial(p_1/p_2)}\cdot\frac{p_1/p_2}{x_1/x_2}.$$
As printed: for every real ${\rho},$ ${\xi_{12}(p,w)=1/(1-\rho)};$ that is, every elasticity of substitution equals ${1/(1-\rho)},$ and ${1/(1-\rho)}$ is the elasticity whenever demand contains a strictly positive bundle.

assumptions.text: Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$

statements.title: For ρ ≠ 0, 1, the CES elasticity of substitution is 1/(1 − ρ)
statements.statement:
Let ${u_\rho(x)=(x_1^\rho+x_2^\rho)^{1/\rho}}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+},$ and let ${p\gg 0}$ and ${w>0}.$ Walrasian demand ${x(p,w)}$ is the set of utility-maximizing bundles in ${B(p,w)},$ and the value of the problem is the indirect utility. A number ${\xi}$ is the elasticity of substitution at ${(p,w)}$ if, for ${p_1}$ near its value with ${p_2}$ fixed, demand is a single strictly positive bundle ${(x_1,x_2)}$ whose ratio ${x_1/x_2}$ is differentiable in ${p_1},$ and
$$\xi=-\frac{\partial(x_1/x_2)}{\partial(p_1/p_2)}\cdot\frac{p_1/p_2}{x_1/x_2}.$$
If ${\rho\neq 0}$ and ${\rho\neq 1},$ every elasticity of substitution at ${(p,w)}$ equals ${1/(1-\rho)},$ and ${1/(1-\rho)}$ is the elasticity whenever demand contains a strictly positive bundle:
$$\xi_{12}(p,w)=\frac{1}{1-\rho}.$$

assumptions.text: ${\rho\neq 0}.$
${\rho\neq 1}.$
Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$

statements.title: Walrasian demand for CES utility

assumptions.text: ${\rho\neq 0}.$
Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$

statements.title: Indirect utility for CES utility
statements.statement:
Let ${u_\rho(x)=(x_1^\rho+x_2^\rho)^{1/\rho}}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+},$ and let ${p\gg 0}$ and ${w>0}.$ Walrasian demand ${x(p,w)}$ is the set of utility-maximizing bundles in ${B(p,w)},$ and the value of the problem is the indirect utility. If ${\rho\neq 0},$ the value of the utility maximization problem is ${v(p,w)=w/\min(p_1,p_2)}$ when ${\rho\ge 1},$ and when ${\rho<1}$ it is, with ${r=\rho/(\rho-1)},$
$$v(p,w)=w\,\big(p_1^{r}+p_2^{r}\big)^{-1/r}.$$

assumptions.text: ${\rho\neq 0}.$
Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$

statements.title: Walrasian demand for linear utility
statements.statement: Let ${u(x)=x_1+x_2}$ (the CES function at ${\rho=1}$), ${p\gg 0}$ and ${w>0}.$ A bundle is in the Walrasian demand if and only if it lies on the budget line ${p\cdot x=w}$ and buys none of a good whose price is strictly higher than the other’s.

assumptions.text: Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$

statements.title: Indirect utility for linear utility
statements.statement:
Let ${u(x)=x_1+x_2},$ ${p\gg 0}$ and ${w>0}.$ The value of the utility maximization problem is
$$v(p,w)=\frac{w}{\min(p_1,p_2)}.$$

assumptions.text: Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$

statements.title: Walrasian demand for Leontief utility
statements.statement:
Let ${u(x)=\min(x_1,x_2)},$ ${p\gg 0}$ and ${w>0}.$ The Walrasian demand is the single bundle
$$x_1=x_2=\frac{w}{p_1+p_2}.$$

assumptions.text: Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$

statements.title: Indirect utility for Leontief utility
statements.statement:
Let ${u(x)=\min(x_1,x_2)},$ ${p\gg 0}$ and ${w>0}.$ The value of the utility maximization problem is
$$v(p,w)=\frac{w}{p_1+p_2}.$$

assumptions.text: Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$

statements.title: CES demand approaches linear and Leontief demand in the limits
statements.statement:
Let ${u_\rho(x)=(x_1^\rho+x_2^\rho)^{1/\rho}}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+},$ and let ${p\gg 0}$ and ${w>0}.$ Walrasian demand ${x(p,w)}$ is the set of utility-maximizing bundles in ${B(p,w)},$ and the value of the problem is the indirect utility. Then, at the fixed ${(p,w)}$:

- for every ${\varepsilon>0}$ there is ${\delta>0}$ such that whenever ${0<|\rho-1|<\delta},$ CES demand is nonempty and each of its bundles lies within ${\varepsilon},$ coordinate by coordinate, of a bundle demanded under linear utility ${x_1+x_2};$ and the CES indirect utility converges to that of linear utility as ${\rho\to1};$
- for every ${\varepsilon>0}$ there is ${M}$ such that whenever ${\rho\le M},$ CES demand is nonempty and each of its bundles lies within ${\varepsilon},$ coordinate by coordinate, of the bundle demanded under Leontief utility ${\min(x_1,x_2)};$ and the CES indirect utility converges to the Leontief one as ${\rho\to-\infty}.$

assumptions.text: Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$

statements.title: Linear utility has no elasticity of substitution
statements.statement: Let ${u(x)=x_1+x_2},$ ${p\gg 0}$ and ${w>0},$ with the elasticity of substitution defined as in part (d). Then no real number is the elasticity of substitution at ${(p,w)}.$

assumptions.text: Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$

statements.title: Leontief utility has elasticity of substitution 0
statements.statement: Let ${u(x)=\min(x_1,x_2)},$ ${p\gg 0}$ and ${w>0},$ with the elasticity of substitution defined as in part (d). Then the elasticity of substitution at ${(p,w)}$ is ${0},$ and no other real number is.

assumptions.text: Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$

statements.title: Cobb–Douglas utility has elasticity of substitution 1
statements.statement: Let ${u(x)=x_1x_2},$ ${p\gg 0}$ and ${w>0},$ with the elasticity of substitution defined as in part (d). Then the elasticity of substitution at ${(p,w)}$ is ${1},$ and no other real number is.

assumptions.text: Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$

entries.title: What utility maximization implies for two demand functions

statements.title: Walras’ law gives the demand for the third good
statements.statement:
Let ${\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta}$ be nonzero constants, and let ${x_1(p,w)}$ and ${x_2(p,w)}$ be given by
$$\begin{aligned}x_1&=100-5\,\frac{p_1}{p_3}+\beta\,\frac{p_2}{p_3}+\delta\,\frac{w}{p_3},\\[4pt] x_2&=\alpha+\beta\,\frac{p_1}{p_3}+\gamma\,\frac{p_2}{p_3}+\delta\,\frac{w}{p_3}.\end{aligned}$$
Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^3_+}$ whose preference is locally nonsatiated, and let ${p\gg 0}$ and ${w>0}$ be such that demand at ${(p,w)}$ is nonempty and every demanded bundle buys exactly ${x_1(p,w)}$ of good 1 and ${x_2(p,w)}$ of good 2. Then every demanded bundle buys the same amount of good 3, namely
$$x_3=\frac{w-p_1x_1(p,w)-p_2x_2(p,w)}{p_3}.$$

assumptions.text: ${\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta}$ are nonzero.
the preference represented by ${u}$ is locally nonsatiated: near every bundle there is a strictly better one.
Prices and wealth are positive: ${p\gg 0},$ ${w>0}.$
Demand at ${(p,w)}$ for goods 1 and 2 is given by the two formulas.

statements.title: Both demand formulas are homogeneous of degree zero
statements.statement:
Let ${\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta}$ be nonzero constants, and let ${x_1(p,w)}$ and ${x_2(p,w)}$ be given by
$$\begin{aligned}x_1&=100-5\,\frac{p_1}{p_3}+\beta\,\frac{p_2}{p_3}+\delta\,\frac{w}{p_3},\\[4pt] x_2&=\alpha+\beta\,\frac{p_1}{p_3}+\gamma\,\frac{p_2}{p_3}+\delta\,\frac{w}{p_3}.\end{aligned}$$
For every ${p\gg 0},$ ${w>0}$ and ${\lambda>0},$
$$\begin{aligned}x_1(\lambda p,\lambda w)&=x_1(p,w),\\ x_2(\lambda p,\lambda w)&=x_2(p,w).\end{aligned}$$

assumptions.text: ${\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta}$ are nonzero.

statements.title: Utility maximization forces α = 100 and β = γ = −5
statements.statement:
Let ${\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta}$ be nonzero constants, and let ${x_1(p,w)}$ and ${x_2(p,w)}$ be given by
$$\begin{aligned}x_1&=100-5\,\frac{p_1}{p_3}+\beta\,\frac{p_2}{p_3}+\delta\,\frac{w}{p_3},\\[4pt] x_2&=\alpha+\beta\,\frac{p_1}{p_3}+\gamma\,\frac{p_2}{p_3}+\delta\,\frac{w}{p_3}.\end{aligned}$$
There is a utility function ${u}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^3_+}$ and a nonempty open set ${D}$ of price–wealth pairs, each with ${p\gg 0}$ and ${w>0},$ such that at every ${(p,w)\in D}$ demand is nonempty and every demanded bundle buys exactly ${x_1(p,w)}$ of good 1 and ${x_2(p,w)}$ of good 2, if and only if
$$\alpha=100,\qquad \beta=-5,\qquad \gamma=-5.$$

assumptions.text: ${\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta}$ are nonzero.

entries.title: Quasi-linear preferences have no wealth effects

statements.title: Demand for goods 2 to n does not depend on wealth
statements.statement:
The consumption set is ${X=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-1}_+}$ with ${n\ge 1}$ goods: any real amount of the first good, and nonnegative amounts of the others. A preference ${\succsim}$ on ${X}$ is *strictly convex* if ${a\succsim y},$ ${b\succsim y}$ and ${a\neq b}$ imply that every strict mixture of ${a}$ and ${b}$ is strictly better than ${y},$ and *quasi-linear in the first good* if ${x\succsim y}$ implies $x+\varepsilon e_1\succsim y+\varepsilon e_1$ for every real ${\varepsilon}.$ Prices are normalized so that ${p_1=1},$ and a bundle is demanded at ${(p,w)}$ if it is affordable, ${p\cdot x\le w},$ and at least as good as every affordable bundle. If ${x}$ is demanded at ${(p,w)}$ and ${x'}$ at ${(p,w')},$ then, for every good ${k=2,\dots,n},$
$$x_k=x'_k.$$

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is strictly convex.
${\succsim}$ is quasi-linear in the first good.
Prices are normalized: ${p_1=1}.$
${x}$ is demanded at ${(p,w)}$ and ${x'}$ at ${(p,w')}.$

statements.title: Hicksian demand for goods 2 to n does not depend on the target utility
statements.statement:
The consumption set is ${X=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-1}_+}$ with ${n\ge 1}$ goods: any real amount of the first good, and nonnegative amounts of the others. A preference ${\succsim}$ on ${X}$ is *strictly convex* if ${a\succsim y},$ ${b\succsim y}$ and ${a\neq b}$ imply that every strict mixture of ${a}$ and ${b}$ is strictly better than ${y},$ and *quasi-linear in the first good* if ${x\succsim y}$ implies $x+\varepsilon e_1\succsim y+\varepsilon e_1$ for every real ${\varepsilon}.$ Prices are normalized so that ${p_1=1},$ and a bundle is demanded at ${(p,w)}$ if it is affordable, ${p\cdot x\le w},$ and at least as good as every affordable bundle. Let ${u}$ represent ${\succsim}.$ A bundle ${h}$ is a Hicksian demand at ${(p,\bar u)}$ if ${u(h)\ge\bar u}$ and ${p\cdot h\le p\cdot y}$ for every ${y}$ with ${u(y)\ge\bar u}.$ If ${h}$ is a Hicksian demand at ${(p,\bar u)}$ and ${h'}$ at ${(p,\bar u')},$ then, for every good ${k=2,\dots,n},$
$$h_k=h'_k.$$

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is strictly convex.
${\succsim}$ is quasi-linear in the first good.
${u}$ represents ${\succsim}$: ${x\succsim y}$ if and only if ${u(x)\ge u(y)}.$
Prices are normalized: ${p_1=1}.$
${h}$ is a Hicksian demand at ${(p,\bar u)}$ and ${h'}$ at ${(p,\bar u')}.$

statements.title: Indirect utility takes the form v(p, w) = w + φ(p)
statements.statement:
The consumption set is ${X=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-1}_+}$ with ${n\ge 1}$ goods: any real amount of the first good, and nonnegative amounts of the others. A preference ${\succsim}$ on ${X}$ is *strictly convex* if ${a\succsim y},$ ${b\succsim y}$ and ${a\neq b}$ imply that every strict mixture of ${a}$ and ${b}$ is strictly better than ${y},$ and *quasi-linear in the first good* if ${x\succsim y}$ implies $x+\varepsilon e_1\succsim y+\varepsilon e_1$ for every real ${\varepsilon}.$ Prices are normalized so that ${p_1=1},$ and a bundle is demanded at ${(p,w)}$ if it is affordable, ${p\cdot x\le w},$ and at least as good as every affordable bundle. Let ${u}$ represent ${\succsim}.$ A function ${v(p,w)}$ is an indirect utility function on normalized prices if, whenever ${x}$ is demanded at ${(p,w)}$ and ${x'}$ at ${(p',w')}$ with ${p_1=p'_1=1},$ ${x\succsim x'}$ holds exactly when ${v(p,w)\ge v(p',w')}.$ Then for some function ${\varphi}$ of prices,
$$v(p,w)=w+\varphi(p)$$
is an indirect utility function on normalized prices.

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is strictly convex.
${\succsim}$ is quasi-linear in the first good.
${u}$ represents ${\succsim}$: ${x\succsim y}$ if and only if ${u(x)\ge u(y)}.$

statements.title: The expenditure function takes the form e(p, ū) = c(ū) − φ(p)
statements.statement:
The consumption set is ${X=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-1}_+}$ with ${n\ge 1}$ goods: any real amount of the first good, and nonnegative amounts of the others. A preference ${\succsim}$ on ${X}$ is *strictly convex* if ${a\succsim y},$ ${b\succsim y}$ and ${a\neq b}$ imply that every strict mixture of ${a}$ and ${b}$ is strictly better than ${y},$ and *quasi-linear in the first good* if ${x\succsim y}$ implies $x+\varepsilon e_1\succsim y+\varepsilon e_1$ for every real ${\varepsilon}.$ Prices are normalized so that ${p_1=1},$ and a bundle is demanded at ${(p,w)}$ if it is affordable, ${p\cdot x\le w},$ and at least as good as every affordable bundle. Let ${u}$ represent ${\succsim}.$ A bundle ${h}$ is a Hicksian demand at ${(p,\bar u)}$ if ${u(h)\ge\bar u}$ and ${p\cdot h\le p\cdot y}$ for every ${y}$ with ${u(y)\ge\bar u}.$ Call ${e}$ an expenditure at ${(p,\bar u)}$ if ${e=p\cdot h}$ for some Hicksian demand ${h}$ at ${(p,\bar u)}.$ A function ${v(p,w)}$ is an indirect utility function on normalized prices if, whenever ${x}$ is demanded at ${(p,w)}$ and ${x'}$ at ${(p',w')}$ with ${p_1=p'_1=1},$ ${x\succsim x'}$ holds exactly when ${v(p,w)\ge v(p',w')}.$ Then there are functions ${c}$ of the target utility and ${\varphi}$ of prices such that ${w+\varphi(p)}$ is an indirect utility function on normalized prices and, for every ${p}$ with ${p_1=1},$ every expenditure at ${(p,\bar u)}$ is
$$e(p,\bar u)=c(\bar u)-\varphi(p).$$

assumptions.text: ${\succsim}$ is strictly convex.
${\succsim}$ is quasi-linear in the first good.
${u}$ represents ${\succsim}$: ${x\succsim y}$ if and only if ${u(x)\ge u(y)}.$

entries.title: Demand for the utility max{ax, ay} + min{x, y}

statements.title: Indifference curves are kinked on the diagonal
statements.statement:
Let ${0<a<1}$ and $u(x,y)=\max\{ax,ay\}+\min\{x,y\}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}.$ Let ${\succsim}$ be the preference that ${u}$ represents. A bundle ${z}$ is indifferent to ${b}$ if and only if ${z}$ lies on the indifference curve at level ${c=u(b)}$:
$$\begin{gathered}\{z:\ z_2\le z_1,\ az_1+z_2=c\}\\ \cup\ \{z:\ z_1\le z_2,\ z_1+az_2=c\}.\end{gathered}$$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ represents ${\succsim}$: ${s\succsim t}$ if and only if ${u(s)\ge u(t)}.$

statements.title: Marshallian demand: a corner, the kink, or a segment
statements.statement:
Let ${0<a<1}$ and $u(x,y)=\max\{ax,ay\}+\min\{x,y\}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}.$ Let ${p\gg 0}$ and let ${w}$ be any wealth level. A bundle ${x}$ is in the Marshallian demand at ${(p,w)}$ if and only if:

- ${p_2<ap_1}$: ${x=(0,\,w/p_2)};$
- ${p_2=ap_1}$: ${p\cdot x=w}$ and ${x_1\le x_2};$
- ${ap_1<p_2}$ and ${ap_2<p_1}$: ${x_1=x_2=w/(p_1+p_2)};$
- ${p_1=ap_2}$: ${p\cdot x=w}$ and ${x_2\le x_1};$
- ${p_1<ap_2}$: ${x=(w/p_1,\,0)}.$

assumptions.text: prices are positive: ${p\gg 0}.$

statements.title: Hicksian demand: a corner, the kink, or a segment
statements.statement:
Let ${0<a<1}$ and $u(x,y)=\max\{ax,ay\}+\min\{x,y\}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}.$ Let ${p\gg 0}$ and let the target ${\bar u}$ be at least ${u(0,0)=0}.$ A bundle ${h}$ is in the Hicksian demand, that is ${u(h)\ge\bar u}$ and ${p\cdot h\le p\cdot y}$ for every ${y}$ with ${u(y)\ge\bar u},$ if and only if:

- ${p_2<ap_1}$: ${h=(0,\,\bar u/a)};$
- ${p_2=ap_1}$: ${h_1+ah_2=\bar u}$ and ${h_1\le h_2};$
- ${ap_1<p_2}$ and ${ap_2<p_1}$: ${h_1=h_2=\bar u/(1+a)};$
- ${p_1=ap_2}$: ${ah_1+h_2=\bar u}$ and ${h_2\le h_1};$
- ${p_1<ap_2}$: ${h=(\bar u/a,\,0)}.$

assumptions.text: prices are positive: ${p\gg 0}.$
the target is at least the utility of the zero bundle: ${\bar u\ge u(0,0)=0}.$

statements.title: Rented and owned housing, a question for discussion
statements.statement: The question asks for a discussion of how rental and purchased housing enter a family’s utility function, and of how a fixed stock of houses bears on their relative prices. It contains no formal statement to check.

entries.title: Recovering utility from the expenditure function

statements.title: Bundles costing at most e(1, p₂, u₀) give at most u₀
statements.statement: Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ that is continuous, strictly increasing and quasi-concave, with expenditure function ${e(p_1,p_2,\bar u)=p_1p_2\bar u/(p_1+p_2)}$: at all prices ${p_1,p_2>0},$ the cheapest bundle at least as good as a bundle ${x}$ costs exactly ${e(p_1,p_2,u(x))}.$ Let ${u_0}$ be a utility level and ${0\le x_1\le u_0}.$ As printed: fixing ${p_1=1},$ for a price ${p_2},$ every ${x_2}$ such that ${(x_1,x_2)}$ is affordable at prices ${(1,p_2)}$ with wealth ${e(1,p_2,u_0)=p_2u_0/(1+p_2)}$ has ${u(x_1,x_2)\le u_0}.$ No condition is placed on ${p_2}.$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is continuous.
${u}$ is strictly increasing: a bundle with at least as much of each good and more of one has higher utility.
${u}$ is quasi-concave.
The expenditure function is ${e(p_1,p_2,\bar u)=p_1p_2\bar u/(p_1+p_2)}$ at all prices ${p_1,p_2>0}.$
${0\le x_1\le u_0},$ the range found in part (b).

statements.title: With p₂ > 0, bundles costing at most e(1, p₂, u₀) give at most u₀
statements.statement: Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ that is continuous, strictly increasing and quasi-concave, with expenditure function ${e(p_1,p_2,\bar u)=p_1p_2\bar u/(p_1+p_2)}$: at all prices ${p_1,p_2>0},$ the cheapest bundle at least as good as a bundle ${x}$ costs exactly ${e(p_1,p_2,u(x))}.$ Let ${u_0}$ be a utility level, ${0\le x_1\le u_0}$ and ${p_2>0}.$ Then every ${x_2}$ such that ${(x_1,x_2)}$ is affordable at prices ${(1,p_2)}$ with wealth ${e(1,p_2,u_0)=p_2u_0/(1+p_2)}$ has ${u(x_1,x_2)\le u_0}.$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is continuous.

${u}$ is quasi-concave.
The expenditure function is ${e(p_1,p_2,\bar u)=p_1p_2\bar u/(p_1+p_2)}$ at all prices ${p_1,p_2>0}.$
${0\le x_1\le u_0},$ the range found in part (b).

statements.title: Utility on the axes: u(x₁, 0) = x₁ and u(0, x₂) = x₂
statements.statement:
Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ that is continuous, strictly increasing and quasi-concave, with expenditure function ${e(p_1,p_2,\bar u)=p_1p_2\bar u/(p_1+p_2)}$: at all prices ${p_1,p_2>0},$ the cheapest bundle at least as good as a bundle ${x}$ costs exactly ${e(p_1,p_2,u(x))}.$ Then, for all ${x_1,x_2\ge 0},$
$$\begin{aligned}u(x_1,0)&=x_1,\\ u(0,x_2)&=x_2.\end{aligned}$$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is continuous.
${u}$ is strictly increasing: a bundle with at least as much of each good and more of one has higher utility.
${u}$ is quasi-concave.
The expenditure function is ${e(p_1,p_2,\bar u)=p_1p_2\bar u/(p_1+p_2)}$ at all prices ${p_1,p_2>0}.$

statements.title: Which amounts of good 1 lie on the indifference curve u = u₀
statements.statement:
Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ that is continuous, strictly increasing and quasi-concave, with expenditure function ${e(p_1,p_2,\bar u)=p_1p_2\bar u/(p_1+p_2)}$: at all prices ${p_1,p_2>0},$ the cheapest bundle at least as good as a bundle ${x}$ costs exactly ${e(p_1,p_2,u(x))}.$ For real numbers ${u_0}$ and ${x_1},$ some ${x_2\ge 0}$ gives ${u(x_1,x_2)=u_0}$ if and only if
$$0\le x_1\le u_0.$$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is continuous.
${u}$ is strictly increasing: a bundle with at least as much of each good and more of one has higher utility.
${u}$ is quasi-concave.
The expenditure function is ${e(p_1,p_2,\bar u)=p_1p_2\bar u/(p_1+p_2)}$ at all prices ${p_1,p_2>0}.$

statements.title: The largest affordable x₂ bounds the indifference curve from below
statements.statement:
Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ that is continuous, strictly increasing and quasi-concave, with expenditure function ${e(p_1,p_2,\bar u)=p_1p_2\bar u/(p_1+p_2)}$: at all prices ${p_1,p_2>0},$ the cheapest bundle at least as good as a bundle ${x}$ costs exactly ${e(p_1,p_2,u(x))}.$ Let ${u_0}$ be a utility level, ${0\le x_1\le u_0}$ and ${p_2}$ any price, and suppose ${m}$ is the largest ${x_2}$ such that ${(x_1,x_2)}$ is affordable at prices ${(1,p_2)}$ with wealth ${p_2u_0/(1+p_2)},$ the formula for ${e(1,p_2,u_0)}.$ Then:

- ${(x_1,m)}$ costs exactly that wealth: ${x_1+p_2m=p_2u_0/(1+p_2)};$
- for every bundle ${(x_1,x_2)}$ with utility ${u_0},$ ${m\le x_2},$ with equality exactly when ${(x_1,x_2)}$ is a cheapest bundle at prices ${(1,p_2)}$ among those with utility at least ${u_0}.$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is continuous.
${u}$ is strictly increasing: a bundle with at least as much of each good and more of one has higher utility.
${u}$ is quasi-concave.
The expenditure function is ${e(p_1,p_2,\bar u)=p_1p_2\bar u/(p_1+p_2)}$ at all prices ${p_1,p_2>0}.$
${0\le x_1\le u_0},$ the range found in part (b).

statements.title: The indifference curve is x₂ = (√u₀ − √x₁)²
statements.statement:
Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ that is continuous, strictly increasing and quasi-concave, with expenditure function ${e(p_1,p_2,\bar u)=p_1p_2\bar u/(p_1+p_2)}$: at all prices ${p_1,p_2>0},$ the cheapest bundle at least as good as a bundle ${x}$ costs exactly ${e(p_1,p_2,u(x))}.$ Let ${u_0}$ be a utility level and ${0\le x_1\le u_0}.$ A bundle ${(x_1,x_2)}$ has utility ${u_0}$ if and only if
$$x_2=\big(\sqrt{u_0}-\sqrt{x_1}\big)^2.$$

assumptions.text: ${u}$ is continuous.
${u}$ is strictly increasing: a bundle with at least as much of each good and more of one has higher utility.
${u}$ is quasi-concave.
The expenditure function is ${e(p_1,p_2,\bar u)=p_1p_2\bar u/(p_1+p_2)}$ at all prices ${p_1,p_2>0}.$
${0\le x_1\le u_0},$ the range found in part (b).

statements.title: The utility function is u = (√x₁ + √x₂)²
statements.statement:
Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}.$ Then ${u}$ is continuous, strictly increasing and quasi-concave, with expenditure function ${e(p_1,p_2,\bar u)=p_1p_2\bar u/(p_1+p_2)}$ at all prices ${p_1,p_2>0},$ if and only if, for all ${x_1,x_2\ge 0},$
$$u(x_1,x_2)=\big(\sqrt{x_1}+\sqrt{x_2}\big)^2.$$

entries.title: An economy with no positive representative consumer

statements.title: Fixed wealth shares need not yield a positive representative consumer
statements.statement:
Aggregate demand under wealth shares ${\alpha_i\ge0}$ with ${\sum_i\alpha_i=1}$ is ${x(p,w)=\sum_i x_i(p,\alpha_iw)}.$ A *positive representative consumer* is a rational preference ${\succsim}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^L_+}$ such that, at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and wealth ${w>0},$ ${x(p,w)\succ y}$ for every other bundle ${y}$ with ${p\cdot y\le w}.$

There are a number of goods ${L},$ consumers ${i=1,\dots,I}$ with utility functions ${u_i}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^L_+}$ whose demand ${x_i(p,w)}$ is the unique utility-maximizing bundle at all ${p\gg0}$ and ${w\ge0},$ and wealth shares ${\alpha_i\ge0}$ summing to ${1},$ such that the economy admits no positive representative consumer.

entries.title: How deadweight loss changes with the tax

statements.title: Both deadweight-loss measures start flat, then rise
statements.statement:
A consumer with utility function ${u}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^L_+}$ has wealth ${w>0}$ and faces initial prices ${p^0\gg0}.$ A tax ${t}$ per unit of good 1 moves the prices to ${p^1},$ with good-1 price ${p_1^0+t>0}$ and all other prices unchanged. Let ${u^0=v(p^0,w)}$ be the maximal utility on the budget set ${B(p^0,w)},$ with ${u^0>u(0)},$ and for good-1 prices ${r}$ between ${p_1^0}$ and ${p_1^0+s},$ for all taxes ${s}$ near ${t},$ let ${h(r)}$ be a Hicksian demand bundle at level ${u^0},$ other prices fixed at ${p^0}.$ With ${\bar p_1=p_1^0+t},$ the measure (3.I.6) is
$$L_6(t)=\int_{p_1^0}^{\bar p_1}\big[h_1(r)-h_1(\bar p_1)\big]\,dr.$$
For every tax ${s}$ near ${t},$ let ${x(s)}$ be a Walrasian demand bundle at the taxed prices and wealth ${w},$ with utility ${u^1(s)}$ above ${u(0)},$ and let ${E(s)=e(p^0,u^1(s))}$ be the least cost at the initial prices of reaching ${u^1(s)}.$ The deadweight loss (3.I.5) is
$$L_5(t)=w-t\,x_1(t)-E(t).$$
As printed: at ${t=0}$ every derivative of ${L_5}$ and of ${L_6}$ at ${t}$ is ${0};$ and at ${t>0},$ if ${h_1}$ is strictly decreasing in the good-1 price from ${p_1^0}$ on, every derivative of ${L_5}$ and of ${L_6}$ at ${t}$ is positive.

assumptions.text: Wealth and initial prices are positive, ${w>0}$ and ${p^0\gg0},$ and so is the taxed price: ${p_1^0+t>0}.$
${u^0=v(p^0,w)},$ the maximal utility on ${B(p^0,w)},$ exceeds ${u(0)}.$
${h(r)}$ is a Hicksian demand bundle at level ${u^0}$ at every good-1 price ${r}$ between ${p_1^0}$ and ${p_1^0+s},$ for all taxes ${s}$ near ${t}.$
${x(s)}$ is a Walrasian demand bundle at the taxed prices, with utility above ${u(0)},$ for every tax ${s}$ near ${t}.$
${E(s)}$ is the least cost at prices ${p^0}$ of reaching the utility of ${x(s)},$ for every tax ${s}$ near ${t}.$
${h_1}$ is strictly decreasing in the good-1 price from ${p_1^0}$ on (for the claim at ${t>0}$).

statements.title: Measure (3.I.6) has zero slope at t = 0 and positive slope after
statements.statement:
A consumer with utility function ${u}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^L_+}$ has wealth ${w>0}$ and faces initial prices ${p^0\gg0}.$ A tax ${t}$ per unit of good 1 moves the prices to ${p^1},$ with good-1 price ${p_1^0+t>0}$ and all other prices unchanged. Let ${u^0=v(p^0,w)}$ be the maximal utility on the budget set ${B(p^0,w)},$ with ${u^0>u(0)},$ and for good-1 prices ${r}$ between ${p_1^0}$ and ${p_1^0+s},$ for all taxes ${s}$ near ${t},$ let ${h(r)}$ be a Hicksian demand bundle at level ${u^0},$ other prices fixed at ${p^0}.$ With ${\bar p_1=p_1^0+t},$ the measure (3.I.6) is
$$L_6(t)=\int_{p_1^0}^{\bar p_1}\big[h_1(r)-h_1(\bar p_1)\big]\,dr.$$
Then at ${t=0}$ every derivative of ${L_6}$ at ${t}$ is ${0};$ and at ${t>0},$ if ${h_1}$ is strictly decreasing in the good-1 price from ${p_1^0}$ on and has a negative derivative at ${p_1^0+t},$ every derivative of ${L_6}$ at ${t}$ is positive.

assumptions.text: Wealth and initial prices are positive, ${w>0}$ and ${p^0\gg0},$ and so is the taxed price: ${p_1^0+t>0}.$
${u^0=v(p^0,w)},$ the maximal utility on ${B(p^0,w)},$ exceeds ${u(0)}.$
${h(r)}$ is a Hicksian demand bundle at level ${u^0}$ at every good-1 price ${r}$ between ${p_1^0}$ and ${p_1^0+s},$ for all taxes ${s}$ near ${t}.$
${h_1}$ is strictly decreasing in the good-1 price from ${p_1^0}$ on (for the claim at ${t>0}$).
${h_1}$ has a negative derivative at ${p_1^0+t}$ (for the claim at ${t>0}$).

statements.title: Measure (3.I.5) has zero slope at t = 0
statements.statement:
A consumer with utility function ${u}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^L_+}$ has wealth ${w>0}$ and faces initial prices ${p^0\gg0}.$ A tax ${t}$ per unit of good 1 moves the prices to ${p^1},$ with good-1 price ${p_1^0+t>0}$ and all other prices unchanged. For every tax ${s}$ near ${t},$ let ${x(s)}$ be a Walrasian demand bundle at the taxed prices and wealth ${w},$ with utility ${u^1(s)}$ above ${u(0)},$ and let ${E(s)=e(p^0,u^1(s))}$ be the least cost at the initial prices of reaching ${u^1(s)}.$ The deadweight loss (3.I.5) is
$$L_5(t)=w-t\,x_1(t)-E(t).$$
If ${u}$ is locally nonsatiated, then at ${t=0}$ every derivative of ${L_5}$ at ${t}$ is ${0}.$

assumptions.text: Wealth and initial prices are positive, ${w>0}$ and ${p^0\gg0},$ and so is the taxed price: ${p_1^0+t>0}.$
${x(s)}$ is a Walrasian demand bundle at the taxed prices, with utility above ${u(0)},$ for every tax ${s}$ near ${t}.$
${E(s)}$ is the least cost at prices ${p^0}$ of reaching the utility of ${x(s)},$ for every tax ${s}$ near ${t}.$
${u}$ is locally nonsatiated: near every bundle there is a strictly better one.

statements.title: The derivative of measure (3.I.6) is −t times the slope of h₁
statements.statement:
A consumer with utility function ${u}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^L_+}$ has wealth ${w>0}$ and faces initial prices ${p^0\gg0}.$ A tax ${t}$ per unit of good 1 moves the prices to ${p^1},$ with good-1 price ${p_1^0+t>0}$ and all other prices unchanged. Let ${u^0=v(p^0,w)}$ be the maximal utility on the budget set ${B(p^0,w)},$ with ${u^0>u(0)},$ and for good-1 prices ${r}$ between ${p_1^0}$ and ${p_1^0+s},$ for all taxes ${s}$ near ${t},$ let ${h(r)}$ be a Hicksian demand bundle at level ${u^0},$ other prices fixed at ${p^0}.$ With ${\bar p_1=p_1^0+t},$ the measure (3.I.6) is
$$L_6(t)=\int_{p_1^0}^{\bar p_1}\big[h_1(r)-h_1(\bar p_1)\big]\,dr.$$
A number ${D}$ is the derivative of ${L_6}$ at ${t}$ if and only if either ${t=0}$ and ${D=0},$ or ${h_1}$ has a derivative ${k}$ at ${p_1^0+t}$ and ${D=-t\,k}$:
$$L_6'(t)=-t\,\frac{\partial h_1}{\partial p_1}\big(p_1^0+t\big).$$

assumptions.text: Wealth and initial prices are positive, ${w>0}$ and ${p^0\gg0},$ and so is the taxed price: ${p_1^0+t>0}.$
${u^0=v(p^0,w)},$ the maximal utility on ${B(p^0,w)},$ exceeds ${u(0)}.$
${h(r)}$ is a Hicksian demand bundle at level ${u^0}$ at every good-1 price ${r}$ between ${p_1^0}$ and ${p_1^0+s},$ for all taxes ${s}$ near ${t}.$

statements.title: The derivative of the deadweight loss (3.I.5)
statements.statement:
A consumer with utility function ${u}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^L_+}$ has wealth ${w>0}$ and faces initial prices ${p^0\gg0}.$ A tax ${t}$ per unit of good 1 moves the prices to ${p^1},$ with good-1 price ${p_1^0+t>0}$ and all other prices unchanged. For every tax ${s}$ near ${t},$ let ${x(s)}$ be a Walrasian demand bundle at the taxed prices and wealth ${w},$ with utility ${u^1(s)}$ above ${u(0)},$ and let ${E(s)=e(p^0,u^1(s))}$ be the least cost at the initial prices of reaching ${u^1(s)}.$ The deadweight loss (3.I.5) is
$$L_5(t)=w-t\,x_1(t)-E(t).$$
Suppose the indirect utility ${v(p^1,w)}$ is differentiable in the tax at ${t},$ and the expenditure function ${e(p^0,\cdot)}$ is differentiable in the utility level at ${u^1(t)}.$ A number ${D}$ is the derivative of ${L_5}$ at ${t}$ if and only if ${E}$ has a derivative ${b}$ at ${t}$ and either ${x_1}$ has a derivative ${k}$ at ${t}$ and
$$D=-x_1(t)-t\,k-b,$$
or ${t=0},$ ${x_1(s)}$ tends to a limit ${\ell}$ as ${s\to0}$ with ${s\neq0},$ and ${D=-\ell-b}.$

assumptions.text: Wealth and initial prices are positive, ${w>0}$ and ${p^0\gg0},$ and so is the taxed price: ${p_1^0+t>0}.$
${x(s)}$ is a Walrasian demand bundle at the taxed prices, with utility above ${u(0)},$ for every tax ${s}$ near ${t}.$
${E(s)}$ is the least cost at prices ${p^0}$ of reaching the utility of ${x(s)},$ for every tax ${s}$ near ${t}.$
the indirect utility ${v(p^1,w)}$ is differentiable in the tax at ${t}.$
the expenditure function ${e(p^0,\cdot)}$ is differentiable in the utility level at ${u^1(t)}.$

statements.title: Every good has at least one substitute
statements.statement: For a utility function ${u}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^L_+},$ the Hicksian demand ${h(p,\bar u)}$ consists of the bundles of least cost ${p\cdot x}$ among those with ${u(x)\ge\bar u}.$ Goods ${i}$ and ${j}$ are *substitutes* at ${(p,\bar u)}$ if, for good-${j}$ prices near ${p_j}$ with the other prices fixed, the Hicksian demand is a single bundle whose ${i}$-th coordinate has a derivative ${\partial h_i/\partial p_j\ge0}$ at ${p_j}.$ As printed: for every utility function ${u},$ price vector ${p},$ level ${\bar u}$ and good ${i},$ there is a good ${j\neq i}$ such that ${i}$ and ${j}$ are substitutes at ${(p,\bar u)}.$

statements.title: With at least two goods, every good has a substitute
statements.statement: For a utility function ${u}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^L_+},$ the Hicksian demand ${h(p,\bar u)}$ consists of the bundles of least cost ${p\cdot x}$ among those with ${u(x)\ge\bar u}.$ Goods ${i}$ and ${j}$ are *substitutes* at ${(p,\bar u)}$ if, for good-${j}$ prices near ${p_j}$ with the other prices fixed, the Hicksian demand is a single bundle whose ${i}$-th coordinate has a derivative ${\partial h_i/\partial p_j\ge0}$ at ${p_j}.$ Suppose there are at least two goods, ${p\gg0},$ and near ${p}$ the Hicksian demand at level ${\bar u}$ is a single bundle, each coordinate of which is differentiable at ${p}.$ Then every good ${i}$ has a good ${j\neq i}$ such that ${i}$ and ${j}$ are substitutes at ${(p,\bar u)}.$

assumptions.text: there are at least two goods.
prices are positive, ${p\gg0},$ and near ${p}$ the Hicksian demand at level ${\bar u}$ is a single bundle, each coordinate differentiable at ${p}.$

statements.title: Substitutability need not be symmetric
statements.statement: For a utility function ${u}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^L_+},$ the Hicksian demand ${h(p,\bar u)}$ consists of the bundles of least cost ${p\cdot x}$ among those with ${u(x)\ge\bar u}.$ Goods ${i}$ and ${j}$ are *substitutes* at ${(p,\bar u)}$ if, for good-${j}$ prices near ${p_j}$ with the other prices fixed, the Hicksian demand is a single bundle whose ${i}$-th coordinate has a derivative ${\partial h_i/\partial p_j\ge0}$ at ${p_j}.$ It is not the case that, for every utility function, price vector ${p},$ level ${\bar u}$ and goods ${i,j},$ whenever ${i}$ and ${j}$ are substitutes at ${(p,\bar u)},$ so are ${j}$ and ${i}.$

statements.title: Substitutes at one price, complements at another
statements.statement: For a utility function ${u}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^L_+},$ the Hicksian demand ${h(p,\bar u)}$ consists of the bundles of least cost ${p\cdot x}$ among those with ${u(x)\ge\bar u}.$ Goods ${i}$ and ${j}$ are *substitutes* at ${(p,\bar u)}$ if, for good-${j}$ prices near ${p_j}$ with the other prices fixed, the Hicksian demand is a single bundle whose ${i}$-th coordinate has a derivative ${\partial h_i/\partial p_j\ge0}$ at ${p_j}.$ There are a utility function, a level ${\bar u},$ two goods ${i\neq j}$ and two price vectors ${p\neq p'}$ such that ${i}$ and ${j}$ are substitutes at ${(p,\bar u)},$ while at ${p'}$ the Hicksian demand is a single bundle for good-${j}$ prices near ${p'_j}$ and ${\partial h_i/\partial p_j<0}$ at ${p'_j}.$

statements.title: Coffee can raise the payment to keep tea, at a fixed utility
statements.statement: For a utility function ${u}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^L_+},$ the Hicksian demand ${h(p,\bar u)}$ consists of the bundles of least cost ${p\cdot x}$ among those with ${u(x)\ge\bar u}.$ Goods ${i}$ and ${j}$ are *substitutes* at ${(p,\bar u)}$ if, for good-${j}$ prices near ${p_j}$ with the other prices fixed, the Hicksian demand is a single bundle whose ${i}$-th coordinate has a derivative ${\partial h_i/\partial p_j\ge0}$ at ${p_j}.$ Let coffee ${c}$ and tea ${t}$ be distinct goods. On our reading at a utility level, the amount paid at prices ${p}$ and level ${\bar u}$ to avoid losing tea is ${W=e'-e},$ where ${e}$ is the least cost of reaching ${\bar u}$ with the goods available and ${e'}$ the least cost of reaching it without tea. Let ${W_1}$ be this amount with coffee available and ${W_0}$ the amount with coffee unavailable. It is not true that ${W_1\le W_0}$ for every utility function, every two such goods that are substitutes at every price vector ${q\gg0}$ and every level, and all prices ${p}$ and levels ${\bar u}.$

assumptions.text: the premise that coffee and tea are substitutes is read at every price vector with all prices positive, and every level, where the question says “at all ${(p,u)}$”.

statements.title: Coffee can raise the payment to keep tea, at a fixed wealth
statements.statement: For a utility function ${u}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^L_+},$ the Hicksian demand ${h(p,\bar u)}$ consists of the bundles of least cost ${p\cdot x}$ among those with ${u(x)\ge\bar u}.$ Goods ${i}$ and ${j}$ are *substitutes* at ${(p,\bar u)}$ if, for good-${j}$ prices near ${p_j}$ with the other prices fixed, the Hicksian demand is a single bundle whose ${i}$-th coordinate has a derivative ${\partial h_i/\partial p_j\ge0}$ at ${p_j}.$ Let coffee ${c}$ and tea ${t}$ be distinct goods. On our reading at a wealth level, the amount paid at prices ${p}$ and wealth ${w}$ to avoid losing tea is the largest sum ${A}$ such that, with tea available, wealth ${w-A}$ still buys a utility at least as high as wealth ${w}$ buys without tea. Let ${A_1}$ be this amount with coffee available and ${A_0}$ the amount with coffee unavailable. It is not true that ${A_1\le A_0}$ for every utility function, every two such goods that are substitutes at every price vector ${q\gg0}$ and every level, and all prices ${p}$ and wealth levels ${w}.$

assumptions.text: the premise that coffee and tea are substitutes is read at every price vector with all prices positive, and every level, where the question says “at all ${(p,u)}$”.

assumptions.text: the premise that coffee and tea are substitutes is read at every price vector with all prices positive, and every level, where the question says “at all ${(p,u)}$”.

entries.title: From indirect utility to welfare and price indexes

statements.title: The expenditure function is e(p, ū) = ū√(p₁p₂)
statements.statement:
Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ with indirect utility ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$: at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0},$ the greatest utility on the budget set is ${I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}.$ Let ${p\gg0}$ and ${\bar u>u(0)}.$ A number ${E}$ is the least cost of a bundle with utility at least ${\bar u}$ if and only if ${\bar u>0}$ and
$$E=\bar u\sqrt{p_1p_2}.$$

assumptions.text: The indirect utility is ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$ at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0}.$
prices are positive: ${p\gg0}.$
the target exceeds the utility of the zero bundle: ${\bar u>u(0)}.$

statements.title: The Hicksian demand splits spending equally
statements.statement:
Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ with indirect utility ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$: at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0},$ the greatest utility on the budget set is ${I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}.$ Let ${p\gg0}$ and ${\bar u>u(0)}.$ A bundle ${h}$ has utility at least ${\bar u}$ and least cost among such bundles if and only if ${\bar u>0}$ and
$$h=\left(\frac{\bar u}{2}\sqrt{\frac{p_2}{p_1}},\ \frac{\bar u}{2}\sqrt{\frac{p_1}{p_2}}\right).$$

assumptions.text: The indirect utility is ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$ at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0}.$
prices are positive: ${p\gg0}.$
the target exceeds the utility of the zero bundle: ${\bar u>u(0)}.$

statements.title: A fourfold rise in p₁ has compensating variation −400
statements.statement:
Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ with indirect utility ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$: at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0},$ the greatest utility on the budget set is ${I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}.$ The price of good 1 rises from ${100}$ to ${400},$ the price of good 2 stays at ${100},$ and income is ${I=400}.$ Let ${u^0}$ be the greatest utility at the initial prices, and let the compensating variation be ${CV=400-E},$ where ${E}$ is the least cost at the new prices of reaching ${u^0}.$ Then ${u^0}$ and ${E}$ exist, and a number ${c}$ is the compensating variation if and only if
$$c=-400.$$

assumptions.text: The indirect utility is ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$ at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0}.$

statements.title: Laspeyres index 5/2, Paasche index 8/5
statements.statement:
Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ with indirect utility ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$: at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0},$ the greatest utility on the budget set is ${I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}.$ The price of good 1 rises from ${100}$ to ${400},$ the price of good 2 stays at ${100},$ and income is ${I=400}.$ The Laspeyres index is the cost at the new prices over the cost at the old prices of the bundle demanded before the change; the Paasche index is the same ratio for the bundle demanded after it. Numbers ${l}$ and ${q}$ are the Laspeyres and Paasche indexes if and only if
$$l=\frac{5}{2}\quad\text{and}\quad q=\frac{8}{5}.$$

assumptions.text: The indirect utility is ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$ at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0}.$

statements.title: Paasche < cost-of-living adjustment < Laspeyres
statements.statement:
Let ${u}$ be a utility function on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}$ with indirect utility ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$: at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0},$ the greatest utility on the budget set is ${I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}.$ The price of good 1 rises from ${100}$ to ${400},$ the price of good 2 stays at ${100},$ and income is ${I=400}.$ Let the cost-of-living adjustment suggested by the compensating variation ${c}$ be ${a=(400-c)/400}.$ Then every Laspeyres index ${l},$ every Paasche index ${q}$ and every such adjustment ${a}$ satisfy
$$q<a<l.$$

assumptions.text: The indirect utility is ${v(p,I)=I/\sqrt{p_1p_2}}$ at all prices ${p\gg0}$ and income ${I>0}.$

entries.title: A monopolist’s output never rises with marginal cost

statements.title: Monopoly output is weakly decreasing in the unit cost
statements.statement:
Let the demand curve be any set ${D}$ of price–quantity points ${(p,x)},$ and let ${q(c)}$ be an output chosen at each unit cost ${c}.$ Consider the costs ${c}$ at which ${q(c)}$ is the quantity of a point of ${D}$ that maximizes profit ${px-cx}$ over ${D}.$ On those costs ${q}$ is weakly decreasing:
$$c<c'\ \Longrightarrow\ q(c)\ge q(c').$$

statements.title: A monotone change of variable preserves increasing differences
statements.statement:
A function ${f(x,y)}$ has *increasing differences* if, for all ${x\le x'},$ the difference ${f(x',y)-f(x,y)}$ is non-decreasing in ${y}.$ Let ${g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be non-decreasing and let ${f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}}$ have increasing differences. Then ${h(x,y)=f(g(x),y)}$ has increasing differences: for all ${x\le x'},$ the difference
$$f\big(g(x'),y\big)-f\big(g(x),y\big)$$
is non-decreasing in ${y}.$

assumptions.text: ${g}$ is non-decreasing.
${f}$ has increasing differences.

statements.title: h(x − θ) has increasing differences exactly when h is concave
statements.statement: A function ${f(x,y)}$ has *increasing differences* if, for all ${x\le x'},$ the difference ${f(x',y)-f(x,y)}$ is non-decreasing in ${y}.$ Let ${h:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}}$ be twice differentiable. Then ${f(x,\theta)=h(x-\theta)}$ has increasing differences if and only if ${h}$ is concave.

assumptions.text: ${h}$ is twice differentiable: ${h}$ and ${h'}$ are differentiable.

entries.title: Pricing against a shifting demand curve

statements.title: Concave demand makes the profit function concave
statements.statement: Let ${P}$ be an open interval of prices and ${Q(p,\theta)}$ a demand curve that, for every ${\theta},$ is non-increasing, differentiable and strictly positive in ${p}$ on ${P}.$ The firm chooses ${p\in P}$ to maximize the profit ${(p-c)\,Q(p,\theta)}$ for a constant unit cost ${c}.$ As printed: concave demand is sufficient to ensure that the profit function is concave. Nothing is said about how ${c}$ relates to the prices in ${P}.$

assumptions.text: The region of prices ${P}$ is an open interval.
Demand slopes downward: ${Q(\cdot,\theta)}$ is non-increasing on ${P}$ for every ${\theta}.$
${Q}$ is differentiable in ${p}$ on ${P}.$
${Q}$ is strictly positive on ${P}.$

statements.title: With price at least cost, concave demand makes profit concave
statements.statement: Let ${P}$ be an open interval of prices and ${Q(p,\theta)}$ a demand curve that, for every ${\theta},$ is non-increasing, differentiable and strictly positive in ${p}$ on ${P}.$ The firm chooses ${p\in P}$ to maximize the profit ${(p-c)\,Q(p,\theta)}$ for a constant unit cost ${c}.$ If ${c\le p}$ for every ${p\in P},$ then for every ${\theta}$: whenever ${Q(\cdot,\theta)}$ is concave on ${P},$ so is the profit ${p\mapsto(p-c)\,Q(p,\theta)}.$

assumptions.text: The region of prices ${P}$ is an open interval.
Demand slopes downward: ${Q(\cdot,\theta)}$ is non-increasing on ${P}$ for every ${\theta}.$
${Q}$ is differentiable in ${p}$ on ${P}.$
${Q}$ is strictly positive on ${P}.$
the unit cost is at most every price in the region: ${c\le p}$ for all ${p\in P}.$

statements.title: Demand grows more inelastic iff log Q has increasing differences
statements.statement: Let ${P}$ be an open interval of prices and ${Q(p,\theta)}$ a demand curve that, for every ${\theta},$ is non-increasing, differentiable and strictly positive in ${p}$ on ${P}.$ Let $\varepsilon(p,\theta)=p\,Q_p(p,\theta)/Q(p,\theta)$ be the price elasticity. ${\log Q}$ has *increasing differences* if, for all ${p\le p'}$ in ${P},$ ${\log Q(p',\theta)-\log Q(p,\theta)}$ is non-decreasing in ${\theta}.$ Then ${|\varepsilon(p,\theta)|}$ is non-increasing in ${\theta}$ at every ${p\in P}$ if and only if ${\log Q}$ has increasing differences.

assumptions.text: The region of prices ${P}$ is an open interval.
Demand slopes downward: ${Q(\cdot,\theta)}$ is non-increasing on ${P}$ for every ${\theta}.$
${Q}$ is differentiable in ${p}$ on ${P}.$
${Q}$ is strictly positive on ${P}.$

statements.title: Increasing differences of log Q make the price rise with θ
statements.statement: Let ${P}$ be an open interval of prices and ${Q(p,\theta)}$ a demand curve that, for every ${\theta},$ is non-increasing, differentiable and strictly positive in ${p}$ on ${P}.$ The firm chooses ${p\in P}$ to maximize the profit ${(p-c)\,Q(p,\theta)}$ for a constant unit cost ${c}.$ ${\log Q}$ has *increasing differences* if, for all ${p\le p'}$ in ${P},$ ${\log Q(p',\theta)-\log Q(p,\theta)}$ is non-decreasing in ${\theta}.$ If ${\log Q}$ has increasing differences then, for all ${\theta\le\theta'},$ the largest optimal price at ${\theta}$ is at most the largest optimal price at ${\theta'},$ whenever both exist. Moreover, ${\log Q}$ has increasing differences if and only if the absolute price elasticity ${|\varepsilon(p,\theta)|=|p\,Q_p(p,\theta)/Q(p,\theta)|}$ is non-increasing in ${\theta}$ at every ${p\in P}.$

assumptions.text: The region of prices ${P}$ is an open interval.
Demand slopes downward: ${Q(\cdot,\theta)}$ is non-increasing on ${P}$ for every ${\theta}.$
${Q}$ is differentiable in ${p}$ on ${P}.$
${Q}$ is strictly positive on ${P}.$

statements.title: Concave demand is not necessary for the prediction: first reading
statements.statement: Let ${P}$ be an open interval of prices and ${Q(p,\theta)}$ a demand curve that, for every ${\theta},$ is non-increasing, differentiable and strictly positive in ${p}$ on ${P}.$ The firm chooses ${p\in P}$ to maximize the profit ${(p-c)\,Q(p,\theta)}$ for a constant unit cost ${c}.$ ${\log Q}$ has *increasing differences* if, for all ${p\le p'}$ in ${P},$ ${\log Q(p',\theta)-\log Q(p,\theta)}$ is non-decreasing in ${\theta}.$ On our first reading of “necessary”: there is no demand curve, region ${P}$ and cost ${c}$ with these properties, with ${\log Q}$ having increasing differences and ${Q(\cdot,\theta)}$ not concave for some ${\theta},$ for which it fails that for all ${\theta\le\theta'},$ the largest optimal price at ${\theta}$ is at most the largest optimal price at ${\theta'},$ whenever both exist.

statements.title: Concave demand is not necessary for the prediction: second reading
statements.statement: Let ${P}$ be an open interval of prices and ${Q(p,\theta)}$ a demand curve that, for every ${\theta},$ is non-increasing, differentiable and strictly positive in ${p}$ on ${P}.$ The firm chooses ${p\in P}$ to maximize the profit ${(p-c)\,Q(p,\theta)}$ for a constant unit cost ${c}.$ On our second reading of “necessary”: it is not the case that every such demand curve and cost ${c}$ for which for all ${\theta\le\theta'},$ the largest optimal price at ${\theta}$ is at most the largest optimal price at ${\theta'},$ whenever both exist has ${Q(\cdot,\theta)}$ concave on ${P}$ at every ${\theta}.$

entries.title: Skill and the choice of technology

statements.title: Increasing differences make computer users buy more skill
statements.statement:
Let ${G}$ and ${H}$ be the production functions of the computer and the old-fashioned technology, and ${c}$ the total cost of skill, all functions of the skill level ${s}.$ The pair has *increasing differences in skill* if, whenever ${s\le s'},$
$$H(s')-H(s)\le G(s')-G(s),$$
that is, if ${G-H}$ is non-decreasing.
If ${G}$ and ${H}$ have increasing differences in skill then, for every cost of skill ${c}$ and every set ${S}$ of available skill levels, the largest maximizer of ${H(s)-c(s)}$ on ${S}$ is at most the largest maximizer of ${G(s)-c(s)}$ on ${S},$ whenever both exist.

statements.title: No weaker condition works for every cost of skill: first reading
statements.statement:
Let ${G}$ and ${H}$ be the production functions of the computer and the old-fashioned technology, and ${c}$ the total cost of skill, all functions of the skill level ${s}.$ The pair has *increasing differences in skill* if, whenever ${s\le s'},$
$$H(s')-H(s)\le G(s')-G(s),$$
that is, if ${G-H}$ is non-decreasing. Call a condition on pairs ${(G,H)}$ *sufficient* if, for every pair meeting it, every cost of skill ${c}$ and every set ${S}$ of available skill levels, the largest maximizer of ${H-c}$ on ${S}$ is at most the largest maximizer of ${G-c}$ on ${S},$ whenever both exist. On our first reading of “weaker”: no sufficient condition is implied by increasing differences and also holds at some pair without increasing differences.

statements.title: No weaker condition works for every cost of skill: second reading
statements.statement:
Let ${G}$ and ${H}$ be the production functions of the computer and the old-fashioned technology, and ${c}$ the total cost of skill, all functions of the skill level ${s}.$ The pair has *increasing differences in skill* if, whenever ${s\le s'},$
$$H(s')-H(s)\le G(s')-G(s),$$
that is, if ${G-H}$ is non-decreasing. Call a condition on pairs ${(G,H)}$ *sufficient* if, for every pair meeting it, every cost of skill ${c}$ and every set ${S}$ of available skill levels, the largest maximizer of ${H-c}$ on ${S}$ is at most the largest maximizer of ${G-c}$ on ${S},$ whenever both exist. On our second reading of “weaker”: no sufficient condition holds at a pair without increasing differences. Equivalently, every sufficient condition implies increasing differences.

statements.title: Selected skill can jump as computers get cheaper
statements.statement:
Let ${G}$ and ${H}$ be the production functions of the computer and the old-fashioned technology, and ${c}$ the total cost of skill, all functions of the skill level ${s}.$ The pair has *increasing differences in skill* if, whenever ${s\le s'},$
$$H(s')-H(s)\le G(s')-G(s),$$
that is, if ${G-H}$ is non-decreasing.
The cost ${k(t)}$ of the computer technology changes over dates ${t}.$ At each date the firm chooses a technology and a skill level ${s\in S}$ together, earning ${G(s)-c(s)-k(t)}$ with computers and ${H(s)-c(s)}$ with the old technology, and ${\sigma(t)}$ is the largest skill level in an optimal choice. The cost path is admissible if it is continuous and non-increasing, exceeds any given level at some date, and is ${0}$ from some date on. On our first reading of “smoothly”: it is not true that, for all pairs with increasing differences, every cost of skill ${c},$ every set ${S}$ and every admissible cost path ${k},$ the selected skill ${\sigma}$ is continuous in ${t}.$

statements.title: Selected skill can jump even in typical cases
statements.statement:
Let ${G}$ and ${H}$ be the production functions of the computer and the old-fashioned technology, and ${c}$ the total cost of skill, all functions of the skill level ${s}.$ The pair has *increasing differences in skill* if, whenever ${s\le s'},$
$$H(s')-H(s)\le G(s')-G(s),$$
that is, if ${G-H}$ is non-decreasing.
The cost ${k(t)}$ of the computer technology changes over dates ${t}.$ At each date the firm chooses a technology and a skill level ${s\in S}$ together, earning ${G(s)-c(s)-k(t)}$ with computers and ${H(s)-c(s)}$ with the old technology, and ${\sigma(t)}$ is the largest skill level in an optimal choice. The cost path is admissible if it is continuous and non-increasing, exceeds any given level at some date, and is ${0}$ from some date on. On our second reading, “smoothly in the typical case”: it is not true that, for every set ${S}$ of skill levels, there is a dense open set of data ${(G,H,c,k)}$ meeting the conditions above, in the topology of pointwise convergence, at every point of which ${\sigma}$ is continuous in ${t}.$

statements.title: Cobb–Douglas utility has a demand function
statements.statement: Let ${0\le\alpha\le1}$ and ${U(x_A,x_B)=x_A^\alpha x_B^{1-\alpha}}$ on ${\mathbb{R}^2_+}.$ There are demand functions ${x(p_A,p_B,M)}$ such that, at all ${p_A,p_B,M>0},$ the bundle ${x(p_A,p_B,M)}$ is affordable, ${p_Ax_A+p_Bx_B\le M},$ and maximizes ${U}$ over the budget set.

assumptions.text: the exponent is nonnegative: ${0\le\alpha}.$
the exponent is at most one: ${\alpha\le1}.$

statements.title: Slutsky symmetry for the linear demand system
statements.statement:
For all ${p_A,p_B,M>0}$ the consumer demands
$$\begin{aligned}x_A&=a_1\frac{M}{p_A}+a_2\frac{M}{p_B},\\[4pt] x_B&=b_1\frac{M}{p_A}+b_2\frac{M}{p_B}.\end{aligned}$$
The demands are *Slutsky symmetric* if at all ${p_A,p_B,M>0}$ the two cross substitution terms agree:
$$\frac{\partial x_A}{\partial p_B}+x_B\,\frac{\partial x_A}{\partial M}=\frac{\partial x_B}{\partial p_A}+x_A\,\frac{\partial x_B}{\partial M}.$$
For these demands, Slutsky symmetry holds exactly when $\partial x_A/\partial p_B=\partial x_B/\partial p_A$ at all positive prices and income.

statements.title: Slutsky symmetry holds exactly when a₂ = b₁ = 0
statements.statement:
For all ${p_A,p_B,M>0}$ the consumer demands
$$\begin{aligned}x_A&=a_1\frac{M}{p_A}+a_2\frac{M}{p_B},\\[4pt] x_B&=b_1\frac{M}{p_A}+b_2\frac{M}{p_B}.\end{aligned}$$
These demands are Slutsky symmetric, in the sense of the reading above, if and only if
$$a_2=0\quad\text{and}\quad b_1=0.$$

statements.title: A preference gives rise to the demands: best-element reading
statements.statement:
For all ${p_A,p_B,M>0}$ the consumer demands
$$\begin{aligned}x_A&=a_1\frac{M}{p_A}+a_2\frac{M}{p_B},\\[4pt] x_B&=b_1\frac{M}{p_A}+b_2\frac{M}{p_B}.\end{aligned}$$
A bundle is a *best element* of a budget set under a complete and transitive preference ${\succsim}$ if it is affordable and no affordable bundle is strictly better. On our first reading, a complete and transitive preference ${\succsim}$ *gives rise to* these demands if at all ${p_A,p_B,M>0}$ the observed bundle ${(x_A,x_B)}$ is a best element of the budget set.

statements.title: A preference gives rise to the demands: unique-best reading
statements.statement:
For all ${p_A,p_B,M>0}$ the consumer demands
$$\begin{aligned}x_A&=a_1\frac{M}{p_A}+a_2\frac{M}{p_B},\\[4pt] x_B&=b_1\frac{M}{p_A}+b_2\frac{M}{p_B}.\end{aligned}$$
A bundle is a *best element* of a budget set under a complete and transitive preference ${\succsim}$ if it is affordable and no affordable bundle is strictly better. On our second reading, a complete and transitive preference ${\succsim}$ *gives rise to* these demands if at all ${p_A,p_B,M>0}$ the observed bundle ${(x_A,x_B)}$ is the unique best element of the budget set.

statements.title: Best-element reading: a₂ = b₁ = 0, a₁, b₂ ≥ 0, a₁ + b₂ ≤ 1
statements.statement:
For all ${p_A,p_B,M>0}$ the consumer demands
$$\begin{aligned}x_A&=a_1\frac{M}{p_A}+a_2\frac{M}{p_B},\\[4pt] x_B&=b_1\frac{M}{p_A}+b_2\frac{M}{p_B}.\end{aligned}$$
Under the first reading, some complete and transitive preference gives rise to these demands if and only if ${a_2=b_1=0},$ ${a_1\ge0},$ ${b_2\ge0}$ and
$$a_1+b_2\le1.$$

statements.title: Unique-best reading: a₂ = b₁ = 0, and a₁ + b₂ = 1 or a₁ = b₂ = 0
statements.statement:
For all ${p_A,p_B,M>0}$ the consumer demands
$$\begin{aligned}x_A&=a_1\frac{M}{p_A}+a_2\frac{M}{p_B},\\[4pt] x_B&=b_1\frac{M}{p_A}+b_2\frac{M}{p_B}.\end{aligned}$$
Under the second reading, some complete and transitive preference gives rise to these demands if and only if ${a_2=0},$ ${b_1=0},$ ${a_1\ge0},$ ${b_2\ge0},$ and
$$a_1+b_2=1\qquad\text{or}\qquad a_1=b_2=0.$$

statements.title: Does this utility index imply risk aversion?
statements.statement: Let ${u(x)=\sqrt{x}}$ for ${x\le100}$ and ${u(x)=10+\sqrt{x-100}}$ for ${x>100},$ and consider preferences over lotteries with nonnegative prizes represented by the expected value of ${u}.$ The question asks whether every such preference is risk averse: whether, for every lottery ${p},$ receiving its mean for sure is at least as good as ${p}.$

statements.title: This utility index does not imply risk aversion
statements.statement: Let ${u(x)=\sqrt{x}}$ for ${x\le100}$ and ${u(x)=10+\sqrt{x-100}}$ for ${x>100},$ and consider preferences over lotteries with nonnegative prizes represented by the expected value of ${u}.$ Not every such preference is risk averse. Moreover, a single lottery ${p}$ works against all of them: none ranks the sure prize equal to the mean of ${p}$ at least as high as ${p}.$

statements.title: Can an expected-utility order rank L₁ ≻ L₂ ≻ L₃?
statements.statement:
Let
$$\begin{aligned}L_1&=\big(200,\tfrac1{18};\,100,\tfrac19;\,40,\tfrac29;\,0,\tfrac{11}{18}\big),\\ L_2&=\big(100,\tfrac13;\,40,\tfrac23\big),\\ L_3&=\big(200,\tfrac1{12};\,0,\tfrac{11}{12}\big).\end{aligned}$$
An *expected-utility order*, on our reading, is a preference over lotteries on the prizes ${0,40,100,200}$ represented by the expected value of some function ${v}$ of the prize.
The question asks whether some expected-utility order ranks ${L_1\succ L_2\succ L_3}.$

statements.title: No expected-utility order ranks L₁ ≻ L₂ ≻ L₃
statements.statement:
Let
$$\begin{aligned}L_1&=\big(200,\tfrac1{18};\,100,\tfrac19;\,40,\tfrac29;\,0,\tfrac{11}{18}\big),\\ L_2&=\big(100,\tfrac13;\,40,\tfrac23\big),\\ L_3&=\big(200,\tfrac1{12};\,0,\tfrac{11}{12}\big).\end{aligned}$$
An *expected-utility order*, on our reading, is a preference over lotteries on the prizes ${0,40,100,200}$ represented by the expected value of some function ${v}$ of the prize.
No expected-utility order ranks ${L_1\succ L_2\succ L_3}.$

entries.title: Pricing a call option by no arbitrage

statements.title: The stock-and-bond market is arbitrage-free
statements.statement: There are two states, ${s=1,2}.$ A stock with price ${1}$ pays ${R_s}$ in state ${s};$ a bond with price ${B\ge0}$ pays ${r>0}$ in each state; and ${R_1>rB>R_2>0}.$ A portfolio holds some amount of each security, and it is an *arbitrage* if it costs at most ${0},$ pays at least ${0}$ in each state, and either costs strictly less than ${0}$ or pays strictly more than ${0}$ in some state. As printed: this security market is arbitrage-free.

assumptions.text: The bond has price ${B\ge0}$ and pays ${r>0}.$

statements.title: With R₂B < r < R₁B, the market is arbitrage-free
statements.statement: There are two states, ${s=1,2}.$ A stock with price ${1}$ pays ${R_s}$ in state ${s};$ a bond with price ${B\ge0}$ pays ${r>0}$ in each state; and ${R_1>rB>R_2>0}.$ A portfolio holds some amount of each security, and it is an *arbitrage* if it costs at most ${0},$ pays at least ${0}$ in each state, and either costs strictly less than ${0}$ or pays strictly more than ${0}$ in some state. If also ${R_2B<r<R_1B},$ then no portfolio, short positions included, is an arbitrage.

assumptions.text: The bond has price ${B\ge0}$ and pays ${r>0}.$

statements.title: Without short sales, the market is arbitrage-free
statements.statement: There are two states, ${s=1,2}.$ A stock with price ${1}$ pays ${R_s}$ in state ${s};$ a bond with price ${B\ge0}$ pays ${r>0}$ in each state; and ${R_1>rB>R_2>0}.$ A portfolio holds some amount of each security, and it is an *arbitrage* if it costs at most ${0},$ pays at least ${0}$ in each state, and either costs strictly less than ${0}$ or pays strictly more than ${0}$ in some state. If only portfolios with nonnegative holdings are allowed, none of them is an arbitrage.

assumptions.text: The bond has price ${B\ge0}$ and pays ${r>0}.$
only portfolios with nonnegative holdings are considered: no short sales.

statements.title: With short sales, the option has a single arbitrage-free price
statements.statement:
There are two states, ${s=1,2}.$ A stock with price ${1}$ pays ${R_s}$ in state ${s};$ a bond with price ${B\ge0}$ pays ${r>0}$ in each state; and ${R_1>rB>R_2>0}.$ A portfolio holds some amount of each security, and it is an *arbitrage* if it costs at most ${0},$ pays at least ${0}$ in each state, and either costs strictly less than ${0}$ or pays strictly more than ${0}$ in some state. A call option with strike ${c},$ ${0<c<R_1},$ pays ${\max\{0,R_s-c\}}$ in state ${s}$ and trades at price ${q}.$ Allowing all portfolios, the market of all three securities admits no arbitrage if and only if ${R_2B<r<R_1B}$ and
$$\begin{aligned}q&=\pi_1\max\{0,R_1-c\}\\&\quad+\pi_2\max\{0,R_2-c\},\end{aligned}$$
where ${\pi_1=(r-R_2B)/(r(R_1-R_2))}$ and ${\pi_2=(R_1B-r)/(r(R_1-R_2))}.$

assumptions.text: The bond has price ${B\ge0}$ and pays ${r>0}.$
The strike satisfies ${0<c<R_1}.$

statements.title: Without short sales, any positive option price is arbitrage-free
statements.statement: There are two states, ${s=1,2}.$ A stock with price ${1}$ pays ${R_s}$ in state ${s};$ a bond with price ${B\ge0}$ pays ${r>0}$ in each state; and ${R_1>rB>R_2>0}.$ A portfolio holds some amount of each security, and it is an *arbitrage* if it costs at most ${0},$ pays at least ${0}$ in each state, and either costs strictly less than ${0}$ or pays strictly more than ${0}$ in some state. A call option with strike ${c},$ ${0<c<R_1},$ pays ${\max\{0,R_s-c\}}$ in state ${s}$ and trades at price ${q}.$ If only portfolios with nonnegative holdings are allowed, the market of all three securities admits no arbitrage if and only if ${q>0}.$

assumptions.text: The bond has price ${B\ge0}$ and pays ${r>0}.$
The strike satisfies ${0<c<R_1}.$
only portfolios with nonnegative holdings are considered: no short sales.

statements.title: Do the arbitrage-free option prices depend on the probabilities?
statements.statement: There are two states, ${s=1,2}.$ A stock with price ${1}$ pays ${R_s}$ in state ${s};$ a bond with price ${B\ge0}$ pays ${r>0}$ in each state; and ${R_1>rB>R_2>0}.$ A portfolio holds some amount of each security, and it is an *arbitrage* if it costs at most ${0},$ pays at least ${0}$ in each state, and either costs strictly less than ${0}$ or pays strictly more than ${0}$ in some state. A call option with strike ${c},$ ${0<c<R_1},$ pays ${\max\{0,R_s-c\}}$ in state ${s}$ and trades at price ${q}.$ For a set of allowed portfolios, consider the option prices ${q}$ at which no allowed portfolio of the three securities is an arbitrage, as a function of the probabilities of the two states. On our reading, the answer *depends on the probabilities* if, for some market data meeting all the printed conditions, two probability assignments give different sets of such prices.

statements.title: The arbitrage-free option prices do not depend on the probabilities
statements.statement: There are two states, ${s=1,2}.$ A stock with price ${1}$ pays ${R_s}$ in state ${s};$ a bond with price ${B\ge0}$ pays ${r>0}$ in each state; and ${R_1>rB>R_2>0}.$ A portfolio holds some amount of each security, and it is an *arbitrage* if it costs at most ${0},$ pays at least ${0}$ in each state, and either costs strictly less than ${0}$ or pays strictly more than ${0}$ in some state. A call option with strike ${c},$ ${0<c<R_1},$ pays ${\max\{0,R_s-c\}}$ in state ${s}$ and trades at price ${q}.$ For a set of allowed portfolios, consider the option prices ${q}$ at which no allowed portfolio of the three securities is an arbitrage, as a function of the probabilities of the two states. On our reading, the answer *depends on the probabilities* if, for some market data meeting all the printed conditions, two probability assignments give different sets of such prices. Then, for every set of allowed portfolios, the answer does not depend on the probabilities.

Here all portfolios are allowed, short positions included.
