entries.title: Equilibria of a three-player game tree

statements.title: The game in normal form
statements.statement:
Player 1 chooses ${a},$ ${b}$ or ${c}.$ A strategy of player 2 is a pair ${(x,y)}$: an action ${x\in\{d,e\}}$ after ${b}$ and an action ${y\in\{g,f\}}$ after ${c}.$ Player 3 chooses ${h}$ or ${i}$ at a single information set containing the nodes after ${bd},$ ${be}$ and ${cf}.$ Each strategy profile reaches one terminal history, and its payoffs to players 1, 2 and 3 are those of that history:

- ${a}$: ${(1,0,0)};$
- ${b,d,h}$: ${(3,0,2)},$ and ${b,d,i}$: ${(0,2,1)};$
- ${b,e,h}$: ${(0,1,1)},$ and ${b,e,i}$: ${(4,1,2)};$
- ${c,g}$: ${(2,2,0)};$
- ${c,f,h}$: ${(1,1,1)},$ and ${c,f,i}$: ${(0,3,2)}.$

statements.title: Pure-strategy Nash equilibrium of the game
statements.statement: Player 1 chooses ${a},$ ${b}$ or ${c}.$ A strategy of player 2 is a pair ${(x,y)}$: an action ${x\in\{d,e\}}$ after ${b}$ and an action ${y\in\{g,f\}}$ after ${c}.$ Player 3 chooses ${h}$ or ${i}$ at a single information set containing the nodes after ${bd},$ ${be}$ and ${cf}.$ On our reading, a pure-strategy profile is a *Nash equilibrium* if no player can raise his own payoff by changing his own strategy alone, the others’ strategies held fixed.

statements.title: The three pure-strategy Nash equilibria
statements.statement:
Player 1 chooses ${a},$ ${b}$ or ${c}.$ A strategy of player 2 is a pair ${(x,y)}$: an action ${x\in\{d,e\}}$ after ${b}$ and an action ${y\in\{g,f\}}$ after ${c}.$ Player 3 chooses ${h}$ or ${i}$ at a single information set containing the nodes after ${bd},$ ${be}$ and ${cf}.$ A pure-strategy profile is a Nash equilibrium if and only if it is one of
$$\begin{gathered}(a,(d,f),i),\qquad (a,(e,f),h),\\ (c,(e,g),h).\end{gathered}$$

statements.title: Belief systems on the game tree
statements.statement: Player 1 chooses ${a},$ ${b}$ or ${c}.$ A strategy of player 2 is a pair ${(x,y)}$: an action ${x\in\{d,e\}}$ after ${b}$ and an action ${y\in\{g,f\}}$ after ${c}.$ Player 3 chooses ${h}$ or ${i}$ at a single information set containing the nodes after ${bd},$ ${be}$ and ${cf}.$ The tree has six decision nodes: the root, the nodes after ${b}$ and after ${c},$ and player 3’s nodes after ${bd},$ ${be}$ and ${cf}.$ They form four information sets: three singletons and player 3’s set of three nodes. A *belief system* gives each node a nonnegative weight, summing to one over each information set.

statements.title: Which Nash equilibria are weak perfect Bayesian equilibria?
statements.statement: Player 1 chooses ${a},$ ${b}$ or ${c}.$ A strategy of player 2 is a pair ${(x,y)}$: an action ${x\in\{d,e\}}$ after ${b}$ and an action ${y\in\{g,f\}}$ after ${c}.$ Player 3 chooses ${h}$ or ${i}$ at a single information set containing the nodes after ${bd},$ ${be}$ and ${cf}.$ The tree has six decision nodes: the root, the nodes after ${b}$ and after ${c},$ and player 3’s nodes after ${bd},$ ${be}$ and ${cf}.$ They form four information sets: three singletons and player 3’s set of three nodes. A *belief system* gives each node a nonnegative weight, summing to one over each information set. On our reading, a profile is *supported as a weak perfect Bayesian equilibrium* if some belief system makes it one: beliefs follow Bayes’ rule on the equilibrium path, and at each information set the player who moves there maximizes his expected continuation payoff given the beliefs.

statements.title: Two of the three equilibria are weak perfect Bayesian
statements.statement: Player 1 chooses ${a},$ ${b}$ or ${c}.$ A strategy of player 2 is a pair ${(x,y)}$: an action ${x\in\{d,e\}}$ after ${b}$ and an action ${y\in\{g,f\}}$ after ${c}.$ Player 3 chooses ${h}$ or ${i}$ at a single information set containing the nodes after ${bd},$ ${be}$ and ${cf}.$ The tree has six decision nodes: the root, the nodes after ${b}$ and after ${c},$ and player 3’s nodes after ${bd},$ ${be}$ and ${cf}.$ They form four information sets: three singletons and player 3’s set of three nodes. A *belief system* gives each node a nonnegative weight, summing to one over each information set. The profiles ${(a,(d,f),i)}$ and ${(c,(e,g),h)}$ are supported as weak perfect Bayesian equilibria, and ${(a,(e,f),h)}$ is not.

statements.title: Sequential equilibrium of the game
statements.statement: Player 1 chooses ${a},$ ${b}$ or ${c}.$ A strategy of player 2 is a pair ${(x,y)}$: an action ${x\in\{d,e\}}$ after ${b}$ and an action ${y\in\{g,f\}}$ after ${c}.$ Player 3 chooses ${h}$ or ${i}$ at a single information set containing the nodes after ${bd},$ ${be}$ and ${cf}.$ The tree has six decision nodes: the root, the nodes after ${b}$ and after ${c},$ and player 3’s nodes after ${bd},$ ${be}$ and ${cf}.$ They form four information sets: three singletons and player 3’s set of three nodes. A *belief system* gives each node a nonnegative weight, summing to one over each information set. On our reading, a profile and a belief system form a *sequential equilibrium* if the beliefs are the limit of those that Bayes’ rule derives from a sequence of completely mixed behavior profiles converging to the profile, and at each of the four information sets the player who moves there maximizes his expected continuation payoff.

statements.title: A Nash equilibrium that is a sequential equilibrium
statements.statement: Player 1 chooses ${a},$ ${b}$ or ${c}.$ A strategy of player 2 is a pair ${(x,y)}$: an action ${x\in\{d,e\}}$ after ${b}$ and an action ${y\in\{g,f\}}$ after ${c}.$ Player 3 chooses ${h}$ or ${i}$ at a single information set containing the nodes after ${bd},$ ${be}$ and ${cf}.$ The tree has six decision nodes: the root, the nodes after ${b}$ and after ${c},$ and player 3’s nodes after ${bd},$ ${be}$ and ${cf}.$ They form four information sets: three singletons and player 3’s set of three nodes. A *belief system* gives each node a nonnegative weight, summing to one over each information set. Some pure-strategy Nash equilibrium, together with some belief system, is a sequential equilibrium.

entries.title: A sales tournament as an incentive contract

statements.title: First-best contracts under observable effort
statements.statement: Agents ${r}$ and ${e}$ achieve sales ${x_i=a_i+\varepsilon_i},$ where ${a_i}$ is effort and the noise terms are independent with a common density ${g}.$ Agent ${r}$’s payoff is ${w_r-a_r^2/2}$ and agent ${e}$’s is ${w_e-\beta a_e^2/2},$ with ${0<\beta<1},$ where ${w_i}$ is the wage; both have the outside option ${\bar U}.$ The company’s payoff is ${x_r+x_e-w_r-w_e}.$ A pair of contracts, efforts ${(a_r,a_e)}$ with wages ${(w_r,w_e)},$ is *first-best under observable effort* if it gives each agent at least ${\bar U}$ and no other pair doing so gives the company a higher payoff. On our reading, the comparison is made at every realization of the noise.

statements.title: First-best contracts exist
statements.statement: Agents ${r}$ and ${e}$ achieve sales ${x_i=a_i+\varepsilon_i},$ where ${a_i}$ is effort and the noise terms are independent with a common density ${g}.$ Agent ${r}$’s payoff is ${w_r-a_r^2/2}$ and agent ${e}$’s is ${w_e-\beta a_e^2/2},$ with ${0<\beta<1},$ where ${w_i}$ is the wage; both have the outside option ${\bar U}.$ The company’s payoff is ${x_r+x_e-w_r-w_e}.$ A pair of contracts, efforts ${(a_r,a_e)}$ with wages ${(w_r,w_e)},$ is *first-best under observable effort* if it gives each agent at least ${\bar U}$ and no other pair doing so gives the company a higher payoff. For every ${0<\beta<1}$ and every ${\bar U},$ a first-best pair of contracts exists.

statements.title: Expected payoffs in the tournament
statements.statement:
Agents ${r}$ and ${e}$ achieve sales ${x_i=a_i+\varepsilon_i},$ where ${a_i}$ is effort and the noise terms are independent with a common density ${g}.$ Agent ${r}$’s payoff is ${w_r-a_r^2/2}$ and agent ${e}$’s is ${w_e-\beta a_e^2/2},$ with ${0<\beta<1},$ where ${w_i}$ is the wage; both have the outside option ${\bar U}.$ The company’s payoff is ${x_r+x_e-w_r-w_e}.$ In the tournament, agent ${i}$ receives the salary ${L_i},$ plus the bonus ${B}$ if his sales are strictly higher than his rival’s. With ${P_r}$ and ${P_e}$ the probabilities that ${r},$ respectively ${e},$ has the strictly higher sales, the expected payoffs are
$$\begin{aligned}U_r&=L_r+B\,P_r(a_r,a_e)-\tfrac12a_r^2,\\ U_e&=L_e+B\,P_e(a_r,a_e)-\tfrac12\beta a_e^2.\end{aligned}$$

statements.title: The expressions are the agents’ expected payoffs
statements.statement:
Agents ${r}$ and ${e}$ achieve sales ${x_i=a_i+\varepsilon_i},$ where ${a_i}$ is effort and the noise terms are independent with a common density ${g}.$ Agent ${r}$’s payoff is ${w_r-a_r^2/2}$ and agent ${e}$’s is ${w_e-\beta a_e^2/2},$ with ${0<\beta<1},$ where ${w_i}$ is the wage; both have the outside option ${\bar U}.$ The company’s payoff is ${x_r+x_e-w_r-w_e}.$ In the tournament, agent ${i}$ receives the salary ${L_i},$ plus the bonus ${B}$ if his sales are strictly higher than his rival’s. With ${P_r}$ and ${P_e}$ the probabilities that ${r},$ respectively ${e},$ has the strictly higher sales, the expected payoffs are
$$\begin{aligned}U_r&=L_r+B\,P_r(a_r,a_e)-\tfrac12a_r^2,\\ U_e&=L_e+B\,P_e(a_r,a_e)-\tfrac12\beta a_e^2.\end{aligned}$$
If ${g}$ is a density, each of ${U_r}$ and ${U_e}$ equals the expectation, over the noise, of the agent’s payoff at the wage the tournament pays him.

assumptions.text: ${g}$ is a density: ${g\ge0}.$
${g}$ integrates to one.

statements.title: A bonus meets the first-order conditions at first-best
statements.statement:
Agents ${r}$ and ${e}$ achieve sales ${x_i=a_i+\varepsilon_i},$ where ${a_i}$ is effort and the noise terms are independent with a common density ${g}.$ Agent ${r}$’s payoff is ${w_r-a_r^2/2}$ and agent ${e}$’s is ${w_e-\beta a_e^2/2},$ with ${0<\beta<1},$ where ${w_i}$ is the wage; both have the outside option ${\bar U}.$ The company’s payoff is ${x_r+x_e-w_r-w_e}.$ In the tournament, agent ${i}$ receives the salary ${L_i},$ plus the bonus ${B}$ if his sales are strictly higher than his rival’s. With ${P_r}$ and ${P_e}$ the probabilities that ${r},$ respectively ${e},$ has the strictly higher sales, the expected payoffs are
$$\begin{aligned}U_r&=L_r+B\,P_r(a_r,a_e)-\tfrac12a_r^2,\\ U_e&=L_e+B\,P_e(a_r,a_e)-\tfrac12\beta a_e^2.\end{aligned}$$ A pair of contracts, efforts ${(a_r,a_e)}$ with wages ${(w_r,w_e)},$ is *first-best under observable effort* if it gives each agent at least ${\bar U}$ and no other pair doing so gives the company a higher payoff.
As printed: ignoring participation constraints, there is a bonus ${B}$ that satisfies necessary first-order conditions for the first-best effort pair to be a Nash equilibrium of the tournament.

assumptions.text: The setup of the question, with the tournament of part (b).
Participation constraints are ignored.

statements.title: A bonus meets the first-order conditions at the first-best efforts
statements.statement:
Agents ${r}$ and ${e}$ achieve sales ${x_i=a_i+\varepsilon_i},$ where ${a_i}$ is effort and the noise terms are independent with a common density ${g}.$ Agent ${r}$’s payoff is ${w_r-a_r^2/2}$ and agent ${e}$’s is ${w_e-\beta a_e^2/2},$ with ${0<\beta<1},$ where ${w_i}$ is the wage; both have the outside option ${\bar U}.$ The company’s payoff is ${x_r+x_e-w_r-w_e}.$ In the tournament, agent ${i}$ receives the salary ${L_i},$ plus the bonus ${B}$ if his sales are strictly higher than his rival’s. With ${P_r}$ and ${P_e}$ the probabilities that ${r},$ respectively ${e},$ has the strictly higher sales, the expected payoffs are
$$\begin{aligned}U_r&=L_r+B\,P_r(a_r,a_e)-\tfrac12a_r^2,\\ U_e&=L_e+B\,P_e(a_r,a_e)-\tfrac12\beta a_e^2.\end{aligned}$$ A pair of contracts, efforts ${(a_r,a_e)}$ with wages ${(w_r,w_e)},$ is *first-best under observable effort* if it gives each agent at least ${\bar U}$ and no other pair doing so gives the company a higher payoff. The *first-order conditions* at an effort pair hold if each agent’s expected payoff is stationary in his own effort there: ${\partial U_r/\partial a_r=0}$ and ${\partial U_e/\partial a_e=0}.$
Let ${(a_r,a_e)}$ be the efforts of a first-best pair of contracts. If ${P_r(\cdot,a_e)}$ has a derivative ${m\neq0}$ at ${a_r},$ then for any salaries there is a bonus ${B}$ at which the first-order conditions hold at ${(a_r,a_e)}.$

assumptions.text: ${g}$ is a density: ${g\ge0}.$
${g}$ integrates to one.
The contracts ${(a_r,w_r)},$ ${(a_e,w_e)}$ are first-best under observable effort.
agent ${r}$’s winning probability is differentiable in his own effort at the first-best efforts, with derivative ${m}.$

statements.title: Can the tournament achieve first-best profit?
statements.statement:
Agents ${r}$ and ${e}$ achieve sales ${x_i=a_i+\varepsilon_i},$ where ${a_i}$ is effort and the noise terms are independent with a common density ${g}.$ Agent ${r}$’s payoff is ${w_r-a_r^2/2}$ and agent ${e}$’s is ${w_e-\beta a_e^2/2},$ with ${0<\beta<1},$ where ${w_i}$ is the wage; both have the outside option ${\bar U}.$ The company’s payoff is ${x_r+x_e-w_r-w_e}.$ In the tournament, agent ${i}$ receives the salary ${L_i},$ plus the bonus ${B}$ if his sales are strictly higher than his rival’s. With ${P_r}$ and ${P_e}$ the probabilities that ${r},$ respectively ${e},$ has the strictly higher sales, the expected payoffs are
$$\begin{aligned}U_r&=L_r+B\,P_r(a_r,a_e)-\tfrac12a_r^2,\\ U_e&=L_e+B\,P_e(a_r,a_e)-\tfrac12\beta a_e^2.\end{aligned}$$ A pair of contracts, efforts ${(a_r,a_e)}$ with wages ${(w_r,w_e)},$ is *first-best under observable effort* if it gives each agent at least ${\bar U}$ and no other pair doing so gives the company a higher payoff. The *first-order conditions* at an effort pair hold if each agent’s expected payoff is stationary in his own effort there: ${\partial U_r/\partial a_r=0}$ and ${\partial U_e/\partial a_e=0}.$ The tournament *achieves first-best profit* if each agent’s expected payoff is at least ${\bar U}$ and the company’s expected payoff equals its expected payoff under the first-best contracts.
The question asks, on our reading of achieving first-best profit, whether for every noise density, every ${0<\beta<1},$ every ${\bar U}$ and every first-best pair of contracts there are salaries, a bonus and efforts at which the first-order conditions hold and the tournament achieves first-best profit.

statements.title: First-best profit is not always achievable
statements.statement:
Agents ${r}$ and ${e}$ achieve sales ${x_i=a_i+\varepsilon_i},$ where ${a_i}$ is effort and the noise terms are independent with a common density ${g}.$ Agent ${r}$’s payoff is ${w_r-a_r^2/2}$ and agent ${e}$’s is ${w_e-\beta a_e^2/2},$ with ${0<\beta<1},$ where ${w_i}$ is the wage; both have the outside option ${\bar U}.$ The company’s payoff is ${x_r+x_e-w_r-w_e}.$ In the tournament, agent ${i}$ receives the salary ${L_i},$ plus the bonus ${B}$ if his sales are strictly higher than his rival’s. With ${P_r}$ and ${P_e}$ the probabilities that ${r},$ respectively ${e},$ has the strictly higher sales, the expected payoffs are
$$\begin{aligned}U_r&=L_r+B\,P_r(a_r,a_e)-\tfrac12a_r^2,\\ U_e&=L_e+B\,P_e(a_r,a_e)-\tfrac12\beta a_e^2.\end{aligned}$$ A pair of contracts, efforts ${(a_r,a_e)}$ with wages ${(w_r,w_e)},$ is *first-best under observable effort* if it gives each agent at least ${\bar U}$ and no other pair doing so gives the company a higher payoff. The *first-order conditions* at an effort pair hold if each agent’s expected payoff is stationary in his own effort there: ${\partial U_r/\partial a_r=0}$ and ${\partial U_e/\partial a_e=0}.$ The tournament *achieves first-best profit* if each agent’s expected payoff is at least ${\bar U}$ and the company’s expected payoff equals its expected payoff under the first-best contracts.
It is not the case that for every noise density, every ${0<\beta<1},$ every ${\bar U}$ and every first-best pair of contracts there are salaries, a bonus and efforts at which the first-order conditions hold and the tournament achieves first-best profit.

statements.title: With a responsive winning chance, the tournament attains first-best
statements.statement:
Agents ${r}$ and ${e}$ achieve sales ${x_i=a_i+\varepsilon_i},$ where ${a_i}$ is effort and the noise terms are independent with a common density ${g}.$ Agent ${r}$’s payoff is ${w_r-a_r^2/2}$ and agent ${e}$’s is ${w_e-\beta a_e^2/2},$ with ${0<\beta<1},$ where ${w_i}$ is the wage; both have the outside option ${\bar U}.$ The company’s payoff is ${x_r+x_e-w_r-w_e}.$ In the tournament, agent ${i}$ receives the salary ${L_i},$ plus the bonus ${B}$ if his sales are strictly higher than his rival’s. With ${P_r}$ and ${P_e}$ the probabilities that ${r},$ respectively ${e},$ has the strictly higher sales, the expected payoffs are
$$\begin{aligned}U_r&=L_r+B\,P_r(a_r,a_e)-\tfrac12a_r^2,\\ U_e&=L_e+B\,P_e(a_r,a_e)-\tfrac12\beta a_e^2.\end{aligned}$$ A pair of contracts, efforts ${(a_r,a_e)}$ with wages ${(w_r,w_e)},$ is *first-best under observable effort* if it gives each agent at least ${\bar U}$ and no other pair doing so gives the company a higher payoff. The *first-order conditions* at an effort pair hold if each agent’s expected payoff is stationary in his own effort there: ${\partial U_r/\partial a_r=0}$ and ${\partial U_e/\partial a_e=0}.$ The tournament *achieves first-best profit* if each agent’s expected payoff is at least ${\bar U}$ and the company’s expected payoff equals its expected payoff under the first-best contracts.
Let ${(a_r,a_e)}$ be the efforts of a first-best pair of contracts. If ${P_r(\cdot,a_e)}$ has a derivative ${m\neq0}$ at ${a_r},$ there are salaries ${L_r,L_e}$ and a bonus ${B}$ at which the first-order conditions hold at ${(a_r,a_e)}$ and the tournament achieves first-best profit.

assumptions.text: ${g}$ is a density: ${g\ge0}.$
${g}$ integrates to one.
The contracts ${(a_r,w_r)},$ ${(a_e,w_e)}$ are first-best under observable effort.
agent ${r}$’s winning probability is differentiable in his own effort at the first-best efforts, with derivative ${m}.$

statements.title: Λ-convex preferences
statements.statement:
Let ${X}$ be a set and ${\Lambda}$ a set of primitive orderings on ${X}.$ A preference relation ${\succsim}$ on ${X},$ complete and transitive, is *${\Lambda}$-convex* if for all ${a,b\in X}$: whenever every ordering ${\ge_\lambda}$ in ${\Lambda}$ admits some ${y_\lambda}$ with
$$b\ge_\lambda y_\lambda\qquad\text{and}\qquad y_\lambda\succsim a,$$
then ${b\succsim a}.$

statements.title: Convexity equals Ψ-convexity for continuous preferences
statements.statement: Let ${X}$ be a convex and closed subset of ${\mathbb{R}^N}.$ Each nonzero vector ${v}$ defines the *algebraic linear ordering* ${x\ge_v y}$ if ${v\cdot x\ge v\cdot y};$ let ${\Psi}$ be the set of all of them. A preference ${\succsim}$ on ${X}$ is *convex* in the standard sense if ${a\succsim b}$ implies ${\alpha a+(1-\alpha)b\succsim b}$ for every ${\alpha\in[0,1]}.$ Then, for a continuous preference ${\succsim}$ on ${X},$ standard convexity is equivalent to ${\Psi}$-convexity in the sense of Definition 1.

assumptions.text: ${X}$ is convex.
${X}$ is closed.
${\succsim}$ is continuous.

statements.conclusion: ${\succsim}$ is convex if and only if it is ${\Psi}$-convex.

statements.title: The textbook’s Λ-convexity implies the paper’s, not conversely
statements.statement:
Let ${X}$ be a set, ${\succsim}$ a preference relation on ${X}$ and ${\Lambda}$ a set of orderings on ${X};$ for ${\trianglerighteq\in\Lambda}$ write ${\triangleright}$ for its strict part. The textbook (Lecture 4) calls ${\succsim}$ *${\Lambda}$-convex* if for every ${y\in X}$ some ${\trianglerighteq\in\Lambda},$ a critical ordering at ${y},$ satisfies
$$\{x: x\succ y\}\subseteq\{x: x\triangleright y\}.$$
The paper’s notion is that of Definition 1. Then:

- (b) a preference that is ${\Lambda}$-convex in the textbook’s sense is ${\Lambda}$-convex in the paper’s sense;
- (a) the converse fails: for some ${X},$ ${\succsim}$ and ${\Lambda},$ the preference is ${\Lambda}$-convex in the paper’s sense but not in the textbook’s.

assumptions.text: For direction (b): ${\succsim}$ is ${\Lambda}$-convex in the textbook’s sense.

statements.conclusion: The textbook’s ${\Lambda}$-convexity implies the paper’s, and the converse implication does not hold in general.
